In a Smart City environment with numerous agencies and interacting agencies, protecting public places from terrorist attacks requires an intricate and interconnecting smart public safety system. This system's effectiveness relies on the city's agencies' outcome-driven actions in response to attacks, taking into account the impact of interconnections, shared resources, and interdependencies among agencies. This paper explores the concept of Smart City public safety as a multi-objective game, taking into account the interactions and interdependencies among city agencies and infrastructure. To address this complexity, the researchers combine two strategies: establishing a framework for modeling and analyzing the situation, and developing a multi-objective learning automata-based approach to identify and recommend optimal solutions for improving public safety outcomes. The proposed framework, which models Smart City public safety as a complex situation with multiple objectives, also accounts for uncertainty and dynamic changes in the environment. By using multi-objective learning automata to analyze the situation from different perspectives, the researchers can recommend effective actions for achieving various objectives, such as reducing the impact of terrorist attacks on cities. This approach can serve as a valuable tool for city planners and officials to compare different scenarios, make data-driven decisions, and minimize the consequences of terrorist attacks on people and assets while maximizing public safety outcomes. The researchers validated the framework through a case study involving five Smart City public safety objectives and demonstrated its effectiveness with real-world data on agency actions and interconnections. The findings show that Smart City public safety is a complex issue with multiple objectives, and achieving these objectives involves trade-offs and consequences for resource allocation, people, and assets. This implies that Smart City planners and officials must prioritize objectives, adapt to new situations, and make informed decisions to achieve specific outcomes and mitigate the consequences of terrorist attacks. Based on this knowledge, the researchers identified effective actions for achieving different objectives and provided a comparative analysis of the consequences using metrics such as regret factor, hit-and-miss factor, and the Hit and Miss graphs. Ultimately, the research highlights the significance of leveraging smart technologies and intelligent systems for mitigating the consequences of terrorist attacks on people and assets in Smart Cities. The proposed framework and techniques provide a valuable tool for city officials and planners to analyze Smart City public safety as a complex situation with multiple objectives, comparing different scenarios, prioritizing objectives, and avoiding resource wastage and negative consequences. Future research directions are proposed to address emerging challenges in Smart City public safety. Our model sets a new standard for long document retrieval, surpassing prior benchmarks across various settings and datasets. Moreover, we show that our memory module can be flexibly applied to other information retrieval tasks, like top-N document retrieval. Despite the exceptional performance of Graph Neural Networks in semi-supervised node classification, they face significant challenges when dealing with an extremely limited number of labels. The semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is often employed to mitigate this issue, which aims to supplement the training set with high-confidence, pseudo-labeled nodes in a self-training cycle. Nevertheless, current pseudo-labeling techniques have several shortcomings. Primarily, they expand the label set cautiously by choosing only the most confident, yet potentially uninformative nodes, which merely amplify minor improvements. Secondly, they combine these pseudo-labels with the original training set through simple data augmentation, failing to fully leverage their value. To address these limitations, we propose InfoGNN, an innovative pseudo-labeling framework. InfoGNN focuses on generating robust and informative pseudo-labels by initially extracting node features from local neighborhoods, then utilizing an informed pseudo-labeling method to select a diverse set of nodes that significantly contribute to model improvement. Information from these selected pseudo-labels is then integrated back into the model through modified GNN augmentation, which enables the model to absorb knowledge from the label information. Our comprehensive experiments on seven datasets demonstrate that InfoGNN outperforms the state-of-the-art methods, including both pseudo-labeling and active learning techniques, by an average of 4.2% in terms of accuracy. Moreover, information theory-based evaluation methods reveal that InfoGNN yields more informative pseudo-labels, while the proposed GNN augmentation method effectively transfers knowledge from the pseudo-labels to the model. Our source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/mengxiao81/InfoGNN. In conclusion, InfoGNN offers a superior solution to semi-supervised GNN node classification under extreme label scarcity. As an alternative approach, it may also be adapted for semi-label propagation in transfer learning and graph classification tasks. Our research indicates that pseudo-labeling can be both safe and effective when the pseudo-labels are made informative, which is contrary to the limitations of current pseudo-labeling methods. Based on our findings, we speculate that the semi-supervised pseudo-labeling method is essentially a special case of unsupervised meta-learning, where the model aims to learn informative pseudo-labels to achieve better generalization. With the rapid advancements in meta-learning research, we hope that our research will inspire the development of more sophisticated pseudo-labeling methods in the future. Ultimately, our work may pave the way for the application of pseudo-labeling in scenarios where labeling costs are extremely high, such as in Graph Neural Networks

Building upon our previous research \cite{Liu:2019xhn}, we examine the prospect of primordial black holes emerging from the second inflationary process caused by the curvaton's oscillation. We employ the instability of the Mathieu equation to leverage the $\delta$ function, which enables a comprehensive representation of the power spectrum. Given the varying curvaton mass, we simulate a broad range of primordial black hole masses, highlighting three distinct scenarios, one of which may explain some aspects of dark matter due to the black holes' typical masses of $10^{17}-10^{18}$ grams. We further optimize our model to align the gravitational wave background with observations from the Advanced LIGO/Virgo Collaborations. We also improve upon our previous model by making the initial curvature perturbation follow a delta function, which yields better results for the primordial black hole abundance. Finally, primordial black holes can decay into other particles including neutrinos, which may impact the decay products' distribution ratio and help constrain our model. We utilize Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and primordial black hole abundance to limit the parameter space of our model. We observed that our model cannot be completely ruled out with current data and future observations of the primordial black hole contribution to cold dark matter are essential for a comprehensive understanding of the cosmological scenario. We further explored the possibility of dark matter consisting of black holes that have masses of $10^{22}$ grams, which may explain the observed receding velocity of Andromeda galaxy denoted by M31. We found that our model's prediction of the power spectrum matches findings from the analysis of South Pole Telescope data at a level of agreement better than $1\%$. Moreover, we found that primordial black holes can significantly influence the decay products' distribution ratio, which may impact the $\mu\mu$ decay rate and ultimately lead to a constraint of our model with a level of precision of $0.01\%$. Ultimately, an understanding of the primordial black hole contribution to cold dark matter and accurate measurements of the power spectrum will be essential for a comprehensive explanation of the characteristics of our standard $\Lambda$CDM model. We hope our model's predictions will be substantiated by the ongoing and future research with current and improved instruments. To assess the effectiveness of each configuration, the distance between vehicles is analyzed based on each driver's perspective. It's demonstrated that, regardless of the information network configuration used, the distance is governed by the same differential equation, with disparate initial conditions acting as key parameters. To analyze the motion patterns of the vehicles, the spectral properties of the state space equation are examined. One of the widely applied optimization methods in machine learning is Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), which tackles optimization problems by iteratively selecting and computing gradients of small data subsets before updating the solution. When executed in parallel, SGD demands communication among involved processes at each iteration. Our innovation is a communication-optimizing approach for utilizing SGD to solve logistic regression. This strategy organizes computations into phases where communication is exclusively required at the commencement and conclusion. This modification yields a significant time savings by reducing the total communication needs by a factor of $O(|B|^2)$, where $|B|$ is the batch size. Our analysis is confirmed through direct Combinatorial Recursive Recurrence Equation calculations and experimental verifications using up to 96 CPU cores, that shows our approach results in a communication efficiency rate of $2.65\times10^{-7}$ seconds per iteration, providing a solid ground for large-scale parallel computing. This method also exhibits exceptional scalability, as our research reveals that it is susceptible to a linear relationship between batch size and communication overhead. Additionally, our technique is adaptable to various SGD algorithms such as mini-batch SGD and Magnus, as well as other optimization methods like parallel Newton-CG for solving linear systems. We also observed that the main bottleneck is typically the computation of the gradient across the batch, allowing us to leverage a parallel optimization method while still maintaining accuracy, as confirmed by our experimental results. This method has the potential to be highly beneficial for training deep neural networks. This research is an initial step to extending this technique to utilize asynchronous communication using SGD, an exploration of which is presented in the appendix. Our aspiration is that this innovation may contribute towards an optimization technique that is efficient in terms of training, computation, and memory, as well as an understanding of how to tackle parallelization of neural networks. This research is an initial exploration into using asynchronous communication using SGD, where our appendix outlines a number of open challenges associated with parallelizing deep neural networks. Future large-scale radio interferometers, aiming to detect 21\,cm signals across vast distances, may struggle with computing cross-correlations given traditional architectures, requiring $O(N^2)$ computations, a challenge that could exceed a hundred thousand cores even with relatively modest numbers of antennas. Thankfully, specialized FFT-correlator architecture, traditionally used in ultrasound, speech, and MRI imaging, offers a significant computational advantage. These machines, originally developed to handle specific data types, surprisingly aligns perfectly with the discrete nature of radio interferometry data. By implementing the FFT-correlator technique, the computational demand is reduced to a more manageable $O(N\log N)$, a substantial improvement. Our study explores and adapts FFT-correlator architecture for application in radio interferometry, proposing necessary enhancements, identifying areas for further optimization, and outlining a roadmap for its practical implementation and testing. The success and effective integration of this technique could vastly impact the field, influencing the design of future radio telescopes and their computational frameworks. Furthermore, this work serves as a case study for the broader scientific community, demonstrating the benefits of "importing in novelty" from one field to another to address challenges, and also highlights a more practical aspect of "exporting capabilities" from one field to another. For several decades, the Markowitz framework has been used for in-depth portfolio analysis but it places an excessive focus on understanding market uncertainty, failing to prioritize trend prediction. While researchers have applied generative adversarial networks and their variants to generate financial time series and portfolio return distributions, the resulting models often struggle to capture the intricacies of future financial data or achieve desired portfolio returns. Therefore, this paper outlines a novel Markovian conditional mixture model to combine the benefits of Markowitz and generative models, effectively analyzing time series patterns and portfolio composition. Unlike traditional GANs, this model prioritizes trend prediction and portfolio optimization. A numerical study demonstrates that our approach outperforms conventional portfolios, and the underlying methodology shows significant promise in marking a new direction for portfolio analysis under uncertainties. Additionally, the potential applications of the proposed model extend beyond portfolio analysis to encompass a broader range of hydrometeorological and future causal data. Initially targeting crop yield forecasting, the integration of causal models could significantly enhance the predictive capabilities of the proposed Markovian conditional mixture model. A subsequent implementation plan is presented to key stakeholders and decision-makers in the agricultural sector to derive informed insights from the proposed model. Given the availability of the necessary input data, the proposed method can be applied in various high-impact areas, including the analysis of geophysical features, climate change, and public health issues. In the future, the integration of causal models will provide informed answers to questions such as 'What factors contribute to changes in crop yields over time?' and 'Which factors are most influential on crop yields?'. For portfolio optimization, the proposed model will provide solutions to questions such as 'What is the optimal composition of a portfolio given uncertainty levels?' and 'What is the likelihood of a portfolio achieving a specified return with a certain level of uncertainty?' The detailed implementation plan is presented in Section 7. A related GitHub repository at https://github.com/AI4Portfolios/MCMC-port holds the implementation of the proposed model. A related video explanation is available at https://vimeo.com/795289997. A technical explanation of the proposed model is provided in the study's supplementary information, referenced as [34].

A groundbreaking method utilizing Bayesian neural networks enhances the accuracy of label assignment in text-based classification tasks. We applied this method to distinguish between two subclasses of active galactic nuclei: Fermi-LAT BL Lac candidates (FBBAC) and Gamma-Ray Blazar Candidates (GRBC). Our study involved a dataset of 219 texts, with FBBAC having more instances than GRBC, and focused on identifying GRBC given the characteristics associated with these sources are often irregular and inconsistent, complicating classification. A neural network with two layers of Bayesian nodes was trained on the data, with each node representing a Bayesian variable that depends on input features. Following training, we assessed the network's performance using a variety of metrics to validate its capacity to generalize, incorporate prior knowledge, and accommodate uncertainty. Our results indicate that the Bayesian neural network is an effective tool for assigning labels in the presence of uncertainty, a capability that is threshold-free in contrast to traditional methods. With this approach, the accuracy of the classification task is unaffected by the level of uncertainty in the data. Importantly, our study reveals a high degree of correlation between the Bayesian neural network's classification and scientific understanding of the sources. Notably, the network is capable of identifying sources that were not considered candidates prior to the analysis as well as recognizing inconsistencies in the data. A notable benefit of the network is its ability to assign an uncertainty range to each classification, effectively creating a continuum of labels that is free from thresholds. A second outcome of the network is the identification of potential sources that could serve as reference points for constraining particle acceleration in BL Lac jets. Moreover, the network is an advanced, sophisticated tool that is capable of reading scientific papers and drawing inferences from them. A demonstration of its potential for active learning and sample selection is presented, an area that is sure to be of importance in the future, particularly in the analysis of data with an extremely high dimension. A Jupyter notebook that illustrates how to utilize the Bayesian neural network is provided as an additional resource. In this paper, we propose a new approach to defining hypergraph operations using tensor joins and demonstrate their mathematical structure. We establish two types of joins - one incorporating external hyperedges and the other with external vertex set modifications - and investigate their properties. These tensor join operations facilitate the introduction of a hierarchical framework for hypergraphs and allow for the seamless integration of existing hypergraph operations into our tensor join scheme. We examine and compare the structural characteristics of hypergraphs formed by different types of joins from various initial structures. Various methods of constructing new hypergraphs using tensor joins are explored, and the independence numbers of the resulting hypergraphs are calculated via a ranking-type extension of the algorithm used by Máčka and the algebraic method proposed by Alon. We further investigate the cases where the resulting hypergraphs have maximum degree one and demonstrate schemes to produce cospectral hypergraphs under certain conditions. Additionally, we discuss strategies for grouping hypergraphs based on their tensor representation and independence lattice structure, and examine the long-term goals and possible applications of this framework in computer science and mathematics. A corresponding website provides access to a collection of open-source tools and examples for working with tensor join operations. The associated algorithms and mathematical concepts are presented in the context of a hypergraph theory that is part of the Zetzsche-Sibley theorem, as well as the tensor version of the Brualdi-Conca theorem. We conclude with potential future areas of study, including exploring new tensor join schemes, extending our findings to graded hypergraphs, examining the computational complexity of tensor join-related problems, and applying the framework to other graph and hypergraph structures. A brief overview of relevant research is provided in the appendix, along with references to related studies. We have included a publicly accessible repository containing the implementation of the framework in Mathematica, along with a collection of examples that illustrate the computational efficacy of the algorithm when applied to small to medium-sized problems. A novel methodology has been introduced to investigate non-equilibrium transitions to alternative reaction pathways through the Onsager-Machlup action principle. Although the action formally relates equilibrium free energies, it provides a path-based framework to examine nonequilibrium pathways. To apply the action framework, we develop a linear approximation method to determine the nonequilibrium rate constant without simulating the detailed dynamics of a system undergoing an equilibrium shift. This method involves two key steps: first generating a transition pathway via the string method and then calculating the linear change in the pathway's free energy with time. Based on these steps, we derive a simple expression for the rate constant. To validate the approach, we examined three systems: a small enzyme-catalyzed reaction, an ordinary Michaelis-Menten reaction, and the linear ubiquitin chain activation pathway. Our numerical results show good agreement between the new method and comprehensive nonequilibrium molecular dynamics simulations. Additionally, we evaluated the method's performance in complex systems of various dimensions. This method offers an efficient means to model multipathway competition in chemical and biological systems, where the transition between equilibrium states may be induced by a trigger, revealing the dynamic origin of the pathways. This new understanding resolves disagreements that have previously arisen over the question of which pathways are dominant. This research proposes a novel two-stage approach using a genetic algorithm (GA) to generate user-specific sequences for low-latency grant-free uplink access. First, the initial GA finds a subsampling strategy to transform a unitary matrix into a closely-packed, uniform pattern. Subsequently, a second-stage GA is employed to conceal 'distortion-inducing' data within the matrix, ensuring even power distribution for multi-carrier transmissions. These modified sequences are proposed for mMTC uplink grant-free access, where simulation results showcase superior performance for joint activity detection and channel estimation using compressed sensing. Lastly, the research into sequence-based mMTC uplink access is placed within the broader context of mMTC research. Several open issues relevant to GA-based sequence generation are also identified. Ultimately, this work is intent on contributing novel ideas to the mMTC community. A recently investigated explanation suggests that these structures form when magnetic field eddies caused by edge-localized modes trigger the development of a PTM seed island. However, this study instead seeks to provide an alternate explanation based on observations of edge plasma turbulence. A distinct feature of plasma turbulence is the existence of persistent structures known as blobs. To better comprehend how these blobs influence PTM formation, researchers analyzed data from scenarios featuring edge sub-steady ELMs and discovered a unique association between these blobs and PTM. Specifically, they identified a particular type of fluctuation, with a poloidal frequency below 100 kHz, that appears prior to a PTM, suggesting that a blob may serve as a PTM seed. To confirm this relationship, the researchers examined PTM development alongside associated blob behavior. Interestingly, this study found that, following the initial transient phase of a sub-steady ELM, fluctuations show reduced amplitude but continue to exhibit a distinct relationship with PTM. We explore the impact of varying degree distributions on biological networks, 
focusing on pairs of excitatory and inhibitory neurons with diverse connection 
patterns based on random graphs. Using mean-field analysis and numerical simulations, 
our research demonstrates that broadening the distribution of incoming connections 
inhibits oscillations in inhibitory networks but fosters oscillations in excitatory 
networks. Additionally, our models suggest that as a network becomes more complex, 
its dynamics are dominated by a dominant slow timescale related to node activity. 
We also observe that in highly connected networks, inhibition can lead to a temporary 
and significant drop in oscillations, however in less complex networks, our analysis 
indicates an inverse relationship between in-degree distribution and oscillations in 
excitatory networks, and a direct relationship in inhibitory networks. Furthermore, our 
research shows that in highly connected networks, excitation levels are directly 
related to in-degree distribution, and when the distribution is broadened, 
excitation levels are both higher and oscillations are less frequent. 

All the findings from our models align well with actual experimental results, 
providing valuable insights into the natural world and its complexities. 
Mean-field analysis, a theoretical method where variables are reduced to lower 
dimensions, contributes to an enhanced understanding of complex biological issues.

complex one with mixed results, suggesting the use of simpler models to study 
complexity in nature. 

Our research primarily utilizes visualizations and statistical methods to create a 
link between random graph theory and biological observations, and our findings may 
stimulate fresh ideas within the neuroscience and network dynamics fields.

suggests the possibility of extending this to more specialized areas within the 
brain, such as spatial and limbic systems. 
Moreover, our work suggests that differing degree distributions could serve as 
distinct markers for identifying varied neuronal dynamics across distinct brain 
regions, allowing for a deeper understanding of paired excitatory and inhibitory 
neurons through simple biological observations.

A Graph Neural Network (GNN) is an effective neural network architecture that processes graph data, extensively applied across multiple domains. Unlike traditional neural network models, GNN can operate in a decentralized manner, facilitating communication among neighboring nodes and potentially leading to more efficient control mechanisms in wireless communication systems. However, wireless channel disruptions significantly reduce the robustness of GNN predictions. To overcome this limitation, we develop methods to assess the robustness of decentralized GNN predictions in wireless communication systems, focusing on a binary classification model. Since real-world data is scarce, we introduce synthetic data generation and simulate a decentralized GNN training process to obtain knowledge. We also establish boundaries for predicted outputs by training models on knowledge from intact graphs to anticipate GNN behavior on partially damaged graphs. We evaluate our approach using four benchmarks and find that our method effectively approximates the true GNN predictions in damaged graph settings, even with a 50% node damage ratio. These results demonstrate that our technique can reliably estimate GNN predictions in dynamic wireless environments. Moreover, our decentralized approach outperforms a centralized model subject to damage. A significant advantage of our approach is its ability to adapt to unfamiliar test data, as confirmed through real-world data applications. The code and configuration for this study are available online. We believe that our proposed method has significant implications for applying GNNs to large-scale dynamic wireless systems. We propose LDT, a novel model compression approach, combining the principles of knowledge distillation and layer decomposition. Existing methods have difficulties in tackling large models due to their multi-layered nature and intricate architecture. To overcome these challenges, we leverage knowledge distillation to transfer knowledge from a large teacher model to a series of student models, each consisting of a single layer. These student models are trained in succession, utilizing the outputs of their predecessors as inputs. A unique characteristic of LDT is the use of decomposed intermediate knowledge, enabling targeted learning for specific layers and improving overall compression performance. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of LDT in achieving superior compression quality on ResNet-50 and DenseNet-201 models, utilizing various backbones and datasets. Ecosystems that naturally thrive in dry environments have unique patterns of plant life due to factors like soil type, rainfall, temperature, and wildlife influence. This study focuses on how spatial plant patterns affect the amount of forage available to grazing animals in semi-arid areas through a dynamic model that involves animal activity modulating their hunger levels and navigating spatial distribution patterns. The researchers investigated how this dynamic influence impacts the plant ecosystem using mathematical and computational methods, analyzing minimum and maximum outcomes of key system variables. The findings suggest that dry land ecosystems can experience significant variations in available forage due to changes in animal population and spatial distribution patterns of plants, with or without herbivorous influence, and that this forage variability can have considerable economic implications for such ecosystems. Furthermore, the study reveals that in certain instances of over-grazing, local equilibrium can help to mitigate the extent of this forage variability. The researchers also explored the limitations of current mathematical methods in capturing the complexities of these ecosystems, advocating for the incorporation of ideas drawn from plant water use theories to enhance the predictive accuracy of these models. The study's outcomes emphasize the importance of considering the intricate connections within dry land ecosystems that involve feedback loops between physical and biological factors, and that this consideration is essential for developing practical strategies to mitigate the impacts of climate change on these sensitive ecosystems. The research demonstrates that through a deeper understanding of the relationships within dry land ecosystems, it may be possible to develop tailored interventions that could have a positive impact on the amount of forage available to such ecosystems. The study proposes that its framework has the potential to be expanded to investigate other factors such as water availability and financial implications within these ecosystems. The research identifies that its model is capable of capturing the time-tested practices of managing two-grazer dynamics that have been employed by dry land herders for centuries. The study concludes by highlighting that its framework is designed to be inclusive, capturing the perspectives of both scientists and traditional herders who have spent years studying and living off these sensitive ecosystems. The research outcomes provide insight into the practical implications of developing robust mathematical models to analyze the dynamics of ecosystems that have significant cultural and economic significance. The study demonstrates that its framework is applicable to other similar ecosystem systems, emphasizing the importance of incorporating the perspectives of those who interact with such ecosystems on a daily basis in order to capture their full complexity. The research aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about how dry land ecosystems may adapt to face the challenges posed by climate change, highlighting the crucial role that animal grazing may play in this transformation process. A well-known dimensionality reduction technique called CountSketch employs randomized linear measurements to map vectors into a lower-dimensional space, particularly effective at identifying the top elements (with the largest squared magnitude) of a given vector. However, the CountSketch sketch falls short in situations where subsequent vectors rely on feedback from previous inputs. Under such circumstances, the classic estimator can be compromised by a relatively low number of inferences, essentially making it vulnerable to manipulation. A more resilient estimator was proposed, which, albeit requiring quadratically more queries in proportion to the sketch size, significantly enhances the safety by a factor of k (with k being the number of key components) when compared to prior studies on CountSketch sketches. A distributed version of this estimator was also proposed, which achieves improved safety while maintaining quadratic relationship between distributed queries and sketch size. Interestingly, the proposed solutions maintain the exact rate of success as the classic CountSketch procedure. A novel learning technique for CountSketch was introduced, dubbed COUNTSketchLearn. It involves training a linear classifier on a trained CountSketch sketch, which offers better performance than the classic CountSketch procedure in subsequent classification tasks. Furthermore, the COUNTSketchLearn method outperforms prior techniques relying on non-convex optimization. COUNTSketchLearn curvature-guided is another version of this technique, which provides an alternative to GAN training, by identifying the most prominent CountSketchLearn generators. These generative adversarial networks compete to recognize underlying latent representations and can be used in various applications, such as classification, by identifying the most suitable learned CountSketch sketches. A novel Counting Generative Adversarial Network was introduced, which rivals state-of-the-art generative models pre-trained on ImageNet. A counting function derived from CountSketch enables accurate counting in situations with occlusions by leveraging top element identification. EXPERIMENTAL results show the COUNTSketchLearn curvature-guided's capability of automatically labeling ImageNet data with vector magnitudes, which can then be utilized for follow-up classification by a linear classifier. Moreover, the CGAN developed an accurate estimator for recognizing birds with attached feathers from the bird SNIPES dataset. Lastly, the COUNTSketchLearn curvature-guided achieved high accuracy in recognizing densely packed crowds with attached overcoats from the mulan dataset. We examine a mechanism design problem for selling $k$ items to unit-demand buyers with private valuations for each item, who can choose between participating directly in the auction or being represented by an intermediary. The aim is to develop robust auction designs that don't rely on the buyer-demand distribution and work well across diverse demand distributions. Mechanisms are considered robust if they don't advantage any particular distribution and are stable in the sense that small changes in the buyer-demand distribution do not lead to significant increases in payment for the same outcome. Our research focuses on the case of $k$ identical items. Previous studies have shown that efficient mechanisms are inherently complex, unless either the item demand distribution is uniform or the buyer valuations follow a Laplace distribution. Building on this, we present a mechanism that ensures robust, efficient, and truthful trade of $k$ identical items for the first time when the item demand distribution is unknown. Furthermore, we show the mechanism is optimal by proving the nonexistence of simpler, consistent, and truthful mechanisms. When considering separate valuations for each item, we design an efficient mechanism that ensures minimal payment for the same outcome as the optimal mechanism. The approach leverages a piecewise linear approximation of the buyer valuation's probability distribution, which features $O(\sqrt{k})$ pieces. Importantly, the mechanism features payment that only scales linearly with $k$. On the other hand, when the item demand distribution is uniform, we present an efficient mechanism that relies on $O(\log k)$ pieces of the demand distribution, without sacrificing its efficiency and robust properties. Notably, the mechanism can handle cases with $k$ items where $k$ is large, by maintaining constant scaling for the payment. Finally, we show the nonexistence of robust, efficient, and truthful mechanisms with constant scaling for the payment when the item demand distribution is separate and the buyer valuations for each item follow a Laplace distribution. The approach bypasses existing mechanisms with constant scaling for the payment, which were shown to be incomplete in achieving this demand distribution. The research rewards an improved outcome when the item demand distribution is separate. Human vocal synchronization in social contexts provides valuable information about a person's cognitive behaviors, suggesting the importance of understanding entrainment patterns in conversational voice. To measure this synchronization accurately in two people interacting, we developed a dynamic approach that combines statistical and machine learning methods for entrainment assessment. This approach consists of two components: (1) a high-performance computer model simulating N persons talking, with a sub-millisecond state update rate, and (2) an entropy-based measure of entrainment among N persons with a sub-10 millisecond computation time. Our experimental model reveals linear relationships between the number of participants and computational time or error rate. Specifically, when three participants are involved, the simulation reaches a high degree of accuracy, taking about 4 milliseconds to update and 0.8 milliseconds to determine entrainment while maintaining a mean error rate of 3.27%. Moreover, to demonstrate practical application, we successfully integrated our entrainment model into a Facebook avatar system called Voogie, allowing users to see how interaction synchronizes voices and participant information. This technology can be used in various scenarios such as training systems for salesforce or customer service representatives. Furthermore, it can also be applied in online role-playing contexts like forums for role-playing games or shared stories, enabling users to engage in synchronized voice interactions with one another. In order to protect user privacy, we ensured that our technology does not collect any user data; instead, it operates solely within the browser and relies on JavaScript. Our future work will involve expanding our study to other types of social interactions and including multimodal communication such as keyboard typing into our framework. This will not only allow us to gain a deeper understanding of how participants interact across different communication methods, but it will also enable us to devise new applications that utilize our technology in areas like privacy-related sales systems or voice assisted search. In the event that voice and text are used separately, voice entrainment assessment will outperform text entropy in capturing rich context from live interactions, indicating a deep and significant advancement in capturing live interaction richness. Furthermore, our technology is inclusive in the sense that it operates across various domains and domains' complexity. Ultimately, our technology has the capability of creating a deeper and more realistic user experience in virtual role-players through an automatic statistical estimation of real user interaction richness. This research focuses on a specific scenario involving a 2D marine ice sheet with a grounding line, though the approach can be extended to other contact issues like subglacial cavitation. A primary challenge arises from the analysis due to ice's nonlinear rheology and the presence of rigid boundaries, both factors that complicate the modelling. This study derives a precise expression for the divergence of the implicit constitutive matrix, one that directly relates to the given driving potential. This research lays crucial groundwork for future full dynamics analyses in other contact-related issues. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, examining how star formation-driven gas outflows are linked to other properties of the galaxy. Our data show a nearly linear relationship between outflow mass and star formation rates, as well as a significant correlation between outflow mass and gas expulsion velocities, all within the galaxy's central region. Furthermore, we found that outflowing gas is missing about half of its mass by the time it's emitted. Our findings align with predictions from simplified models of outflow dynamics, suggesting these models adequately describe outflow behavior, especially at high velocities. However, we also observe outflowing gas at velocities much lower than expected using these simple models, implying these low velocities may be due to outflows being disrupted by surrounding interstellar material. Additionally, we found no evidence that outflows affect the shape of our star formation rate distribution. This could be because outflows aren't able to reach sufficiently high intensities to impact the formation of stars, or that outflows operate on a larger timescale than the lifetime of individual super star clusters. Finally, we found that outflows account for less than a tenth of the gas that's recycled back into the galaxy through processes such as gas re-accretion and supernova explosion. This discovery highlights the importance of self-sustaining gas circulation in maintaining the gas content of galaxy central regions. Our research stresses the need for studies to be done at high angular resolution, as this reveals unique aspects of galaxy behavior, like outflows that're directed perpendicular to the galaxy plane. Our research paves the way for further high-resolution studies of outflow properties across a range of galaxy types and environments. Future studies using advanced techniques like VLASPECS and PANPS will allow us to make comparisons between outflows in the gas phase and outflows in the dust phase, examining the role of outflowing gas in dispersing galaxy magnetic fields and the effects of outflows on galaxy rotation. If outflows are able to propagate perpendicular to the galaxy plane, this would provide strong evidence for outflows playing a significant role in galaxy disk formation and evolution, as outflows would provide the necessary momentum to allow gas to fall onto central regions, being re-accreted, while outflows perpendicular to the galaxy plane would provide the necessary pressure to allow gas to fall onto central regions, as outflows would provide the necessary pressure to allow gas to fall onto central regions, as outflows would provide the necessary pressure to allow gas to fall onto central regions, as outflows.

Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum relationships. Understanding the underlying causes of these connections remains a crucial area of future investigation. Our simulation also indicated that $v_3$ and $v_2$ exhibit comparable transverse momentum elliptic and triangular flow correlations. Ultimately, these findings may serve as a basis for further exploration of the initial conditions of heavy ion collisions through experimental analysis of $v_2$ and $v_3$ in differential analysis. In support of upcoming experiments with p+Pb and $p+$Pt collisions, we provide predictions for $v_3$ in relation to centrality and particle transverse momentum. Our research and its implications will be presented at the 9th International Conference on Clusters and Cluster Associates.

Deep neural network training requires substantial computational resources, so to develop a more effective approach with fewer requirements, we utilized unlabeled videos for a deep learning model's initial training stages. Specifically, we discovered that extracting depth information can serve as an excellent representation for various objects in a scene, making it beneficial for tasks like semantic segmentation. To test this idea, we created a method called Depth Projection Consistency (DPC) that enforces depth estimation to conform to known ground truths, resulting in improved depth estimators that can outperform traditional ones. Moreover, DPC can be adapted for other tasks, such as unsupervised keypoint learning, and, notably, it requires no training with scene labels to achieve superior results. Interestingly, DPC's success stems from leveraging the principle of depth consistency that governs the relationship between point features and 3D scene geometry, a concept that was previously applied to supervise the learning of keypoint detectors. Furthermore, we utilized our depth estimators as pre-training methods for a wide range of semantic segmentation tasks, including ones with outdoor scenes, fine-grained categories, and talking head images. Importantly, cross-dataset evaluations indicate that DPC's effectiveness stems from general principles of computer vision, meaning it can excel in other domains as well. To support the community, we created publicly available depth datasets, training code, and challenge platforms that can be utilized for various deep learning applications. Overall, DPC presents a novel and efficient approach for unsupervised pre-training that significantly enhances deep neural network performance for diverse tasks. Our experiments show that DPC's depth estimates can surpass those generated by other unsupervised and supervised models, achieving better results when evaluated using a variety of unsupervised and supervised semantic segmentation benchmarks. Notably, DPC's efficacy extends beyond object recognition tasks, enabling unsupervised pre-training for keypoint detection, depth estimation, occlusion detection, and even raw image representation learning. Furthermore, extending DPC to unsupervised pre-training for dense pixel-level scene parsing appears to be a promising area of research, considering the significant improvements observed in depth, semantic segmentation, and keypoint detection tasks. In the future, we aim to further refine DPC as well as develop it for more complex tasks like dense pixel-level scene parsing. To facilitate this, we are making public several challenge platforms that allow researchers to evaluate their unsupervised depth estimators and semantic segmentation models. The Hirsch Conjecture was a theory claiming that a d-dimensional polytope with n faces cannot exceed a diameter of n - d. This assumption was contested by Santos, whose findings led to the conclusion that some linear programming methods cannot perform optimally within n - d iterations. This series of research was initiated by a novel algorithm, the facet pivot method, proposed in the first paper. This second paper verifies the efficacy of the facet pivot method, confirming it completes in at most n - d iterations. Consequently, the efficacy of certain linear programming processes, such as the simplex method of Boruvka, Mancini, and Kramer, is also validated, alongside other algorithms, like Papadimitrius' method. The final paper in this series will further explore the capabilities of the facet pivot method and extend its applications to related problems. Our objective is to quantify the magnitude of off-shell and non-resonant influences on the forms of various differential distributions that will be crucial for top quark mass determination via template fitting techniques. Although the proposed study pertains to the LHC experiments, it may serve as a starting point for analogous investigations within the context of future electron-positron colliders. Current approaches have shown limitations, often becoming overly specialized in training datasets and struggling to adapt to unseen attack methods and environments. Experimental results conducted on widely accessible datasets showcase the superiority of our proposed solution, outperforming state-of-the-art methods significantly in zero-shot scenarios within the HQ-WMCA and SiW-M datasets. The concept of an effective, time-independent Floquet Hamiltonian underpins the Floquet engineering of isolated systems, describing their evolution over driving periods and often obtained through analytical high-frequency expansions. However, extending these ideas to open quantum systems, modelled by a system-system-bath framework, poses a significant challenge due to the need to project onto the system's degrees of freedom. In this work, a mean-field approximation is applied to analyze the effects of high-frequency driving on open quantum systems, focusing on the case of a solid interacting with a surface-emitted light wave and exploring its floquet engineering. Despite the need for a more sophisticated description in this scenario, numerical simulations indicate a phase transition within the system, with the possibility of generating a floquet Hamiltonian describing two distinct quantum states. These findings have implications for controlling quantum systems, enabling the creation of entangled states and potentially shielding internal degrees of freedom from environmental influences. Furthermore, our model's general applicability suggests that these phenomena could also influence other environmental systems, such as graphene. Finally, our analysis outlines a route to implement a highly secure key distribution protocol based on the principles of quantum teleportation. A thorough discussion of the practical feasibility of this concept is also undertaken, involving experimental estimates of the actualization of these ideas. In particular, it is investigated whether the required conditions for floquet engineering can be achieved using current technologies and experimental methods such as photolithography, laser cutting and atomic layering to create the required nanostructures. Additionally, the interaction with a surface plamon and radiation of a dipole also offers alternative possibilities for applying Floquet engineering. These ideas may contribute towards the development of highly secure communication methods, like quantum key distribution, and enhance our understanding of the complex relationships between quantum systems and their highly fluctuating environments. It is evident that deep neural networks excel in extracting relevant features from a given dataset, but they may not necessarily excel in adapting these features to datasets with different underlying characteristics. In this report, we compare the effectiveness of four domain adaptation methods for image classification: DeepCORAL, DeepDomainConfusion, CDAN, and CDAN+E, which employ an unsupervised learning approach given the absence of target labels. Our analysis is based on a test of these methods across four target datasets derived from the ImageNet corpus. Interestingly, despite each method claiming to facilitate domain adaptation, our results show that target dataset performance lags behind that of the source dataset in three out of four cases, with significant discrepancies observed between the methods. A potential explanation for these "domain shift" discrepancies is offered. Additionally, to facilitate replication of our research, accompanying this report is a fully documented code package available at https://github.com/sustocht/DeepUnsupDomainShift. Our work highlights a crucial, previously overlooked aspect of deep neural network evaluation - domain shift - which needs to be carefully addressed when deploying such networks in real-world applications. Our research also underscores the more straightforward task of unsupervised domain adaptation as a "proof-of-concept" rather than a solved problem. Ultimately, the findings of our report are intended to stimulate further research to develop more robust domain adaptation methods that effectively adapt to target datasets with distinct underlying characteristics. Our work also includes an accompanying preprint document available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05326. Our research draws inspiration from a work reporting on domain shift in context image classification - (Zhang et al. 2018, MachineVision) - where across four target datasets derived from ImageNet a significant disparity exists between the adaptation performance of the DeepCORAL method and its source dataset performance. Our research extends that of (Zhang et al. 2018) by investigating whether domain shift actually exists across five other target datasets derived from ImageNet and testing three alternative unsupervised domain adaptation methods for image classification. Our research finds that domain shift indeed exists across six target datasets (including numerical evidence) and reveals domain shift exists across all tested target datasets derived from ImageNet. Our research offers insights into a potential explanation for domain shift, our results show that domain shift cannot be completely overcome but can be mitigated through a simple approach. Our research draws out the underlying implications from the findings presented. Despite recent advancements in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), explaining their predictive decisions remains an unresolved issue. Traditional visualization methods are limited in handling GNNs, as they require assumption of a fixed, static graph, whereas real-world graphs are dynamic and vary by instance. To address this, we propose an unsupervised graph visualization approach that learns node positions in a way that maintains interpretability of GNNs' predictive decisions. Our approach employs a comprehensive, instance-specific graph representation, structured into a core and a extension component. We derive a symmetric True Distance Metric (TDM) for the core graph, enabling effective visualization of labeled datasets. Consequently, we develop a Supervised Graph Visualization (SGV) method that closes the distance between test nodes to class-specific centers, providing clear explanations for GNNs' predictive decisions based on the TDM. Experiments on seven diverse datasets demonstrate that SGV produces robust, instance-independent graphs, outperforms existing graph visualization techniques, and provides clear and precise explanations for GNNs' predictive decisions. Furthermore, SGV's visualizations improve the overall performance of leading GNN models when fine-tuned with node-level labels obtained through TDM-inspired guidance. Our study is open-source at https://github.com/tanl/SDM. Our TDM-inspired visualization approach can also be applied to qualified input data, facilitating the explanation of other black-box models' decisions. Additionally, we develop the first TDM-inspired visualization approach tailored to Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents, providing clear insights into decisions made by agents operating in the OpenAI Gym environment. Results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in generating visually meaningful visualizations of RL agents' decision-making processes. RL code is available at https://github.com/tanl/SDM-RL. Ultimately, our research contributes to the field of Visual Explanation of Black-box Predictors by offering innovative solutions for visualizing the decision-making processes of Graph Neural Networks and Reinforcement Learning agents in diverse application domains. As such, our approach may be applied or extended to explain other types of black-box models' decisions. To promote future research in Visual Explanation, we provide our work as a foundation for similar studies and welcome discussions regarding its potential for extension or application to other domains. Our approach is versatile and can be applied to other types of black-box models with some modifications. For GNNs, our approach is suitable for explaining decisions made by other GNN models, whereas RL agents were chosen due to the availability of open-source environments and the difficulty in developing RL policies

The peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core. To explore its development and composition, we examined archival X-ray data from Chandra and XMM-Newton, examining the dynamic cluster state and searching for gas substructures. Its X-ray brightness distribution exhibits no evident disruption except for an elongation in the North-East to South-West direction. We applied the unsharp masking technique and calculated the morphology parameters to assess disturbance levels. These analyses identified a South-West substructure located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo. This is one of two known systems displaying this anomaly; what are its implications for cosmological studies and our understanding of intracluster medium (ICM) dynamics? Further investigation is necessary to determine if the detected substructure constitutes an extrinsic disruption or part of the system's inherent dynamics. To facilitate this, we present a series of illustrations depicting the likely 3D layout of the cluster based on its X-ray images. Additionally, we propose RXCJ0232.2-4420 as an exemplary benchmark to test both new and existing X-ray telescopes in detecting dynamic clusters in the future. $\diamond$ These findings contribute to an ongoing discussion regarding the prevalence of haloes in clusters and their relation to core cool cores, providing valuable insights for the development of models to predict X-ray morphologies and predict the occurrence of haloes. Furthermore, we advocate for Chandra to thoroughly examine this dynamic system in all its spectral complexity in order to uncover the current system dynamics. $\diamond$ Furthermore, we propose that the peculiar system, RXCJ0232.2-4420, at $z$ = 0.28, is an ideal candidate to represent the typical characteristics of haloes in terms of their length, intensity and location within their parent clusters, requiring in-depth investigation. Upon further investigation, we discovered that the peculiar system, RXCJJ0050.2-2733, at $z$ = 0.026, contains a unique radio halo surrounding its central cluster core, exhibiting similarities to RXCJ0232.2-4420 in terms of its dynamic cluster state, with South-West oriented substructures located at approximately 1 arcminute from the core, indicating the system may possess a quiet core but turbulent surroundings that potentially pump energy to the detected radio halo.

This paper provides an in-depth mathematical examination of the LMU architecture. Initially, the model's equation of state for the LMU cell level and training loss are derived, and it's shown that the LMU can achieve global convergence when optimized using gradient descent. Furthermore, the classification error of the LMU is analyzed and expressed as a function of the model's key non-linear parameters. This paper then investigates the asymptotic behavior of the LMU and identifies a characteristic learning phase transition of the LMU, where the model may encounter difficulty transitioning from an underfit to an overfit state due to vanishing gradients. To address this challenge, several strategies for mitigating this phenomenon in the LMU are presented, including data augmentation, model ensemble methods, and selective transfer of features learned during initial training stages. Finally, the efficacy of these techniques is verified through comprehensive numerical simulations. Our findings have the potential to accelerate the development and refinement of the LMU architecture, and contribute to informed design choices, enabling researchers to effectively utilize this type of model for their specific applications and achieve optimal performance. Language plays a vital role in a culture's fabric, deeply intertwined with human migration patterns. Investigating the migration dynamics through the naming game with migrating entities reveals how migration affects the distribution of languages. It has been discovered that migration significantly contributes to creating monolingual pockets within a population and breaks the symmetry of language distribution. The outcomes of our research affirm that ring-like migration patterns are optimal for achieving uniform language distribution. Additionally, our analysis indicates that a migration network's connectivity and language vocabulary size exert influence on each other, forming a symbiotic relationship. Lastly, our findings indicate that smaller languages are likely to become extinct over time. For further details, refer to the accompanying paper at arXiv:2203.05066. 

As an extension of our work, we analyzed the naming game with migrating entities in a migratory bird context. The migration dynamics of birds have long been studied due to the substantial impact they have on the distribution of species. Focusing on the naming game with bird species that change their names through migration reveals how migration affects the distribution of languages. Interestingly, our research discovered that migration introduces homogeneous and monolingual patches within a population. The key findings of our analysis are as follows: (i) a ring-like migration pattern is most effective in achieving uniform language distribution, (ii) there is a positive relationship between the complexity of migration network and the vocabulary size of the languages, (iii) smaller languages are likely to become extinct over time, and (iv) a migration network and language network co-adapt and evolve together. The outcomes of our research are such that they could potentially explain the distribution of species, the resurrection of local languages, global language co-adaptation phenomena, and may even provide insights into the origin of languages. Despite these achievements, they often struggle to achieve optimal convergence when the target function contains intricate details. By leveraging the properties of neural tangent kernels, we have investigated how PINNs train under a momentum-based stochastic gradient descent. Our findings indicate that incorporating momentum substantially diminishes the impact of spectral bias, leading to better convergence. Additionally, we discovered that using the Adam optimizer not only reduces spectral bias but also accelerates convergence. Our numerical experiments further demonstrate that wide-enough networks using stochastic gradient descent can still converge to optimal solutions, even when the target function contains high-frequency features, highlighting the importance of network width in achieving convergence. Lastly, we have observed from our numerical investigations that cross-validation can unreliable for determining the optimal kernel width of a NTK, given varying initial conditions and stochastic sampling. To resolve this issue, we have proposed using the L-curve method as a more reliable tool for estimating the NTK kernel width. These findings shed new light on the training dynamics of PINNs, shedding insight into their inherent limitations and the development of more effective training techniques. They also pave the way for further optimization of PINNs, enabling the creation of more robust and accurate neural networks. We examine a two-wave system in the interval (-1,1), where one wave absorbs energy and the other does not, with partial damping that mimics a viscoelastic material's behavior. Prior research showed that with damping throughout the entire domain, the system's energy decreases at a rate proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$. Using the frequency domain method in this paper, we demonstrate the system's behavior changes significantly due to the non-standard boundary conditions, specifically exhibiting damped behavior at an exponential rate for high frequencies. Consequently, we prove the system's behavior is like that of a purely resonant problem at high frequencies and low frequencies. With the help of a parameter split, we show the system can be rewritten as wave equations with homogeneous boundary conditions and exhibit nonhomogeneous boundary conditions in the large frequency limit. Consequently, we derive the rate of energy decrease as being proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$ under the condition that the system does not have a resonance. When considering the case where the system does have a resonance, we use a series of simple and efficient estimates to deduce the rate of energy decrease is proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Combining these estimates with the identity that conserves energy in the system allows us to derive the rate of energy decrease for the system as being proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. We apply our findings specifically to a case where the system does not have a resonance and the boundary conditions are $\partial u/\partial x= \alpha_0\partial^2u/\partial x^2$ at $x=-1$ and $x=1$, where $\alpha_0>0$ is a small number. We further derive the rate of energy decrease for this system as being proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$ and show the system does not have a resonance in this case. We also derive general bounds for the system's behavior that hold for all times and show the system does not have a resonance in the large-time limit. We derive the rate of energy decrease for the system as being proportional to $t^{-\frac{1}{4}}$. Recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have led to widespread success across various applications, yet deep RL methods struggle with two major limitations - their experiments frequently fail due to poor exploration, resulting in poorly trained value function approximators, and they often cannot adapt to novel tasks after initially mastering previous tasks. In order to overcome these limitations, researchers have started developing more robust experimental frameworks such as privileged information and multi-task reinforcement learning. We propose a novel model-based multi-task reinforcement learning approach that leverages an accurate dynamics model to enable off-policy transfer, effectively utilizing past experience from source tasks to facilitate learning in target tasks. Our proposed method exploits privileged information to empower the agent to simulate past experiences in new environments. We demonstrate through simulation results the ability of our method to perform successfully off-policy and adapt across diverse traffic scenarios. Additionally, we highlight the benefits of model-based RL methods in controlled autonomous driving environments, showing that they tend to perform better than model-free approaches. We also show through a fusion-based learning technique that it's possible to integrate data collected using model-based and model-free strategies to achieve better performance than either technique alone. Overall, our approach represents an important step forward in the development of reusable autonomous driving systems. Evaluation results confirm the practical applicability of our approach to real-world applications, as our code is available online at https://github.com/asharhamidi/mbRL_for_traffic_jams. Our actual driving simulations can be found here. Pre-trained models and data for the AToC benchmark are available at https://github.com/asharhamidi/mbRL_AToC. For privacy reasons, real driving data is stored encrypted. Blind Image deblurring attempts to estimate an image's point spread function and latent image given a observed blurred image. Advances in deep learning have enabled significant breakthroughs in this field, however the problem remains unresolved. We propose an innovative approach by transforming the deblurring problem into an optimal kernel selection process. This is achieved through a kernel mixture model with unknown kernel counts and shapes within a convex function space. Using the reparameterization trick from variational networks allows the mixture model parameters to be learned end-to-end. This new method, called VMVM, boasts two key advancements - both the kernel count and the convolutional filter matrix can be learned. Experiments demonstrate that this model surpasses the state-of-the-art in both single image and multiple image deblurring tasks. More specifically, it yields superior textural details in both the Textures10Evaluating database and the TASS benchmark for multiple image deblurring. Moreover, it significantly outperishes in the widely used real-world single image deblurring benchmark, YUVAL. Our source code can be found at https://github.com/Attenboros/VMVM. This work contributes substantially to the current state of blind image deblurring research. Furthermore, it provides an innovative solution for discovering and learning unseen or highly complex convolutional filters. This new technique may have a significant positive impact in various research fields where convolutional filters need to be learned. Finally, it can be applied in real-world scenarios where the database of point spread functions is insufficient. With further advancements and optimizations, it is expected to find applications in fields such as autonomous driving, real-time processing and video deblurring. Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances for software,
particularly vital in systems requiring safety and security assurances.
Hoare logic serves as a widely employed formal methodology for thoroughly
examining software adherence to specifications through precondition/postcondition
declarations. The improvement of semantic parsing methodologies and increasing
availability of computationally powerful systems make it feasible to automate
the specification interpretation process, making it possible to leverage automated
inferencing to identify specifications for software programs with observed
behaviors. This research outlines a formal framework for integrating automated proof
techniques with Hoare logic and demonstrates the approach's effectiveness on a real-world
target language by presenting a specification derivation tool for the JavaScript
language, which also includes a concurrent extension. The proposed method involves a
number of novel formal derivations for establishing the meaning of program statements,
as well as a formal connection between observed execution traces and Hoare logic-style
program specifications. The formal framework's limitations are also examined, which
relate to potential non-terminating executions and conflicting specifications. This
research appears to be the first demonstration of a formalization method for
automatically inferring Hoare-style specifications on a practical, widely used software
platform. The research also includes an examination of by-design limitations of the
proposed method in ensuring the non-reusable derivation of specifications. The outcome
of the approach is a practical tool for enabling specification-based development for
practitioners without extensive knowledge of formal methods. A practical case study
demonstrates its effectiveness in inferring specifications for high-stakes, safety-critical
software. The research data associated with this research paper is publicly accessible via
https://doi.org/10.6013/pondi-ml/1234.0. A corresponding implementation of the derived
specifications for verifying concurrency defects is accessible via
https://doi.org/10.6013/pondi-ml/1235. A public repository containing the research
implementation is available at https://doi.org/10.6013/pondi-ml/1236.

Recent studies utilizing neutron spin echo and nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, which examine linear transport properties, have yielded contrasting results when analyzing the impact of cholesterol on the bending modulus of lipid bilayers. This inconsistency arose despite earlier research employing solely equilibrium experiments, not linear transport properties, indicating that one may be misled by data from the latter. A general discussion highlights how this misunderstanding occurs, after which it's demonstrated that the neutron spin echo findings can be reinterpreted to be consistent with the prior equilibrium results, thereby resolving the disparity. Furthermore, in the context of nuclear magnetic resonance relaxation methods, there exists confusion over which modulus is being measured; an alternative interpretation is explored that doesn't conflict with the equilibrium experiment results. Ultimately, it's concluded that lipid bilayers exhibit an unusual characteristic where they can accommodate significant curvature fluctuations, and this is attributed to them functioning as exceptional solid membranes. This conclusion is also substantiated by further observations. Lastly, it's suggested that the neutron spin echo's sensitivity to short-wave fluctuations makes it a valuable tool for investigating the extreme rigidity of certain types of surfaces, which could have important implications for future research.

Researchers have developed uncertainty estimation methods for deep object detectors but encountered difficulties in applying them to tracking algorithms due to the increased demand for sequential data. A novel approach, known as TUNTRAC, has been developed that combines a high-performance object detector with a tracking algorithm to produce a Bayesian representation of targets in a specific area. By implementing this innovative technique, TUNTRAC achieves the ability to generate uncertainty metrics and target distributions for individual objects. Existing tracking systems that utilize deep neural networks for identification and the distribution of probability often fail to account for the detector's uncertainties, which can lead to decreased performance when combined. TUNTRAC's unique architecture allows the uncertainty metric to affect the tracking process, resulting in improved performance during target births, annihilations, and changes in appearance when the old detector model no longer accurately represents the target. Experimental evaluations using various datasets, including AT4K, CORE, and KITTI, demonstrate TUNTRAC's superior performance to current tracking systems that utilize deep neural networks. When compared to the uncertainty metric-only baseline, TUNTRAC produces an increased recall rate of around 10% while maintaining a low false positive rate. Automatic hippocampus segmentation on magnetic resonance imaging is a critical factor in diagnosing and treating neuropsychiatric disorders. Current deep learning-based methods primarily utilize data from patients with healthy or Alzheimer's disease. This paper proposes an innovative, data-efficient approach without the need for patient data. We employ contrast-enhanced, Dauphin-optimized 3DResNet models to create models for hippocampus and mesial temporal lobe segmentation. This approach demonstrates promising results both inside and outside its original dataset, indicating a high potential for use in clinical settings. Detailed experiments and analyses are conducted to understand the impact of different collections of training data on the overall segmentation accuracy. This research showcases the effectiveness of the proposed method in promoting more ethical data usage in medical imaging, particularly through the use of control subjects in MRI studies. We conduct these studies within a controlled environment using the SegMIMI dataset. Additional information regarding code and data is available on https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuclres.2022.102101. We scrutinize an experiment claiming to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by having three parties navigate a two-path interferometer with no pair of them using the same path simultaneously. Through an analysis based on weak values, we uncover inconsistencies in the description. By incorporating transversal modes and examining the emergence of correlations between path and traversal properties, we also investigate the rotational symmetry of the output pattern as an indicator of pairwise interactions. However, our analysis finds that the symmetry bears no evident connection to the probability of three particles exiting the interferometer together. We attribute the alleged demonstration of the quantum pigeonhole effect to an oversimplification of the output statistics rather than the inherent properties of the system in question. Our work utilizes the elastic nature of weak values to reveal previously unexplored aspects of the system, which might find practical applications in testing quantum theory's predictions. As an example, we show how weak measurements can enhance the symmetry of the output pattern even in a classical elastic system by manipulating the weights of three-pattern correlations. Additionally, we propose an alternative method for precisely calculating the probability of three particles exiting the interferometer together that leverages the elastic properties of path transformations, consistent with Clogni, Muntoni, and Bergholm's findings. Ultimately, our work suggests the feasibility of employing weak measurements in future attempts to showcase the quantum pigeonhole effect by harnessing nonlocal properties arising from entangled particle properties. The research, therefore, contributes to an improved understanding and realization of the quantum pigeonhole effect by harnessing the capabilities of elastic path transformations and weak measurements. Furthermore, our study indicates that the quantum nature of the pigeonhole effect can be effectively validated by studying the thermal properties of entangled particle properties. The research, therefore, proposes an innovative method for measuring the elastic characteristics of path transformations applicable to both classical and quantum contexts. By leveraging this phenomenon, our analysis suggests a new approach for measuring the coefficients of elastic particle transformations that might be implemented using interferometric or other suitable setups. We believe that the concepts explored in our study primarily rely on established methods and will not present significant technical difficulties in their implementation. Furthermore, our analysis primarily draws from existing theories and does not contain newly discovered data or findings reported at conferences or internal research meetings. As a final remark, our analysis emphasizes that the quantum pigeonhole effect by entangled properties presents a more feasible approach for demonstrating the effect compared to other possible methods.
