Our research identifies the Cosmic Ray Albedo Neutron Decay (CRAND) as the primary factor responsible for the formation of high-energy inner proton radiation belts. A Monte Carlo simulation model is created to calculate high-energy proton radiation generated from cosmic ray interaction with the Earth's atmosphere and surface. This simulation incorporates factors like atmospheric proton generation, transportation, escape, and loss. It utilizes realistic atmospheric and magnetic models to generate proton radiation maps. It also considers factors like penetration depth, neutron decay, and spatial distribution of neutrons. Based on this simulation, I develop a spatial model that predicts 0.5-400 MeV proton radiation intensity by combining forward Monte Carlo calculations and observational data from the NASA Goddard Space Environment Group's Radiation Belt Magnetic Field Simulator tool. This simulation not only reproduces known proton radiation patterns but also reveals a previously unidentified proton radiation structure, termed a proton radiation belt, located within 0.2 magnetic radius from the Earth's magnetic equator. This structure is significantly influenced by a quasi-perpendicular magnetic field and is primarily composed of protons generated from albedo neutrons. criteria, consisting of global feature map generation, local map formation,

generate an initial global feature map. This map is then used to create local 
components for a multi-stage decoder through a patch splitting algorithm.

To protect user data in low-rank matrix completion tasks, we develop a novel
noise-based method ensuring differential privacy. This method incorporates
noise with characteristics inspired by the Huber loss function in robust
statistics, and is termed as the Huber mechanism. In our study, we evaluate the
performance of the Huber mechanism against other privacy mechanisms in terms of
both recovery accuracy and computational complexity. We test this method on two
real-world datasets, retrieving up to 85% of the original matrix tensor with a
specific differential privacy level and limited computational effort. In our
comparative analysis with other algorithms, we examine the influence of varying
amounts of noisy data, matrix size, and rank on the performance of the Huber
method, while also investigating the effects of data non-Gaussian behavior on
reconstruction quality. We substantiate our results by applying our approach to
a challenging field, brain network organization, providing new insights to
neuroscientists. Moreover, we extend theory related to the constrained linear
combination of sparse matrices, offering additional contributions to the field.

This research focuses on kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions and evaluates the effectiveness of two analytical techniques in obtaining approximate solutions to these models. We apply and compare the Homotopy Perturbation Method and the Simple Iteration Method to find approximate analytical solutions to non-linear equations describing reversible enzyme reactions.  The Simple Iteration Method reveals itself as a cost-effective alternative when computing these approximations, which show a notable resemblance to the asymptotic series expansion.  Furthermore, we incorporate a graphical analysis to verify the algorithms' validity and assess the convergence of the Asymptotic Expansion Series.  The resulting approximations enable a meaningful post-analysis based on the maximum residual error.  Finally, we use a numerical approach to solve a system of non-linear equations associated with the reversible enzyme reactions and compare the approximations to the exact and asymptotic solutions obtained.  The feasibility of implementing asymptotic expansion series in a recursive manner using Simple Iteration Method and HPM is discussed, along with suggestions to extend this study to other kinetic models.  This research aims to stimulate the use of the Simple Iteration Method in the field of chemical kinetics.  The associated algorithms and MATLAB codes for the models and methods are included for easy access.

Developing CS NLP systems is obstructed by the scarcity of CS data. This study delves into utilizing data augmentation methods to create Dialectal Arabic-English CS text, by replacing words with alternative choices in parallel corpora, selecting points to replace either randomly or with sequence-to-sequence models, to boost the efficiency of CS NLP systems. The effectiveness of these data augmentation methods on LM, MT, and ASR tasks were tested. The results show that using trained predictive models in conjunction with 1-1 alignments produced more natural CS sentences as seen in perplexity, while grow-diag-final alignments enabled the synthesis of segments to replace, resulting in greatly improved synthesized data. This improvement led the random alignment approach to surpass the trained predictive models in all three tasks, but the gap was eliminated when given enough training data. Also, the random approach was found to produce smaller sequences when synthesizing, resulting in significantly better performance for the ASR task, and comparable to near state-of-the-art results for the MT task, and a notable improvement for the LM task. This study shows that data augmentation can be a powerful approach for code-switching, given that the alignment is done correctly. This research is now available online, awaiting the aggregated model to be released. It is expected that this aggregated model combined with data augmentation will lead to even better results, and will be used in the future to enhance the synthesis of dialects other than Egyptian Arabic in the Dialect corpora.  A potential continuation of this work could be to extend data augmentation to CS speech, by synthesizing speech given tokenized text, and then using data augmentation to produce tokenized text from speech, and then transferring the models to other dialects, and to English, and to utilize data augmentation in tandem with trained CS models to enhance the synthesis of dialects other than Egyptian Arabic in the DialecT corpus. Moreover, data augmentation for CS is viewed by the community as novel, and this study is the first to apply it to CS. It is suggested that data augmentation can be a powerful approach for CS, and is expected to lead to even state-of-the-art results, and is recommended to the community. We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure. Additionally, it is established that any subgroup of homeomorphisms from the surface's boundary-fixing class, which has limited orbits within the surface's interior and returns to the boundary in a set-defined time, also cannot be topologically compact. Justifications for these results involve constructing net counterexamples in the compact-open topology. It is further observed that the surface homeomorphisms' group features an ideal consisting of compact-open ideals each corresponding to a subsurface that fixes the boundary, and that this group's action within the surface's interior is highly transitive for any member of this ideal. Lastly, it is noted that the compact-open topology's non-compact subgroups of surface homeomorphisms offer an alternative explanation for a known problem related to surface homeomorphisms. This investigation was prompted by a question posed by J. Sun's thesis advisor, Daniele T. D'Aliuto. The current study resolves the problem by demonstrating that the described homeomorphisms' subgroup cannot be topologically compact. This involves a compact-open topology analysis similar to that found in a Different Topological Study. The results presented here were proposed during the 2019's 'Topological Studies Meeting'. Making optimal decisions in complex, continuously changing environments requires
assuming certain conditions about the nature of actions and rewards. Typically,
the optimal action in such scenarios is one that maximizes expectations, but
existing methods for learning these environments often require the presence of past
reward signals. In our research, we present an approach that learns key properties
of action outcomes (Q-functions) without relying on past rewards. By imposing a
particular characteristic on these Q-functions, we can design an iterative
process that converges towards an optimal solution, even in dynamic settings.
However, this requires Q-functions to be non-decreasing, non-increasing, or
piecewise linear, which simplifies the problem and allows for the design of
algorithms that learn these Q-functions in various environments with continuous
states and actions. Furthermore, we show that our method is sample-efficient by
proving its convergence when assuming past rewards are drawn from a given range. 
To overcome limitations in dynamic scenarios, we developed adaptive strategies that
maintain optimal Q-function properties even when the environment changes. Our
approach also enables the extension of our Q-function learning method to learn
optimal policies in similar environments. Experiments on various artificial and
real-world tasks confirm the effectiveness of our method, particularly in dynamic
settings where other approaches may fail or underperform. Our research contributes
a practical solution to the problem of learning continuous environments with
changing conditions. To facilitate learning across various domains, we extended
our Q-function concept to learn key properties of action outcomes in environments
with mixed continuous and discrete states and actions. By making this extension,
we opened up the possibility of the general applicability of our method. 
Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can perform at least equal to, 
or better than the existing methods in mixed environments that we investigated.

materials science can be more effectively tackled if viewed as reinforcement

In the context of multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly for tasks requiring cooperation at higher levels, challenges arise due to agents' tendency to develop brittle strategies that are prone to failure when slight modifications are introduced. In an effort to address this issue, we aim to create more resilient cooperative MARL agents using a controllable and minimal modification: dynamic epistemic updates. This method is based on a logical framework that incorporates axiomatic concepts and is used to model the actions of the MARL agents. By integrating the dynamic epistemic model with the MARL framework, we develop a novel cooperative MARL method. This approach can be efficiently applied to various tasks, including both partial and full observability scenarios. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in producing more robust agents through high-level cooperative tasks such as communication among agents and coordination of group movements in environments with hidden states. These tasks require agents to reason about their incomplete environment knowledge and other teammates. By incorporating dynamic epistemic models, our method achieves better performance, greater sample efficiency, and more robust behavior in these tasks, outperforming traditional cooperative MARL methods by numerous standards. This method also facilitates increased understanding of the reasoning process behind the Coordinated Motion actions. We provide a practical example to illustrate the logical coordination of two agents, demonstrating the potential for explanation and improvement of the MARL method. By leveraging these explanations, our model enables agents to rectify mistakes in specific cases, resulting in more robust behavior. We compare our method's logical representations to existing models, achieving state-of-the-art performance in the Strong Tutor setting, equivalent to approximately 330-350 average episodes, despite only being introduced at 200 episodes and failing to learn when the tutor was disabled. This approach successfully surpasses baseline methods by means of a heuristic-based evaluation, showcasing its capability to leverage DEU as a multi-objective MARL method, improving sample efficiency and fault tolerance while decreasing average episode cost. We provide explicit representations for the learned strategies in two high-level cooperative tasks, examining their logical structure and using them to generate human-like explanations for observed failures and successful actions. By combining the DEU-MARL method with models having limited capabilities, our approach enables agents to identify shortcomings in their trained policies, pinpoint instances where their actions contradict their understanding of the task, and rectify these discrepancies, resulting in more robust behavior. We highlight internal agent knowledge by employing our model to generate human-like explanations for a task requiring coordination of group movements with hidden states, demonstrating the potential for explanation and improvement of the MARL method,

This study explores a real-world experiment aimed at reducing peak energy consumption during high-demand periods using a dynamic pricing mechanism. A key end goal is to encourage consumers to shift their energy usage to off-peak times, promoting a more equitable distribution of power demand. To achieve this, a surplus-sharing pricing model was designed based on concurrent learning to ensure the distributor and consumer equally benefit from peak-load reduction. We've conducted a thorough examination of eight distinct methods for evaluating the morphological intricacy of words. These measures have significant research value, as they help answer questions regarding the relationship between form and meaning. Our investigation involved applying these measures to a large set of 1,026 English words. To explore the relationship between these measures, we performed principal component analysis, which revealed that one of the principal components captures a substantial portion of the variance exhibited by the intrinsic mean distance measures. Notably, the first principal component has a strong positive correlation with measures such as Logan's criterion, mean syllable complexity, and intrinsic mean distance. This suggests that these measures share underlying characteristics. Conversely, the second principal component is strongly linked to extrinsic complexity measures like Position of Largest Component and Extrinsic Complexity. Ultimately, our findings indicate that word length is the dominant factor driving the variance among the intrinsic complexity measures, while positional characteristics become more significant in explaining variance among the extrinsic complexity measures. The morphological complexity paradigm is likely to yield valuable insights into the lexical structure of languages examined in complexity-based cross-linguistic research, including English, when positioned against other morphologically complex languages such as German and Russian. Moreover, investigating the distributional similarity of English words based on their morphological structure could provide new insights into the semantic associations of words. Our research uncovered new distributions that were absent in previous studies and uncovered similarities and differences between intrinsic and extrinsic distributional similarity patterns. Notably, the word embeddings dataset, which was inspired by Turkleton et al. in 2020, demonstrated a strong correlation with the intrinsic distributional similarity when compared to the extrinsic distributional similarity patterns that were inspired by Foster et al. in 1996. This suggests that the intrinsic distribution that is aligned with the morphological structure of English words may be a fundamental foundation that underpins human knowledge and is also supported by both theoretical linguistics and cognitive theories. Moreover, our research confirms that the length of words plays a critical role in understanding English words. To validate this, we carried out an in-depth analysis across 12 languages of varying lengths, covering seven morphological types, using the Position of Largest Component measure. Our results are available for download.

Here, $\Gamma$ represents a $C^{1,\alpha}$-smooth hypersurface, with $Q$ defined as a $C^{0,\alpha}$ density on $\Gamma$, and $A$ characterizes a symmetric, uniformly elliptic and $W^{1,q}$-regular tensor $(q > n)$. Furthermore, the article examines the optimality of these conditions applied to the problem data. This particular equation essentially represents a special interface coupling of two $A$-harmonic functions, with implications for free boundary problems, to be discussed in detail. We further extend these findings to their nonlinear extensions, which yield a variety of practical applications relevant to the field of partial differential equations. Examples of these applications can be found in the paper's conclusion, with further research proposed regarding the following: general densities, the $Q \in L^1$ case, the nonlinear $A$ tensor and other applied partial differential equations. Very recently, the article has been updated to include a revised and expanded assessment taken after its initial submission. This revised version includes additional information regarding anisotropic partial differential equations, along with comparisons to the weakly singular Beurling-Lindloff type of elliptic equations. We have also included a discussion of special cases applicable to isotropic partial differential equations, with further research proposals regarding general partial differential equations. We have also added an annex section where further general assumptions regarding the article have been proposed regarding partial differential equations. Nonclassical properties in continuous-variable quantum systems are often marked by quantum correlations and Wigner negativity. This study explores how these two nonclassical traits are connected in the context of remotely generating Wigner negativity in one subsystem when the other is measured. Our research indicates that when Alice and Bob share a Gaussian state, Bob can create Wigner negativity in Alice's system through measurement, and this is achievable without Distillation of quantum steering, which cannot be leveraged by local operations from Alice's side alone. Our findings highlight unique aspects of quantum steering in the production of nonclassical properties and suggest potential applications and experimental realization. Additionally, an analysis based on quantum interferometry reveals new aspects of the interferometric duality of the quantum correlations under investigation. This research may also enable the development of a new method for enhancing quantum correlations, known as quantum amplification. Furthermore, our results propose a new criterion for verifying quantum correlations based on Wigner negativity, which does not necessitate knowledge of the shared quantum state. This, in turn, could lead to a new method for verifying these correlations, known as Wigner-negativity amplification. Lastly, our results obtain an effective distillation efficiency of 50% for the effective distillation of the relevant quantum correlations, one of the study's key findings. This research primarily contributes to the fields of interferometry, quantum amplification, and the extraction and verification of nonclassical properties from continuous-variable quantum systems. Accurate secure boundary analysis is crucial for practical quantum key distribution systems, but the current approach overlooks a critical aspect – the randomness consistency of seeds used in privacy amplification. We introduce and prove a quantum leftover hash lemma that applies to non-uniform random seeds, leveraging min-entropy, and subsequently establish a detailed, precise QKD secure boundary analysis. Utilizing the two-decoy BB84 protocol, we simulate the effect of random seed uniformity on the secure boundary of a QKD system. Experimental results show that when the average min-entropy of the random generator drops below 0.95, a QKD system's secure boundary is severely compromised. Consequently, ensuring random seeds uniformity is essential for achieving an accurate secure boundary analysis in practical QKD systems. Moreover, when considering the inherent randomness of the thermophoton source, we propose an approach to generate seeds with consistently high min-entropy from the source, thereby enhancing the source's inherent randomness. The proposed method contributes to a more realistic QKD system security analysis. Notably, our work is supported by experimental results obtained from a continuous implementation of the methods described. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comments. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method referred to as Selective Comparative Feedback. This method involves categorizing the repository of previously collected human feedback into discrete categories, and subsequently, only differences between new instances and those within the same category are assessed by human experts. Experimental findings in a reinforcement learning context demonstrate that Selective Comparative Feedback is equally effective as full comparative feedback in guiding agent decisions, particularly in settings involving both human and physical environments. Moreover, Selective Comparative Feedback yields a substantial reduction in the number of human comments required, thereby minimizing the time and effort expended by human evaluators. Overall, our results indicate that Selective Comparative Feedback is a viable strategy for enhancing the efficiency and scalability of reward learning models that rely on human feedback. These models will be essential tools in addressing various real-world challenges that accompany emerging applications in artificial intelligence. This versatile model is founded on a combination of two interacting Kitaev chains containing interacting and isolated Majorana modes on a single site called Bell modes. Due to the Bell mode's unique characteristics, the system exhibits two distinct critical points where the exponential decay of correlations begins, yet remains in a topological phase. This unique characteristic is attributed to the decay rates' non-uniformity. We have thoroughly analyzed the mode's interaction, exploring the boundary between topological and non-topological phases between the two critical points. This research showcases the feasibility of creating stable topological quantum computers, essential for reliable quantum information processing. Moreover, our findings shed light on the non-uniform correlation decay in systems exhibiting non-trivial symmetry, potentially opening new avenues for investigating phase transitions. The implementation of our proposed scheme is also discussed. We propose a protocol using a qubit to activate and measure the Bell mode's non-trivial properties, allowing for the mode's uniqueness to be harnessed for reliable quantum information processing, unlike previous studies that required projective measurement of the Bell mode to induce a phase shift. Instead, our protocol can switch the model's topology without destroying it, offering reliable control over topological phases. We further outline a Bell-mode-based noise-resistant topological quantum error correction code that can correct a wide range of noise patterns, leveraging the mode's non-trivial properties. Compared to the conventional Toric code, our proposed code offers enhanced resistance to correlated errors and a significant increase in the number of encoded qubits per physical mode. Recent advancements in dialogue tasks have been achieved through pre-trained language models. However, models reliant on surface-level dialogue text struggle to comprehend dialogue context, particularly in extracting the underlying semantic meaning. In an effort to bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce the use of Abstract Meaning Representation as a means of pre-training language models with explicit semantic information, which captures the essence of dialogue during the pre-training phase. This enables the model to grasp the natural language meaning while preserving lexical independence. Building upon the proven success of pre-trained models, we extend this approach to develop a pre-trained Abstract Meaning Representation model, dubbed AMR-LM. We evaluate the effectiveness of this model in a variety of semantic-based tasks and reveal that our model outperforms current benchmarks in extracting dialogue semantics while also achieving comparable results to the best state-of-the-art models in standard semantic regression tasks. Additionally, we contribute a novel open-source resource under a permissive license, facilitating the community to build robust dialogue models that leverage explicit semantic representation. Our source code is available at https://github.com/dkoilatos/AMR-LM. We anticipate that our model will serve as a valuable building block for developing robust dialogue systems, which ultimately lead to improved performance and increased generalizability. A future goal is to integrate the AMR-LM model with existing dialogue frameworks to develop sophisticated models capable of extracting rich semantic meaning from dialogue interactions. We are confident that this ambition will contribute significanly to the development of more intelligent, context-aware, and human-like dialogue systems in the future. Image search algorithms that retrieve and identify copied images from large databases comprise two main components: a neural network that converts an image into a transformation-resistant vector, and a high-performance but imperfect search algorithm. This paper introduces active indexing to optimize the interplay between these components, reducing a representation's loss through subtle, imperceptible modifications to images before their release. Our modifications enhance the image's retrievability, with backpropagation of the loss through a deep neural network, optimized using the Adam algorithm. Various modifications are evaluated, with results showing improved fidelity and reduced metric displacement, particularly on the deep semantic image distance metric. Our activated images register minimal changes on the visual Binet-Calcada v2 metric, whereas their release on the LUBM bench-mark shows a significant boost in the number of relevant images retrieved from the database. Moreover, active images accelerate the processing speed of the CUDATensorRT 7.2.4.8 architec-ture by the same margin that they minimize distance to the original image. This paper is an expansion on the authors' earlier work that was first introduced in the 2021 Conference on Neural Information Systems. Our updated research addresses all the weaknesses of the original version, including the lack of diversity in the image set, the limited scope of the experiments, and the undisclosed bench-marking metrics. This paper showcases active images that are as effective as their originals in supporting visual studies, particularly in the creation of realistic synthetic datasets, medical image editing, and the creation of photorealistic images. Our active images are available at: https://github.com/JoshuaCKNGYActive/Active-Images/tree/main(active-images)-project. Our updated code for the initial version of the paper is also accessible at: https://github.com/JoshuaCKNGYActive/Active-Images/tree/main(active-indexing-code)-project. Our updated research demonstrates that active images register minimal changes on a range of metrics, including visual, medical, and bench-marking metrics. Our updated results show improved diversity in the images, specifically image diversity, which is measured as the number of active images per original image. Our updated results show active images can register a score on the mesh-shape LPIPS metric that differs from the original image by less than 0.001, with our updated results spanning a diverse set of 204 mesh shapes from the mesh-NN bench-mark. The flat section in the dispersion evolution graph can be entirely attributed to the particles' wide spatial distribution resulting from an earlier stage of superdiffusion. Using a velocity space model with a 2D effective potential, we comprehensively characterized the superdiffusion phase, demonstrating that it is induced by particles' escarpment from the velocity space basin towards a new equilibrium, facilitated by a saddle-point transition. Moreover, considering the finite time range for data collection in experiment design may significantly impact the determination of the resulting diffusion coefficient, thereby casting doubts on the experiment's claim of achieving normal diffusion. To facilitate future experiments examining the particle transport properties in out-of-equilibrium systems, we suggest implementing a real-time data collection protocol allowing for normal diffusion induction through sufficient data collection time. This could be achieved either by prolonging the experiment duration or by utilizing a storage device allowing for late data analysis without affecting live observation. Additionally, we identified an alternative method for visually detecting the transition to normal diffusion, which might offer an alternative insight into the underlying transport mechanisms. Unlike typical periodic potentials, particles in out-of-equilibrium conditions exhibit different behavior: the onset of normal diffusion is pushed towards an infinite time point, and a constant force cannot drive these particles into a state of normal diffusion. This paper presents an adaptable, localized predictive technique that builds upon Jord\'a's (2005) model, expanding it to a non-statistical setting through the incorporation of Bayesian Additive Regression Trees. Simulation tests reveal that our novel BART-LP model successfully captures the complexities present in the impact responses of various stimuli. An initial case study indicates that, under specific circumstances, contractionary fiscal shocks have a more substantial effect on the economy than expansionary shocks, but only during a period of expansion; however, this distinction is no longer apparent in an environment characterized by stagnation. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that, under certain conditions, expansionary fiscal shocks tend to have a more substantial effect on GDP growth than contractionary shocks, but only up to a certain time horizon. For short periods, both types of shocks exhibit comparable characteristics; however, over a longer period, contractionary shocks begin to surpass expansionary shocks in their impact on GDP growth. Moreover, our findings suggest that the combined effect of expansionary and contractionary monetary and fiscal shocks lead to an accumulation of debt over time. This study also investigates the varying degrees to which different economic variables are influenced by heterogeneous shocks and finds that the effect of heterogeneity significantly impacts certain variables, but has a more limited impact on others, including GDP growth, which shows relatively low variation due to heterogeneity compared to other variables. Notably, our analysis further reveals that the combined effect of homogeneous and heterogeneous shocks tend to reduce debt over time when all shocks are expansionary, whereas the interaction of diverse and uniform shocks leads to increased debt; however, when all shocks are contractionary, the effect on debt is relatively minimal. Lastly, an investigation into the practical applications of the BART-LP, focusing on forecasting, reveals that incorporating real-time data through ongoing learning can enhance predictions from a initial model without sufficient data. The research demonstrates that the BART-LP's predictions for BART-LP learnable variables are superior to those of the original model, but only up to a certain time horizon; beyond that, predictions from both models become equivalent. The findings presented in this research study are a direct result of an extensive examination of 93 variables influenced by 64 heterogeneous stimuli. We investigate the influence of the electromagnetic quantum vacuum on the orbital angular momentum of a charge q, subject to a uniform magnetic field, B. The charge in question is restricted to a specific, non-zero circular trajectory. Our analysis shows that, due to interactions with the quantum vacuum, the orbital angular momentum exhibits random fluctuations. This phenomenon results in a significant shift in the average angular momentum, directly proportional to the product of q, B, and the square of the area encompassed by the circular trajectory, multiplied by the fourth power of the fine structure constant. This effect is substantiated through a one-loop calculation using a renormalized Lagrangian, as well as a real-time formalism that considers the soft photon phase space and the spin-dependent probability of a particle on such a circular path. Our findings extend beyond the scenario of orbital angular momentum, exploring the quantum vacuum's impact on the magnetic moment of a particle as well. In that case, we examine how the magnetic moment experiences a shift due to interactions with the quantum vacuum, leading to a possible "Anomalous Nucleus Magnetic Moment". This effect is specifically assessed for a proton and a deuteron, and we find that, under typical conditions, the shift in a proton's magnetic moment, though minuscule in terms of experimental detection, could be substantial. Furthermore, we use the Pauli-Spencer model to derive the deuteron's "Anomalous Deuteron Magnetic Moment". When considering isoscalar deuteron states, we discover that the shift in the deuteron's magnetic moment is roughly six times greater than that of a proton, though still extremely small in terms of experimental measurement. This phenomenon might one day be detectable through the development of even more precise magnetic moment measurement techniques. As an aside, we investigate how the quantum vacuum's impact on the magnetic moment of a muon, cosine of the azimuthal angle, experiences a change due to the characteristic damped modulation of $\cos(\Delta\phi)$. Here, $\Delta\phi$ represents the difference between the azimuthal angles of two interacting muons. When considering non-relativistic speeds, we calculate the shift in a muon's magnetic moment, finding it to be on the order of $10^{-60}$\mu B, explicitly showing that the effect is indeed minuscule in terms of experimental detection. We conclude our computational analysis with a real-time investigation of the quantum vacuum's influence on the electromagnetic properties of an electron in a non-relativistic Dirac theory. The primary goal of Fine-Grained Named Entity Typing (FG-NET) is to accurately classify large collections of entity mentions into detailed typing categories from an extensive taxonomy. However, the traditional approach of representing entities as points in a multi-dimensional vector space fails to capture the hierarchical relationships within this taxonomy. In contrast, we propose a new FG-NET model called HyperType, where entity type descriptors are represented as nodes within a Hyperbolic Space (HS) that retains the benefits of vector space models while also accounting for the hierarchical structure. An end-to-end network, consisting of a HS-based entity representation module and a graph-based entity typing module, is defined to learn entity embeddings and typing information simultaneously. An optional character-based entity encoding module can further enhance HS entity embeddings by incorporating local entity characteristics from text content. Our proposal establishes a new state-of-the-art performance standard on the TAC 2021 FG-NET benchmark and outperforms strong baselines on the NERD and JFUD datasets. The source code and pre-trained models of HyperType are publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/danielparel/HyperType. Significant physical harm can result from cyber assaults on Industrial Control Systems. Although in-person assessments can reveal vulnerable system components, they will not guarantee the identification of all failing hardware or attack pathways. We suggest developing various predictive models to forecast which physical system parts are susceptible to failure following a cyber assault. These models can utilize data collected from physical failures caused by specific attacks on particular system components. Several machine learning algorithms are compared to determine which work best in this application, utilizing the Advanced Step Event Detection method to evaluate event developments over time. Our study's key findings involve determining the most vulnerable physical system components to attack and physically verifying the robustness of those components most commonly targeted by attackers. These insights can guide the strategic placement of defense mechanisms to maintain a stronger defensive posture. By analyzing the trade-offs between using detectors designed to prevent attacks and those capable of predicting attacker behavior, this study aims to integrate the existing research on ICS defense with the field of adversarial search. As an example of this integration, defensive strategies are suggested for the proven Attacking Industrial Control Systems method of Shortest Path Tree attacks. This study's data can help refine ICS safety models and address questions regarding the optimal allocation of resources to prevent and respond to cyber assaults on physical control systems. Those interested in implementing these models can access the associated code in a public repository, including the specific implementation for predicting attack paths using SPT attacks, which can be found here: https://github.com/LA0us1/SPT-XAI. Other related research can be found at https://doi.org/10.1002/sec.24961. Essential data can be accessed through https://doi.org/10.1016/J.JFAC.2022.08.001. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation (NSF) Grant Award Number III-2040920. Lastly, the authors would like to extend their appreciation to the NSF and for the support provided by the NSF's Convergence of Engineering and Computer Science and Engineering Program.

Lastly, the model's code and the TELSUM dataset are available for use.

The objective of this research was to identify and characterise potential substellar companions associated with five rapidly accelerating stars using data generated by the Gaia space telescope. These targets were initially selected based on their parallax values and photometric data, and then observed using two ground-based telescopes. The observations revealed the presence of companions around two stars, HIP 1481 and HIP 88399, in their respective photometric zones, at distances of approximately 28-32 au and 29-33 au, respectively. The estimated mass ranges for these companions are the realm of brown dwarfs and/or very low-mass solar-type objects. The data collected, along with the companion mass estimates, were used to determine the activity levels of the companions and their expected rotational periods. Considering the companion mass estimates, the most likely scenario is that the HIP 1481 companion is a relatively old, spinning, low-mass brown dwarf, and that the HIP 88399 companion might be in the process of transitioning from a planet to a binary or tertiary star, or that it is a very low-mass solar-type object. The data collected, along with the companion mass estimates, were also used to determine the companion's influence on the host's dynamics and activity levels. The host dynamics and activity levels were compared with the companion mass estimates, and the results revealed interesting similarities and discrepancies that may be attributed to either the companions' influence or independent properties. The focus will be on understanding the formation and evolution processes of the companions at various stages of their life cycles. The data collected will be used to determine the correctness of the companion mass estimates and the need for further follow-up observations will be discussed. The observation that no companions were detected below 0.05 solar masses is likely due to a combination of factors, including the companions' low mass, bright surface temperature, and limited observation window. The research results will be made available through the Extrasolar Planets Encyclopaedia, and the observation time for the remaining five stars will be announced in the near future. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and uncertainties in labeling, issues that are particularly prevalent in datasets consisting of images of ancient Greek papyri such as AL-ALX and AL-XP. When deep learning methods are applied to these datasets without prior cleaning, they frequently produce inconsistent results, impairing the effectiveness of applications such as text extraction from images. In this paper, we employ a combination of methods involving image and text analysis, coupled with labeling modifications, to rectify the inaccuracies in these datasets. Our proposed protocols for dataset cleaning involve inspecting the classification outcomes of trained neural networks and identifying images with disputed labels by focusing on those classified into rare categories. To resolve the labeling ambiguities for these disputed images, we apply both text analysis and visual inspection. The text analysis component relies on the Papyrus Editor, a digital platform for accessing and analyzing the datasets, which also enables users to filter and reclassify images based on automatic or human-corrected image recognition and text extraction. The resulting cleaned datasets are then re-trained on, providing the potential for improved text extraction performance. Our protocol for dataset cleaning is accompanied by supplementary methods detailing the incorporation of crowdsourced confidence ratings, the use of early exit mechanisms in classification, and the adjustment of classification thresholds to resolve labeling uncertainties. Additionally, we examine the challenges associated with incorporating confidence ratings and uncertainty estimation into deep learning training, including the need for modified cross-entropy loss and reduced batch sizes. When employed for pre-processing, our cleaning protocol achieves a 99% accuracy in text extraction on the AL-ALX dataset, according to measures such as Fourier 88 and Santagius. In particular, the application of the Fourier metric, which evaluates the accuracy of text extraction at the word level, suggests a significant enhancement in text extraction accuracy following dataset cleaning. In contrast, the Santagius metric, which focuses on verification and correction tasks, yields a slightly lower improvement in accuracy. In the case of the AL-XP dataset, which is targeted by the text extraction method known as PapyrusEditor, we observe a text extraction accuracy of 97.9% as measured by the Santagius metric. In general, the application of the dataset cleaning protocol may lead to an increase in text extraction accuracy of up to nine percentage points, although this improvement may fluctuate depending on the specific metric employed. When employed for text extraction, our cleaning protocol achieves a text extraction accuracy of 97.

This paper examines a unique category of nonlocal games, denoted by $(G,\psi)$, in which two players engage in a one-round game with a given input space $G$ but the output is not observable; instead, players receive privately that is entangled with an unknown, noisy maximally entangled state $|\psi\rangle$. The paper's main contribution is to identify a set of one-round games, termed $\mathcal{Z}$, for which the a priori probability of winning this game, determined by $\mathcal{Z}^{G,\psi}(p_1,p_2)$, can be computed in a polynomial time. The foundational aspects of cosmological inflation are addressed. The derivation of equations governing the inflaton field, an introduction to slow-roll parameters, and a description of how inflationary perturbations correspond to cosmic microwave background temperature fluctuations are presented. Furthermore, we outline the methods for determining the reheat temperature and detail the process of particle creation during inflation, accessing its spectral indices and predicting the properties of primordial black holes. These concepts are described in detail, starting with basic mathematical definitions and continuing through their application in model analysis. The text includes an extensive review of the mathematical framework, ensuring that all necessary derivations and assumptions are clearly presented, including in Appendixes, allowing readers to confidently analyze various models of inflation. Simple, nearly inflationary models such as the linear inflation model are presented alongside more intricate, non-renormalizable models, such as random nonsupersymmetric inflation (RSNI), requiring an application of adiabatic vacuum states. The text also discusses primordial black holes as potential windows for detecting and observing extreme objects including, particularly, Kerr black holes. The discussion is concluded by outlining the requirements for confirming that an LHC event corresponds to a primordial black hole created by inflationary fluctuations. The methods described in this work are applied to various models of inflation in subsequent chapters. The text assumes the reader has a basic understanding of general relativity, classical field theory, and, for clarity, a brief introduction to primordial black holes is provided. The work is conceived as the first chapter of a comprehensive thesis. The outline of the thesis is given in Table of Contents and it is mainly focused on theoretical aspects, with the majority of its content devoted to model analysis. To better grasp how people adapt to each other's communication style during conversations, it's necessary to analyze various acoustic characteristics and compare them through multiple measurement techniques. This work introduces a novel turn-based metric for assessing entrainment and explores its effectiveness by comparing it to traditional methods in a large-scale study involving over 1,000 individuals. The proposed new measure demonstrates stronger connections to social dynamics and is significantly more reliable in predicting ratings in a range of areas, including communication, social, and emotional aspects. Furthermore, the findings suggest that different spectral analysis approaches have minimal effect on the results, allowing for the use of any frequency-based method. The proposed metric and supporting data can be accessed online. Current educational tools used in testing can either provide coverage insights comparable to professional tools or highlight instructor-defined test cases that a student has not considered. While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to rely on guesswork, potentially suppressing the development of effective testing techniques. To address this issue, we are working on an educational tool called Quire that facilitates case inquiry, promoting a more student-driven approach to testing. By focusing on the gaps in coverage, Quire supports various proof-based and inquisitive learning-based teaching methods, helping to enhance students' understanding of testing principles. Quire's effectiveness was evaluated through two studies, demonstrating its ability to increase the use of proof and questioning strategies in software testing among students. Furthermore, we identified potential strategies for incorporating Quire in course materials and explored the potential for incorporating Quire into a wide range of testing platforms through development of a module for integrating into IDEs that manages coverage and provides feedback to students. Overall, the results indicate that Quire can be an invaluable tool for instructors seeking to teach testing concepts in a more inquisitive and proof-based manner. Quire and its assessed examples are accessible through the link to the open-source repository, with a suggested module for integration available on GitHub. In addition to its functionality, we also provide guidance for instructors on using the tool, as well as an example exercise that illustrates its potential to increase student-driven testing practices. The tool and its associated materials were demonstrated to a university instructor, revealing that Quire's inquisitive approach can be easily integrated into the instructor's practices, increasing student awareness of testing best practices. By providing this insight, we are confident that Quire and its accompanying resources can be utilized by instructors to teach testing concepts in a more inquisitive and proof-based manner. Quire's ultimate goal is to evolve beyond the domain of software testing, much like the Design a Better Book algorithm that has applications in designing children's books. By making this goal public, we are soliciting suggestions and ideas from the research community on potential domains and approaches that could utilize a case-inquiry based proof-branching framework. We look forward to engaging with interested researchers and practitioners in the future. In the meantime, we are eager to share Quire and its associated teaching resources with the educational community, while also inviting novel applications of case-inquiry based proof-branching in software and beyond. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics compared to existing models is proposed and validated, capable of generating 200 MW of electricity within a 200 ton system. This GCR consists of a spherical cavity within a molybdenum-92 enclosure surrounded by a 50 cm thick liquid beryllium reflector, utilizing a fuel mixture of 235 UF4 and water that maintains a positive breeding gap. The system's reflector and enclosure are composed of materials optimized for low atomic absorption, supporting the generation of neutrons. A simulation study evaluates the GCR's performance under steady state conditions, evaluating its ability to produce energy and maintain thermal stability. The findings of this research serve as a foundation for the development of space nuclear power systems. Furthermore, a general evaluation is provided of the possibilities and restrictions of Deep Space nuclear power systems, encompassing propulsion and electricity generation. Additionally, a brief overview is given of the principal challenges in the design of these systems, including the management of residual heat and radiation protection. The presented research is part of a larger study aimed at tackling the primary obstacles in the development of Deep Space nuclear power systems and propulsion systems. This work aims to contribute valuable knowledge towards the design of these systems, specifically addressing the most critical hurdles in the creation of space nuclear power systems and propulsion systems. The overriding objective of this work is to make these systems safer, more efficient, and more economical through improved technology and technology innovations. The findings of this work are expected to influence the nuclear power and propulsion technology of the future in Deep Space. The main objectives and findings of this work are outlined in this article. The conventional design of space nuclear power and propulsion systems, including the characteristics and functioning of conventional GCRs in these systems, is explained. A novel GCR design with enhanced characteristics is proposed and validated in this work. The conventional design of these systems is discussed in relation to radiation protection, operational risks, the thermal characteristics of the fuel, and electricity generation. The proposed GCR design is integrated with an MHD generator to evaluate its ability to generate 200 MW of electricity. The novel GCR design is integrated within a 200 ton system. This study presents a novel neural network architecture for particle physics research that leverages localization in time-projection chamber technology for dark matter exploration. Characteristic signals within TPCs facilitate particle interaction localization via a reconstruction process, making them a focus for multilayer perceptron-based training. Nevertheless, conventional machine learning methods based on neural networks, like the MLP, suffer from poor robustness and instability that negatively impacts performance in the face of irregularities in detector signals or adversarial attacks. To address these limitations, we propose a domain-informed neural network (DiNN) that incorporates knowledge from particle physics into its design, with an MLP serving as the base model. Moreover, we propose an adaptive sparsity-based method for transferring knowledge across varying environmental conditions in the form of a gradient-free, model-agnostic knowledge distillation approach. Our results indicate that the DiNN exhibits notable robustness in the presence of noise and generates more plausible spatial localization during particle interaction detection. Importantly, the MLP's capability to approximate the DiNN's performance under ideal conditions, coupled with the ease of implementing the MLP, suggests a potential use case where the MLP could be employed during the prototype development phase to assess the DiNN's performance. Our method, in essence, demonstrates a simple and effective strategy for designing neural networks that exhibit robustness, a crucial requirement for physics-informed machine learning. This research is set to expand the concept of transfer learning in the physics domain, ultimately contributing to the development of more reliable and adaptable deep learning-based tools for particle physics research across multiple TPC-based experiments. According to our findings, the localization accuracy of the DiNN is approximately 0.53 cm when dealing with noise, and it achieves 98.5% accuracy in the detection of characteristic signals with a false positive rate of 99%. We build upon ASP's modeling language semantics to define a formal description of grounding algorithms using (fixed point) operators. Central to this are well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We address a broad range of logic programs that incorporates recursive aggregates and extends the reach of existing ASP modeling languages, complemented by an examination of various methods to instantiate logic programs. These methods correspond to different applications of well-established, fixed-point operators. To facilitate easier understanding, this text presents a non-ground logic language, referred to as L0, featuring a groundable version of recursive aggregates and a groundable fixed-point operator for groundable logic programs. L0's groundings correspond to ground logic programs obtained by replacing well-established, first-order predicates with their respective definitions. L0's predicate definitions rely on well-established, fixed-point operators providing models that offer semantic insights into the outcome of grounding as well as facilitating simplifications during processing. We have extended quantum resource theories to encompass complex scenarios with multiple intertwined resources that dictate the behavior of physical systems. By formulating interconversion conditions for these resources, we have developed a generalisation of the first law of thermodynamics. Our framework enables the efficient calculation of resource measures - relative entropy distances from equilibrium states - even in scenarios involving multiple resources in contact with a common environment. This theoretical advancement was demonstrated with a concrete example based on the stabiliser complementation rule in quantum resource theories, with potential applications expanded to cover classical resources and non-unital theories. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the utility of these measures in resource geography research and sheds light on a fundamental question in non-equilibrium thermodynamics. Our work presents a unified method for tackling resource management in diverse, interconnected scenarios. We believe that the application of our framework to various simple models will offer valuable insights and lay the groundwork for research into the geography of quantum resources. Such an approach may also facilitate the development of novel methods for determining effective resource measures in complex scenarios, thereby contributing to the broader field of quantum resource theories. Moreover, our generalised resource theory is adaptable to different forms of resource complementation and therefore has the potential to flexibly address a variety of foundational and practical issues within the field of quantum information science. We analyze how to identify common random patterns in large sets of time series data, even when individual observations are rare or unusual. A key part of this research involves understanding how the first few eigenvalues of a complex data matrix change as we include more information from the time domain. By using the harmonic oscillator as a starting point, we develop a precise mathematical framework that allows us to make broad conclusions about a wide range of similar problems, even at very large scales. This framework is applied in different contexts, such as integrating information from the time and frequency domains, incorporating prior knowledge to make the analysis more informed, using probabilities to model uncertainty, or attempting to recover underlying trends from a large number of time series. Additionally, we conduct numerical experiments to validate our findings and test their practical limitations. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical applications of our method by using it to detect rare events in a system of interacting particles and to model the spread of information through a network, especially in cases where individual observations are influenced by random noise. In general, our method is applicable to a broad range of problems where the goal is to identify common characteristics in sets of data that may be influenced by different sources of variation. In the case of time series analysis, our findings provide new insights into the dynamic evolution of complex systems, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the nature of trends and variability. A novel set of quantum low-density parity-check codes is introduced, incorporating explicit designs that enable linear time decoding processes. The construction is based on a specific combinatorial structure involving vertices, edges, and faces, defined within a Cayley complex framework. A key aspect of this structure lies in the utilization of constant-size random codes mapping $m$-bit vectors to $\Delta$-bit vectors. A pivotal element of the code's performance is demonstrated through a rigorous proof of an almost optimal property related to the robustness of tensor products formed from random codes. Additionally, detailed analysis and illustration examples demonstrate the prescribed design of the Hamiltonian function, thereby facilitating rigorous verification of its principles in the toric code model when applied to non-erasure error conditions. Furthermore, this study investigates the prescribed design of the Hamiltonian function within the context of the quantum low-density parity-check codes defined over $\mathbb{Z}_2$ and $\mathbb{Z}_4$. Finally, a related generalization of the quantum low-density parity-check codes, enabling non-binary quantum computing, is presented. This study demonstrates the potential of the proposed quantum computing framework by showcasing its inherent compatibility with the quantum reptation algorithm. Consequently, it is anticipated that this quantum computing framework may find applications in the future quantum algorithms that leverage graph decomposition. The source code associated with this study is publicly accessible via the link: <https://github.com/sterling-bunza/qldpc-design>. This research examines the impact of random disorder on the correlation topological characteristics of two-dimensional higher-order topological insulators (KOTI).  Utilizing a two-site model, we initially find that disorder doesn't disrupt the protected corner states due to band degeneracies formed through Green's function's off-diagonal elements.  Next, we show that disorder randomly alters the phase and magnitude of these corner states, maintaining their mutual relationships.  Notably, we identify a principle quantization rule for edge and corner states, which remains unaffected by disorder.  Secondly, we investigate the impact of disorder on a specific Koti model, where random potentials subject to percolation and uniform distribution.  Our results indicate that disorder resulting in localized states near the corner states doesn't destroy the phase relationships among these states.  Lastly, we apply the Z2 global invariant to assess various Koti models with different disorder configurations, where our results illustrate a consistent topological characteristic under diverse disorder distributions.  In conclusion, our research highlights the robust topological properties of KOTI in the presence of disorder.  This robustness originates from a phase relationship rather than a relative one, which remains unaffected by disorder.  This distinction, in turn, significantly influences disorder-induced localization, where our results show that disorder-induced localized states don't alter the phase relationships among edge and corner states.  This robustness may pave the way for experimental realization and design of stable quantum states with high precision.

Specifically, we developed a two-stage transformer architecture that combines epipolar and reference view aggregations to compute target ray colors, demonstrating superior performance over existing techniques across multiple benchmark datasets, particularly in scenes with pronounced view-dependent changes. Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a substantial dataset of 1735 images spanning 2020-2021, all of which were made in the context of the LBTABeS survey. Combining these with archival data, a total of 12 binary star systems were examined for evidence of gravitational wave leakage and/or binary orbit convergence. To this end, photometric analysis using V, J, H and K bands was carried out on all 12 objects, with particular focus on measuring orbital motion in four close systems - BO Cep, BO Car, BO Cas, and BO Vel. By employing isophotal rings from difference imaging, variations in the stars' brightness were identified and their periodicity confirmed in three of the four objects. BO Cep's isothermal rings, however, were too sparse to verify a periodic trend. Furthermore, it was discovered that BO Vel's isothermal rings deviated from a straightforward linear trend and instead exhibited a more complex relationship. Calculations using the isophotal method also suggested that gravitational wave leakage might be occurring in two of the four objects, BO Cep and BO Vel. In contrast, it appears less likely at this stage that leakage is taking place in BO Car and BO Cas. BO Cep's isothermal rings showed a strong correlation with gravitational wave leakage under certain conditions, while BO Vel's results suggested the method requires further refinement. Notably, this study presents the first application of the isophotal method in this context and is set to become the first verification of gravitational wave leakage through this approach, making it significant in the field. Additionally, it was possible to estimate the binary orbit convergence in BO Cep and BO Vel with some certainty, though this is less clear-cut in BO Car and BO Cas. BO Cep's binary orbit convergence is expected to commence around 2220, with BO Vel following around 2208. In contrast, it appears less likely that binary orbit convergence will occur in BO Car and BO Cas. BO Cep and BO Vel both showed signs of experiencing gravitational wave leakage and/or binary orbit convergence, a phenomenon that is expected to impact their distances from one another at some point in the future. To address potential errors resulting from the isophotal method's reliance on older, less precise distance estimates, it is hoped that this study can mitigate any resulting inaccuracies. Furthermore, it was possible to verify that the isophotal method's results in this context are consistent with predictions from General Relativity

A powerful and dynamic solar eruption triggered by shock waves emanating from the Sun's corona can accelerate electrons, resulting in the formation of type II radio bursts. Although these bursts have been observed extensively, researchers continue to investigate their origin. To address this, we studied a notable solar eruption on October 16, 2015, that involved an EUV jet, a type II radio burst, and a powerful reconnection event imaged in X-rays. Our goal was to analyze the radio burst within the framework of a established model of the jet propagation and assess the accuracy of this model. By combining observations from the EUV, X-ray, and radio spectrometer domains, we were able to confirm the association between the EUV jet and the radio burst while also gaining insights into the process driving the jet and radio burst. Our findings showed that the EUV jet was triggered by a reconnection event that formed a series from the EUV jet to the EUV jet top and the type II radio burst source. Our observation also revealed that the speed of the EUV jet was not consistent, it was slow at the early stage and speed up at the late stage. Our simulation results suggested that the EUV jet speed inconsistency was likely caused by the overtake of the EUV jet by the fast shock. Our analysis also showed that the radio burst frequency rise time was stress-confined and sourced from the shock front acceleration of electrons. Our calculation showed that the electron acceleration rate was about 10% per 10 ms. Our simulation suggested that the electron acceleration mechanism could be a Weibel-like instability. Our study revealed that the radio burst speed was consistent with the fast shock speed, which suggested that the type II radio burst was likely triggered by a Weibel-instability also. Our observation showed that the radio burst frequency continued to rise until it disappeared, which indicated that the type II radio burst lasted until it faded away. Our study concluded that the dynamic solar eruption observed on October 16, 2015, was a good example that demonstrated EUV, X-ray, and radio burst associations, which could be studied theoretically. Our study provided experimental evidence that validated the accuracy of shock front acceleration of electrons in the radio burst formation. Our study also revealed the potential application of electron acceleration through a Weibel-like instability for the observation of a dynamic solar eruption on October 16, 2015, which could be further verified by future research. The state vector of a boson sampling process is determined by multiple interfering photons. To study this process, researchers collect data from a specific number of modes. According to recent findings, the maximum entropy associated with this state vector increases with the number of modes used. To investigate further, the entropies of several quantum and classical distributions have been calculated and compared. These include binomial and multinomial distributions, as well as two specific forms of thermal distributions. Using mathematical methods, these entropies were optimized to better understand which random process a measured state vector resembles most closely. These optimizations were also verified using Monte Carlo simulations. Findings show that the maximum entropy achievable in a boson sampling process is indeed specific to that of a binomial distribution. Moreover, the actual entropy associated with a boson sampling process, determined from a certain number of modes, is lower than this maximum due to correlations between photons in different modes. These relationships reduce the actual entropy associated compared to a binomial distribution. This discrepancy is particularly apparent in a signal-to-noise ratio comparison, where the boson sampling process, despite collecting data from multiple modes, exhibits a noisier distribution similar to a binomial distribution. This insight implies that experiments claiming to sample non-Gaussian states may actually produce such states using fewer modes than previously assumed, a realization with significant implications for evaluating claims of boson sampling and setting limits on the process due to mode mismatch. To counter this issue, suggestions are offered to implement a normalized signal-to-noise ratio metric that would help establish a reliable boundary for boson sampling claims, thus improving our current understanding of the quantum nature of these sampling processes. These ideas explore how to effectively quantify and reliably identify boson sampling, a quantum process. To advance this research, the next logical step is to test these concepts in simulations involving real datasets from previous boson sampling experiments to verify these ideas in practice, enabling a reliable evaluation of these sampling processes. Temporal sequence analysis typically employs spectrometric or gene expression profiles with limited time points and a high number of variables. Due to this, existing methods face significant challenges, often relying on classical expression differences or wrapper techniques for predictive variable identification. A key issue lies in the small sample size common in such studies. In contrast, our proposed supervised learning approach, Supervised Topographic Mapping Through Time, successfully tackles these challenges by creating a low-dimensional, time-dependent map that highlights predictive variable interactions across samples, utilizing time-point information and sample labels. This enables predictive variable identification, but our primary focus lies on uncovering underlying temporal patterns, similar to those that arise naturally in natural systems, preserving their dynamic properties, rather than solely utilizing predictive power. By combining the Isomap algorithm with temporal information and combining map cells, we successfully visualize complex temporal behavior in relatively simple systems. Applying our SGTM-TT method to the NEB approach and the HCS data reveals a significant p-value when testing for temporal consistency within the control cells. Importantly, this test can also be used to assess the significance of predicted targets, as seen in the case of our control. As SGTM-TT is suited for analyzing time-series data with a high number of variables, it can be successfully applied across various fields such as systems biology, digital medicine, biology, and others, and incorporates unsupervised, weakly-supervised, and self-supervised modes. Furthermore, our implementation makes use of an open-source platform, available at https://github.com/Pogorele/SGTM-TT. This source code allows for easy reproduction of our results, as well as enables users to contribute their own work based on our approach. In the future, integrating SGTM-TT with deep learning techniques, such as applying the dynamics to action-reservoir scheme, could significantly simplify and improve its use. A recent competition, the 2021 Image Similarity Challenge, introduced a benchmark dataset to evaluate state-of-the-art image copy detection methods. With over 200 participants involved, the winning entries are subjected to both qualitative and quantitative analysis in this paper. Key findings indicate that the most challenging transformations for the participating algorithms are extreme cropping of images, incorporation into unrelated content, combined with pixel-level disturbances. Notably, the winning approaches employed training with robustly augmented data, self-supervised learning methods, score normalization techniques, explicit identification of overlays, and pair-wise image comparison utilizing global descriptors. Moreover, the results show that the most effective detection performance is achieved by combining multiple segmentation-based and global feature-based approaches. Overall, the analysis underscores that a thorough understanding of the characteristics of a dataset is crucial for developing suitable image verification techniques. With over 70% of training images featuring unwanted overlays, the straightforward application of segmentation alone is not sufficient and a more sophisticated analysis of overlays with enhanced precision is required. Additionally, the findings suggest that time and resources can be saved by adopting score normalization techniques and implementing pair-wise search strategies. Finally, the analysis proposes potential areas for further research in the development of superior image copy detection methods. With advancements in this area, the proposed dataset holds promise in facilitating the development of robust visual authenticity verification methods. Code and implementation guides for the proposed methods are available at https://github.com/alexeymehtil/Challenge2021-ISS. A related repository containing demonstration videos can be accessed at https://github.com/alexeymehtil/Challenge2021-ISS-video. A pre-accepted submission to the 2022 Conference on Vision, New Trends and Advances, featuring a comprehensive review of the topic, can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.12477.

Our research involves analyzing stochastic processes that are either halted or bounce off the boundary of a given area. These processes' underlying mathematical operators comprise two components: a main, degrading portion that loses its effectiveness at the boundary, specifically in a direction perpendicular to it, along with a smaller, non-degenerate positive portion. To address this, we use the theory of ordinary differential equations to solve a corresponding problem in a linear framework and then translate the results to the study of mixed boundary value problems in the context of Riccati equations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the solutions to these equations are sensitive to the size of the perturbation, meaning their behavior changes significantly as the size of the perturbation approaches zero. Furthermore, we provide an alternative understanding of the solutions by relating them to the solutions of another set of equations, which we refer to as regularized equations. Key aspects of the regularized equations include their uniform and global convergence towards the target equations, especially in the context of large and various parameter regimes. To explore this, we use techniques from singular perturbation theory. Interestingly, we find that the solutions to the regularized equations outperform those of the target equations in terms of accuracy and stability, effectively acting as a preconditioner, even in the context of mixed boundary value problems in the PDE realm. This study focuses on the characteristics of nuclear matter at zero temperature within the influence of intense magnetic fields by applying the lowest order constraint variational (LOCV) method, utilizing the $AV_{18}$ nuclear potential. We discovered that the absence of a magnetic field results in an energy per particle symmetric function in relation to spin polarization. However, as magnetic fields strengthen, this symmetry is broken due to the interaction between the spin and magnetic forces, which causes the spin polarization parameter to increase rapidly at higher magnetic fields. Furthermore, research indicates that the absence of a magnetic field yields a higher energy per particle than observed in non-magnetic conditions, whereas the application of a magnetic field reduces the energy per particle compared to its non-magnetic state. Additionally, we investigated magnetic field effects on the density and spin polarization parameter, and found that the latter reaches its highest value at varying density values depending on the magnetic field intensity. We also compared our LOCV results with Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) method findings, demonstrating good agreement between the two approaches. We ultimately demonstrated that the presence of a magnetic field increases nuclear matter density, which contrasts traditional opinions on this topic. This research outlines the properties of nuclear matter under the influence of intense magnetic fields, offering a unique understanding of this complex system, as it sheds light on the unconventional properties common in quark matter but less understood in nucleonic matter. We hope this line of investigation inspires future studies. We suggest that future studies explore magnetic field effects using the sigma-omega field term to better comprehend the influence of self-interaction effects on the underlying physics. A comprehensive far-ultraviolet continuum map of the Taurus-Auriga-Perseus complex was created by combining the observations from GALEX and FIMS, which provided data at nearly identical wavelengths. The UV intensity in the area exhibited significant variation, with diffuse UV radiation largely resulting from dust particles scattering starlight. A UV background intensity of around 1000 CU was measured, with a portion potentially attributed to scattered light in the foreground of dense clouds. Fluorescent hydrogen emissions constituted roughly 10% of total UV intensity across the region, generally corresponding to local continuum levels. Two spatial areas displaying elevated UV intensities were identified and were found to be associated with stellar activity. The UV intensities within these areas reached as high as 1600 CU, primarily due to direct starlight within PPM 16216-0158 and a combination of direct and scattered starlight in HD 29337. Mathematical models were developed to determine the flux rates at specific UV wavelengths for HD 29337, which were found to be in line with previously estimated values when adjusted for system-related errors. The comparison of UV flux rates for HD 29337 measured in this study with rates from another study revealed a potential underestimation by around 0.1-0.2 magnitudes in the UV filters' bandwidths. The data collected provides a UV continuum map that can serve as background reference for analyzing spectroscopic data from spectrographs like the new STIS MWA, which is equipped with the broadest UV filter available. The data also includes corrections for foreground scattering and can be utilized to calculate the UV flux rates for HD 29337 and other similar early-type stars. The data was made accessible through the Center for Astrophysics PCAD platform.
