This work delves into the dynamic cognitive hierarchy theory, developed by Lin and Palfrey (2022), within the context of multi-stage incomplete information games. In such scenarios, players simultaneously uncover peers' relevant characteristics and problem-solving abilities as the game unfolds, with relevant feature discovery by one player affecting the ability of other players to determine the same characteristic. Building on this theory, we examine a new class of two-person games with these characteristics and derive a partial differential equation system to describe the process. Although we are unable to achieve uniform Nash equilibrium in these games, we prove the existence of a unique Nash equilibrium that satisfies a partial differential equation system. This equilibrium can be understood as a solution that simultaneously maximizes U and V, representing updates of player i's belief about his opponent's parameter given observed actions. Researchers have proposed filtering structures to reduce False Positive Rates (FPRs) through the revision of classic problems like set intersection, union, and union-of-intersections. We theoretically investigate in a theoretical paper the formation of a Bose-Einstein condensate from spin zero atoms that interact with a M\"ottola-Predazzi-Sizov (MPS) thruster, utilizing magnetic and optical trapping techniques. In a system containing Bose-Einstein condensate, we identify three processes that contribute to the spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation to form an atom-molecule pair. These processes are: i) a collision that results in spin-exchange, ii) a three-body collision, and iii) photoassociation, all of which act to form an atom-molecule pair. In the present study, their SPH framework, incorporating diverse spatial-temporal resolutions for individual components, is extended to include multi-phase flows, particularly with significant density discrepancies, interacting with rigid or deformable structures. 
To achieve this, a straightforward multi-phase model was developed, incorporating varying density reinitialization strategies instead of employing separate formulations to enforce interface continuity across different scales. 
A unique key idea was introduced, using coarse-grained low-resolution particles to replicate boundary conditions from fine-scale particles, thereby replicating topological features from finer scales to coarser grids without altering the resolution. 
Additionally, the present research focuses on the fundamental issues of the split-add operation in SPH, particularly in interacting structures and multi-phase flows, demonstrating enhanced efficiency and accuracy.
A broad range of simulations, including the breakdown of interfaces near structures in single and multi-phases, the simulated flooding of a submersible vehicle, and interactions between structures and multi-phases, were conducted to validate the efficiency, accuracy, and robustness of the method. 
Comparisons with the Monaghan-Gularananda and V volume-preserving SPH methods demonstrated superior performance and stability, highlighting the potential of the multi-resolution SPH method to analyze multi-phase FSI problems. 
Therefore, it provides an efficient numerical tool for various engineering applications, including marine engineering, aerospace engineering, geophysical fluid modeling, medical fluid mechanics, meteorology, and hydrology.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^{3/2}K^{1/2}\log{P})$ with $N$, $K$, and $P$ representing the number of data points, clusters, and data dimensions, respectively. This study presents a TTS model with enhanced pitch adjustment capabilities. 
A difficulty in achieving pitch shifting in TTS lies in protecting the voice's timbre. 
Our proposed TTS system includes two main components: a supervisor that corrects pitch 
in pre-trained TTS models, and a re-tuning algorithm that ensures the voice's timbre 
is preserved when shifting pitch. 
A neural network-based supervisor was developed using speech from 80+ native 
Mandarin speakers, and was tested with three different TTS models, including Tacotron2, 
FastTacotron2, and EFG Tacotron2, achieving an average root mean square error of 16.2. 
A GMM-based re-tuning algorithm was also proposed to restore the voice's timbre after 
pitch adjustment. 
When comparing the output of our proposed system with the conventional TTS models, 
it was found that the neural supervisor and GMM re-tuning algorithms resulted in a 
significant improvement in the listening quality of the EFG-Tacotron2 model, as 
measured by PESQ+ and listening tests. 
By a margin of 0.95 points, our proposed system outperformed the conventional EFG-Tacotron2. 
A further analysis of the listening test results revealed that 70.91% of the listeners 
preferred the synthesized speech from the proposed system, while only 21.37% 
preferred the conventional EFG-Tacotron2. 
Conversely, it was found that the fast version of the supervisor algorithm, which was 
optimized for processing speed, resulted in a decrease in the listening quality of the EFG-Tacotron2 model. 
A further experiment tested the ability of the proposed system to synthesize speech 
at pitches that were outside of the training data, specifically at 4, 6, and 8. 
The results showed that the conventional EFG-Tacotron2 model failed to synthesize speech 
at these higher pitches in an intelligible manner, whereas the proposed system 
successfully synthesized speech at these more extreme pitches, at an average PESQ+ 
score of 2.81, as measured in a listening test. 
A further analysis of the listening test results revealed that 50.38% of the listeners 
prefered the synthesized speech from a pitch that was outside of the training data.

This research focuses on solving spatiotemporal object-based video reasoning challenges like "things-relationships" from GQA, by employing an unsupervised object detection and tracking approach called object permanence to predict sets of objects within a video clip. Object permanence is an innate concept indicating that removed objects still exist, driving detection and tracking of multiple objects within a video to answer a given question. To accomplish this, we enhance the unsupervised object detection and tracking framework by integrating object attributes and question information into the object detection module, leading to the proposal of object permanence. Our approach utilises three distinct features: using an object detection module pre-trained on ImageNet to accumulate historical information of individual objects. Additionally, we leverage semantic information from object detectors to enhance understanding of the question, and finally integrate the question into the object detection module to gather information on relationships between objects. Our proposed object permanence approach demonstrates strong performance when answering both "things-relationships" and "colors-relationships" question types from GQA, even without fine-tuning the model on GQA, given pre-trained object detection. Further support comes from visualizing our object permanence-based method with selected attention weights from the object detection module, indicating that the object detection and tracking accuracy hinges upon the accurate identification of object attributes. Similarly, we observed that object attribute accuracy impacts our object permanence-based approach, leading to improved overall performance. Our research lays a foundational understanding of object permanence in video-based object recognition and provides an unsupervised object detection and tracking solution for spatiotemporal object-based video reasoning. The code and model used in this research are publicly available at https://github.com/ashishbms/OP. Our results have been visualized at https://github.com/ashishbms/OP/tree/main/OP-vis. Currently, this research holds the top unsupervised result on GQA "things-relationships" challenge, according to anonymous submissions. Our results will be reported in full at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2022). In this study, we revisit the issue of fitting hierarchical models using Bayesian approaches by integrating Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and stochastic gradient descent (SGD) methods. Our primary interest lies in SGD, which can efficiently process large datasets, but requires frequent tuning. To address this challenge, we develop a non-conjugational Bayesian approach, combining SGD with the Hamiltonian Neumann Lanczos algorithm, that leverages data augmentation and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo sampling. This innovative strategy, the covariance SGD algorithm, generates samples from the posterior distribution, whose mode is essentially equivalent to the optimal solution of a convex optimization problem under certain conditions. Our proposal, the SNLN algorithm, facilitates sample generation without requiring conjugation and can fit a wide range of Bayesian linear regression models with covariates. Our numerical simulations confirm that the SNLN algorithm outperforms conventional methods in efficiency and precision. To demonstrate its practicality, we apply the proposed method to a real-world examination dataset, analyzing student performance based on various factors, including gender and examination year. Our analysis, facilitated by the SNLN algorithm, yields meaningful insights and a reliable estimate of the model's predictive accuracy. All the necessary code and software are openly available for replication and further exploration. Additionally, our methods can be extended to accommodate diverse non-Gaussian hierarchical models, including a mix of linear and non-linear combinations, to fit a wide range of applications. To illustrate the applicability of the proposed methods, we simulate data from the Ono model, known for its non-conjugational posterior distribution, and successfully apply the SGD-based algorithms with data augmentation, recovering the simulated data and providing sample fits, including confidence intervals and quantiles. Our findings demonstrate that the SGD algorithms, incorporating data augmentation, significantly outperform conventional methods in precision and efficiency. To the best of our knowledge, the integration of SGD with data augmentation constitutes an innovative extension of the Bayesian algorithm, previously applicable only on conjugational data scenarios. Our method, the proposed extension, is universally applicable to a wide range of Bayesian hierarchical models with covariates, facilitating sample generation from the posterior distribution. Our numerical simulations have shown that the SNLN algorithm, when extended to the Ono model, outperforms conventional approaches with remarkable efficiency and precision. All the necessary code and software have been made openly available for replication, further exploration, and future enhancement. Our primary contribution lies in the integration of two algorithms, SGD and data augmentation, to facilitate sample generation from the posterior distribution, with implications for a variety of applications. depends on intricate electronic transport mechanisms involving the members of the
ensemble. Phenomena such as electron scattering and phonon-assisted interactions
influence conductivity at the nanoscale, leading to equilibrium electron transport
within the ensemble. This phenomenon results in the collective behavior of an
ensemble, even if the individual nanoelements are not connected to one another. 
Using an extensive model, our simulation research has been dedicated to studying
electrical conductivity in disordered nanowire ensembles, focusing on the impact of
phonons. Our models demonstrate that phonons have a significant role in conductivity
at high temperatures, while magnetic interactions only become prominent at extremely low
temperatures, where conductivity is primarily facilitated by coherent electron states. 
This conductivity mechanism is similar to the quantum phenomenon known as conductive
bonding, where shared energy leads to the collective behavior of an ensemble, even without direct contact between individual nanoelements. 
Our simulation research has significant implications, as our models can be applied to a
wide range of different nanomaterials and quantum systems to estimate their average
conductivity levels. Additionally, our data highlights the distinct signatures of various
quantum systems that exhibit collective conductivity.

of different quantum systems, and it can be applied to a broad range of different
nanomaterials and systems to estimate their average conductivity levels.

This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in their significance to the clustering process. To address this issue, the proposed method incorporates a weighted distance measurement that adaptes to the subspaces' structure, using features that are most relevant to distinguish between clusters. The effectiveness of the approach is demonstrated through simulations and real-world data sets comparison. The outcomes show that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques in term of clustering accuracy and average sub-space cardinality. The validity of the approach is further substantiated by statistical tests. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have become crucial components of various neural networks and ensemble learning systems. Nevertheless, traditional algorithms designed for learning MoE models often struggle to converge due to getting stuck in local optima, a challenge that persists despite extensive research over two decades. This paper presents a groundbreaking solution to this long-standing problem by introducing an innovative algorithm capable of consistently learning MoE model parameters for a wide range of non-linear functions. This new algorithm uniquely estimates expert parameters through an analysis of the cross-moment tensor between inputs and outputs. While it still necessitates an EM algorithm to recover gating parameters, the proposed approach simplifies this process and significantly improves convergence compared to existing methods, leading to enhanced performance on both simulated and real-world data sets when compared to standard baselines. Additionally, the framework established in this paper has the potential to be expanded to other statistical models for multi-modal data analysis. Experimental results demonstrate the new algorithm's efficacy on a variety of applications, including symbol sequence classification and motion planning. As such, the presented approach holds vast potential for real-world applications in areas like robotics, video analysis, speech recognition, and medical diagnosis. This set of notes offers a standalone overview of the theory of chip-firing games on metric graphs along with the theory of Jacobians and Prym varieties, stemming from the 2022 Cambridge summer school on combinatorial methods in algebraic geometry. The notes assume no prior knowledge in algebraic or combinatorial geometry but do require background in classical graph theory. Due to their introductory nature, these notes cover the foundational aspects of metric graph theory, discrete linear systems, and tropical curves, in addition to combinatorial properties of Jacobian and Prym varieties. Following the summer school, we also provide an overview of recent research in chip-firing on rooted trees, rooted manifolds, and their algebraic counterparts, the arithmetic Toda structure, and the Deligne-Mumford orbifold. Finally, we discuss the application of CMUMF methods to linear systems on tropical manifolds, a topic largely unexplored to date. These notes are intended for readers without prior expertise in algebraic or combinatorial geometry, or those seeking a concise introduction to the subjects. Moreover, they contain several open questions proposed by the contributors of the summer school, aiming to provide readers with a deeper understanding of the subjects and possible avenues for future research. Appendix A contains a brief overview of Pontryagin Duality, while Appendix B consists of an exhaustive list of references, divided into suggestion lists and general references. Furthermore, Appendix C contains a list of problem sets, proposed by S. Papathanasiou. Several of the results mentioned are originally presented in detail, while others are surveyed from relevant literature. A brief discussion on the history and context as well as future perspectives concluding the summer school is contained in Appendix D. As an additional resource, the organizers have provided links to additional images, examples, and software not included in the notes. Due to space constraints, this document frequently refers to previously established results, assumed to be known but not explicitly stated. Conversely, some novel results are presented, marked with an asterisk. Lastly, we would like to dedicate this document to the memory of our departed colleague, David Eisenbud, who sadly passed away during the summer of 2022. A comprehensive summary of his profound impact on the field of Algebraic Geometry is provided in Appendix E. These notes were approved by David Eisenbud, who sadly did not live to see them completed. While quantum gravitational effects generally break global symmetries, their presence may hold significant value in understanding both particle physics and cosmology. Discovering well-maintained global symmetries could provide a valuable insight into the properties of gravity. A statistically significant detection of cosmic birefringence in the Cosmic Microwave Background may signify a previously undiscovered, though spontaneously broken, global symmetry in nature. A potential explanation for this phenomenon could be a very light, electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field that remains free from gravity's influence. We demonstrate the feasibility of testing an otherwise theoretical framework by proposing that gravitational effects render any field in a state of deformation rather than uniformity. This concept is exemplified in a model where an electromagnetically interacting pseudoscalar field adjusts to another scalar field's minimum. By observing how light behaves in the presence of gravity, we may uncover new principles that could reveal the underlying structure of spacetime, thus further developing our understanding of global symmetries in the universe. Ultimately, this could pave the way for exploring quantum gravitational phenomena in the context of cosmology. By delving into the interactions between gravity, electromagnetism, and the Birefringent Field, we may uncover new principles that could reveal how the very fabric of space-time is constructed. Such findings may pave the way for identifying the boundaries of quantum gravity within cosmological contexts. Our framework provides a novel model that maintains a global symmetry across multiple fields without complicating the field structure. Any gravitational influence on our model induces an asymmetry within the electromagnetic sector without rendering the framework's field structure unstable. Our proposal is primarily based on observations from 2020, but it is compatible with more recent data released in 2021. A future, more precise measurement of the electromagnetic polarization angle should enable us to deduce the gravitational influence on our model. This could significantly expand our understanding of quantum gravity by providing a new perspective within the realm of general relativity. By providing a new framework, we embark on a pioneering journey to identify quantum gravitational phenomena within cosmological contexts, thus opening the door to previously unexplored realms. With our proposal, we initiate this journey and await the future, more precise measurements of the electromagnetic polarization angle. Our proposal may also inspire new experimental technologies that are capable of detecting gravitational influences on our model. Our work principally contributes to the field of quantum gravity by shedding light on one of its core questions: how do matter fields behave in the presence of gravity? Our proposal offers an unusual perspective on both cosmological and particle physics

Our research presents new findings based on far ultraviolet (FUV) observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147 obtained with three specific filters onboard the AstroSat satellite. The goal of deep transfer learning (DTL) is to empower deep neural networks (DNNs) with the ability to leverage knowledge acquired through prior experiences, like pre-training on large, general datasets. This allows DNNs to adapt this knowledge to achieve high performance in a variety of additional tasks. A well-established approach for implementing DTL involves pre-training DNNs on a diverse range of tasks via self-supervised learning, with subsequent fine-tuning for specific downstream tasks. Despite its widespread usage, the process lacks a comprehensive understanding of the factors that influence its effectiveness, particularly when it comes to downscaling it to smaller, task-specific datasets. This downscaling process involves transferring knowledge from pre-trained models to supporting tasks, a challenge that poses considerable challenges due to limited data resources and potential noise in the data. This study aims to build on prior works that investigated factor analysis through extensive experiments, with a specific focus on transfer learning for graph-based tasks. Our research involves an in-depth analysis of several key factors, specifically data source diversity, model design, and dataset size, with the aim of enhancing the transferability of pre-trained CNNs in mind. Our work, which includes the development of new methods and the evaluation of multiple pre-training objectives, not only sheds light on the intricacies of transfer learning but also results in the achievement of state-of-the-art performance in the semantic segmentation of red edge and near-infrared spectra. Our study is the first to investigate transfer learning for spectrum-based tasks, with our results demonstrating the effectiveness of supporting spectral data from diverse sources, such as raw data from monochrome CMOS sensors and data processed using principal component analysis. Our work also proposes a new approach, involving the segmentation of raw data through trained models, outperforming numerous state-of-the-art methods along the way. Our experiments, which also involve supporting tasks, indicate that reducing the model size results in improved transferability, with our fine-tuned models achieving top results among those without access to raw data. Our study culminates in the development of "little transfer," a pioneering method of transferring knowledge from models with reduced capacities, with our results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach for spectrum-based and red edge tasks. Our work, which includes the use of a novel network design featuring dual branches, outperforms state-of-the-art methods, including full transfer learning, feature averaging, model distillation, and subset learning. Our experiments also highlight the effectiveness of "little transfer" in downscaling, with our results similar to state-of-the-art methods when tested

In various scenarios, such as mobilization, pandemic mitigation, and advertising, the swift dissemination of information and social behavior change are paramount. Although straightforward methods like spreading equations (SE) can effectively transmit information in highly interconnected networks, their slow pace might hinder their practicality in networks with regional clusters and limited connectivity between them. This work introduces an enhanced model that leverages the network's structure to minimize SE's limitations. By employing SE in local communities and using target nodes' local connections to efficiently transmit information across the network, the proposed model maintains comparable efficiency while significantly reducing the number of target nodes necessary for a given level of information dissemination. Furthermore, the synergy between SE and other models has been explored, suggesting the potential for developing tailored hybrid strategies that seamlessly integrate the strengths of distinct models via a universal framework. Extensive simulations validate the efficacy of the proposed model and lay the groundwork for the development of next-generation information dissemination techniques. Detailed information on the code used in this research can be found at https://github.com/JayJayCheng/dissemination- code. This work focuses on networks representing social relationships; however, the proposed model is versatile and adaptable to various types of complex networks requiring efficient information dissemination. The reliability of a discrete-time channel model that uses a standard method of perturbation
is numerically investigated for cases without signal amplification. We assess the distance between 
discrete nonlinear interference points and find that this distance can be employed to estimate 
the effective memory length of the communication channel. By utilizing this estimate in a simple 
threshold technique, we are able to predict when a given amplification-free channel becomes 
unreliable, i.e., when its minimum reliable signal transfer rate exceeds a predetermined information 
transfer rate threshold. This prediction is based on a combination of factors, including the average 
signal energy, standard signal energy fluctuation, interference distribution, and the desired rate 
value. We demonstrate that our simple method significantly outperforms an existing continuous-time 
channel model based predictor in most scenarios and reveals the break-down points of commonly used 
amplification-free amplifiers such as the DSB-SC and SS-SS modulators. Furthermore, from a practical 
perspective, the proposed method may contribute to the development of faster prediction tools for 
amplifier selection in devices such as IoT smartphones. We share our numerical findings for standard 
communication devices and share our implementation of the discrete nonlinear interference 
point estimation method in a Python code available online at this URL: 
https://github.com/MagnoLores/discrete-nonlinear-channel.

Unlike robust, topologically protected states like the Pfaffian, this new phase emerges from an intricate interplay between particle-hole symmetry and an energy threshold. Although this analysis focuses on a one-dimensional system, corresponding two-dimensional results can be inferred.  Furthermore, two distinct methods have been employed to verify that this phase cannot be achieved through any particle-hole symmetry-breaking term.  Finally, it is discussed that this phase can potentially be identified through its distinct specific heat signatures in quantum Hall systems.  A preliminary investigation into the specific heat of the Pfaffian state is presented along with a detailed analysis of how this phase might be linked with the unusual specific heat observations found in experiments on the even-denominator quantum Hall states.  Interestingly, quantitative matching has been found between the theoretical specific heat results and the experimental data, which provides strong backing for the proposed phase.  Consequently, it is proposed to utilize specific heat measurements as an additional means to explore the quantum Hall system's topology.  Lastly, it is hypothesized that this phase may also exist in superconductors due to structural anomalies in the energy spectrum triggered by topological defects, an occurrence referred to as topological Anderson tuning.  A corresponding theoretical investigation into this phenomenon is presented in the appendix. Furthermore, it is predicted that this phase can also be realized in the "fluctuon" state, an exotic quantum magnet made from densely packed Bose gases, where the rotation of internal vortices results in a thermal Hall conductivity of unprecedented magnitude. Our analysis reveals that the conditions generating the Thakurta metric, previously investigated in a study by Böhm et al., involve a single black hole feeding on non-interacting isotropic dust throughout the entire universe. This leads to a realization that the processes driving black hole growth are connected to universal properties rather than localized occurrences. Moreover, radiation, primordial black holes, and dark matter cannot provide the required energy to sustain Thakurta black hole growth, and such a solution cannot be applied to binary black hole systems. Ultimately, we conclude that the Thakurta metric does not accurately represent the growth of cosmic black holes, and this failure stems from a flawed assumption that a black hole can exist within an eternal universe. This assumption is analogous to others found to be invalid, such as the assumption that a cosmic string can exist in a steady-state universe. Lastly, we note that the Thakurta metric bears a resemblance to certain exact solutions to Einstein's field equations, including the Droniak-Benjamin metric, and as such, should be classified as an exact or pseudo-exact metric rather than a pseudo-Riemannian metric. This distinction necessitates an revision of methods previously used to derive the Thakurta metric from a vacuum field equation using a paplle curvature approach. These issues highlight the need for critical evaluation of mathematical techniques and their applications to astrophysical systems. Furthermore, our study suggests that future research into novel black hole models derive these from alternative theoretical frameworks, such as emergent gravity theory, which views black holes as emergent entities born from a transition between states where gravity is manifest and where gravity is not. Research into an emergent gravity theory provides an opportunity for a range of novel black holes to emerge, including the Banados-Sottini-Paris metric, or the types of black holes proposed by Aref'ev and Shepelyanov, or the types of black holes proposed by Aref'ev and Saridakis. Research into an emergent gravity theory suggests that the Thakurta metric may describe a state where the black hole is born from an exchange of energy between itself and cosmic dust, and as such, our study indicates that the Thakurva metric, when viewed through the lens of this theory, describes a novel type of black hole rather than being inherently flawed. This idea is consistent with other findings where gravity is viewed as an emergent entity, such as studies into distance and curvature, or the studies into Reissner-Nordström

Specifically, pressure bumps in these discs hold significant implications for planet formation, and can stem from, among other things, binary interactions. Although binarity in disc models is often linked to the evolution of binary systems as a whole, and disc physics is typically treated separately, we investigated how disc models change when binarity is considered within the context of disc physics. In this research, we investigate whether the requirement for massive models might be partly attributed to computational limitations inherent to the learner itself. We also examine whether these constraints are exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our study is predicated on the idea that a learner is computationally restricted if it belongs to a specific complex class of functions that can be optimized through conventional learning methods. We have proven that learners bounded by specific types of complexity are compelled to design extremely large models when handling high-dimensional datasets, even when the model parameters are proportional to the data dimensions. Moreover, our results demonstrate that such constraints are more severe under robust learning conditions. We have also verified these findings with synthetic data points under an empirical loss. Building on this concept, we have investigated learners bounded by complexity based on specific types of distributions, such as the Gaussian distribution, and established similar outcomes. Our studies using Gaussian datasets reveal that the restriction to learn complex functions with high dimensions necessitates extremely large models, and this necessity is more severe under robust learning conditions. Our results provide insights into a fundamental trade-off between the scope of learnable functions, the number of model parameters, and the robustness of learning tasks. Our research suggests that the widespread adoption and success of large, overparameterized models might be partly attributed to computational constraints inherent to the learner, exacerbated under robust learning conditions. Our studies also highlight the significant limitations of the learners bounded by complexity and distribution under robust learning settings and the need to develop more efficient algorithms that can learn complex functions with fewer model parameters while ensuring robustness. Our results might explain why current algorithms based on optimization and gradient descent are insufficient to learn the constraints of volume under various distribution functions and why the state-of-the-art techniques in deep learning have achieved only limited progress in this area. This study addresses the dial-a-ride problem within large urban settings where residents have multiple transportation options at their disposal. To remain competitive, ridepooling services must balance high pool participation rates against minimizing detours for users. This research explores a real-world challenge faced by ridepooling providers in metropolitan areas, where an overemphasis on pool rates can compromise service quality by incurring substantial user costs. To tackle this problem, a computational simulation model was developed to model the dynamics of ridepooling operations and identify strategies to minimize detours while maintaining high pool participation rates. The proposed model was validated using actual data from a metropolitan area and served as the basis for an optimized proactive routing model, which demonstrated a significant potential for reducing detours by up to 26.6%. This optimized model also enabled the identification of optimal threshold values for minimizing passenger costs while maintaining high pool participation rates. Furthermore, a simulation-based analysis revealed that detour reductions are directly linked to the level of over-assignment in the system. This is particularly evident in cases where the over-assignment rate is low (20-40%), but the pool participation rate increases rapidly with higher over-assignment rates (40-100%). Lastly, a comparison with a heuristic-based approach revealed a minimal increase in computational complexity when using the proposed model. This research provides metropolitan areas with a valuable resource for mitigating the drawbacks of ridepooling services due to over-assignment. Optimized solutions derived from the proposed model can help ridepooling providers improve the service quality by minimizing user costs and increasing the efficiency of their operations. Moreover, this research showcases the effectiveness of a computational simulation in addressing a real-world challenge faced by metropolitan ridepooling systems. Its applications can be expanded to other related fields that rely on over-assignment strategies, such as the sharing of taxis or ride-sharing services. Additionally, this research highlights a double standard in current optimization-based models when it comes to representing the goals and motivations of users in ridepooling services. As a result, the proposed model offers an alternative perspective that considers minimizing passenger costs as a top priority, which can be relevant in metropolitan areas with high levels of traffic congestion. In contrast to previous studies, this research focuses on a specific type of customer dissatisfaction (detours) rather than involvement. As a result, the proposed model is complementary to an array of optimization-based models that rely on over-assignment, making it a reliable tool for metropolitan areas with different priorities. This research explores multi-modal pretraining techniques for tables in the context of e-commerce. Due to the complex nature of table structures, which are essentially 2D representations of text, we need to develop novel methods for integrating diverse modalities - images and text. The problem lies in coordinating the existing progress made in vision and language areas with the specific requirements of table data. This work creates a visual language model capable of understanding tables and leveraging co-modal knowledge to refine our understanding of tables based on images and text. To achieve this, we introduce a new dataset called TABC, which contains comprehensive table information, accompanied by corresponding images and text descriptions. Additionally, we propose a new modular pretraining framework called TABC-TVT, which includes three stages: it first teaches the model to recognize tables visually, then encodes semantic meaning and finally correlates the data across different modalities to extract more comprehensive information. Through this approach, we enhance the model's ability to process tables in different situations and achieve a notable breakthrough in our field. Our code and the new dataset are publicly available. Natural Language Processing employs a crucial task called text classification, which sequential models efficiently handle, though their connection to linguistic semantics in output predictions often falls short. This study presents an innovative score called I-score, an efficient search algorithm termed Backward Dropping Algorithm, and an innovative feature engineering technique known as the "dagger technique". Firstly, the paper introduces I-score, an innovative score that identifies and prioritizes crucial linguistic semantics for accurate text classification predictions. Subsequently, the paper suggests using Backward Dropping Algorithm to manage dependencies within large datasets. Additionally, the paper proposes "dagger technique" which ensures an optimal association between the input variables and target variable. These methods can be applied universally across feed-forward ANNs, CNNs, and other neural networks, as demonstrated through an experiment using commercial text classification data. Results show that using I-score and the "dagger technique" together yields an optimal solution, and when employed with a backward dropping algorithm, successfully reduces the size of deployed models by half with minimal loss in accuracy. This study aims to give deeper insights to the deployed models' connections with linguistic semantics. Text classification data was utilized to test the efficiency of the system. The I-score and related code will be made available for public use.

We examine the relationship between spin-orbit coupling and interactions within a two-orbital Hubbard model on a square lattice, employing the variational Monte Carlo method. An effective spin-orbit constant $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is considered in the wave function, focusing primarily on a transition metal oxide material. For electron numbers below four, $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ correlates directly with the original $\lambda$ when there's no interaction, but increases with growing interactions in the paramagnetic phase. As Hund's coupling increases, the difference between $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ with and without interactions diminishes, and the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ equation modifies into a more complicated function of the original $\lambda$ and interaction strength. In the antiferromagnetic phase, the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ is significantly influenced by the orbital anisotropy, becoming much larger than it would be if the orbitals acted independently. Additionally, the two-orbital model yields a magnetic phase diagram that aligns with a corresponding phase diagram for a related model with confined dimensions, where the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ helps account for the differences between the two models' spin-orbit characteristics. Furthermore, the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ helps explain a range of experimental observations related to the spin-orbit coupling in transition metal oxides. Suggestions for future research incorporating more complicated computational methods and an investigation of how the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ evolves within specific materials are provided. A related, highly speculative hypothesis is presented, where the effective $\lambda_{\text{eff}}$ may play a crucial role in the phenomenon of superconductivity observed in iron-based materials. A future study exploring this connection is also proposed. The source code used for the calculations has been made publicly available. A detailed methods section with additional computational details is included at the end of this document. A preprint version of this paper is available online at arXiv arXiv:2103.12158. exceeds the age of the Universe, then it can be a candidate for dark matter.

in the range of $[10^{-6}, 10^{-1}] \, \mathrm{eV/c^2}$ or, if less than

To ensure that AI-powered medical devices operate safely and efficiently in diverse environments before being released to the public, accurately assessing their performance in varying scenarios is crucial. Given the regulatory restrictions on medical software and the scarcity of comprehensive labeled medical datasets, our approach revolves around predicting a model's performance in an unfamiliar setting using its predicted responses alone, without requiring any modifications to its training process or assumptions about its original data source. This "black-box" model assessment technique is based solely on the model's self-generated output samples and estimated probability distributions. By leveraging recent advances in kernel methods, we develop a non-parametric estimate for measuring the difference in performance between a model and a "black-box" model assessment method. We also present a fully automatic, normalized implementation of kernel model assessment that does not rely on any assumptions about the original data distribution, and provide empirical evidence supporting its effectiveness using MNIST images processed through different neural networks as well as a deep model trained on MIMIC-III clinical data. When performing cosmological inferences based on the Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, standard analyses typically only consider one aspect, the distance to the unclustered Ly$\alpha$ emitters. In this research, we investigate whether the full shape of these correlation functions can help break this degeneracy. To find out, we calculate non-linear effects on two relevant correlation function parameters and establish a simplified formula to estimate how the emission line shape affects Ly$\alpha$ monopole data. Our study indicates that incorporating the full shape of Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions, including velocity information and redshift space, can significantly improve the constraints on relevant cosmological parameters without being influenced by the degeneracy mentioned above. Using mock Ly$\alpha$ datasets from the Euclid Sky Lens simulations, our analysis demonstrates that the full shape analysis offers more accurate measurements of cosmological parameters, resulting in reduced errors by a factor of two. The improved precision also makes the full shape analysis more resilient to measurement uncertainties. Our conclusions open up the possibility of utilizing Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions as an independent method for constraining the distance to the unclustered Ly$\alpha$ emitters, a critical component in evaluating the performance of future surveys such as the Euclid satellite. Future work will explore additional potential benefits of this analysis. In addition, there is an accompanying research note that examines potential systematics in Ly$\alpha$ correlation functions due to Lyman beta contamination, where these biases are measured using Ly$\alpha$ and Ly$\beta$ mock spectra and their impact is discussed. Our analysis indicates that the Lyman beta contamination creates an artificial correlation signal, particularly in the direction perpendicular to the redshift axis. To correct this anomaly, these researchers propose a simple method of matching Ly$\alpha$ and Ly$\beta$ flux ratios, a technique that can also be used to detect Ly$\alpha$ Ly$\beta$ absorbers at redshifts greater than 6. Our analysis further reveals that, in the redshift range from 6 to 8.6, the artificial signal represents less than 0.1 percent of total Ly$\alpha$ flux, a percentage that can however contribute up to a third of the uncertainty in measuring the velocity bias. Researchers at Fermilab have successfully conducted an experiment where a beam of particles undergoes an unconventional manipulation, swapping its horizontal and longitudinal beam patterns at the A0 Photoinjector. The new experimental setup, featuring a specially designed deflector accompanied by curved beamsplitting components, has enabled the first observation of a distinct phase shift between the particle beam's trajectory and its time-of-flight. The emittance exchange experiment, a crucial step towards developing advanced acceleration technologies, has also provided scientists with a unique perspective on the performance capabilities of the A0 photoinjector, which has allowed them to measure key parameters of the particle beam, such as its energy and transverse beam patterns, under different operation conditions. The findings from this research have crucially validated the theoretical foundations of emittance exchange theories, reinforcing their validity and guiding future studies. The study has significant implications for the design and optimization of future compact particle accelerators. The researchers have obtained high-quality results for the particle beam's time-of-flight with sub-nanosecond precision and transverse beam patterns with tens-of-micrometer precision, setting Firbino, their analysis software, apart from other analysis tools with similar capabilities. The success of this experiment has paved the way for more innovative particle beam manipulations and may lead to the development of cold undulators in a particle beam's final stage, a feature previously not feasible. The researchers are now investigating the possibility of employing emittance exchange to enhance the capabilities of LCLS-II-HE. A fundamental issue in pedestrian trajectory prediction research is generating accurate and diverse walking paths to enable risk assessment in crowded areas. Most current approaches rely on Markov chains or Gaussian processes to model pedestrian behavior, but they often predict simple or circular movements, failing to account for changes in trajectory direction. In this paper, a novel representation-based method is proposed to capture the diversity of pedestrian trajectories through a motion-neutral representation, specifically based on changes in trajectory direction. This method employs a motion-neutral residual variance model to predict trajectories, demonstrating significant improvements in terms of multi-modality and future trajectory precision compared to state-of-the-art methods, especially in scenarios involving turning movements. Our technique's core technology has been successfully adapted for real-time use on mobile devices, opening up potential applications for pedestrian safety and driver assistance systems. The source code and dataset for this research are available on https://github.com/MGUC-Team/MNP. The dataset, which includes the ECE dataset, can be accessed at https://mguc-team.github.io/project/mnp/. Our model has achieved the state-of-the-art performance on the TOP dataset and the TOP-BD and TOP-Place benchmarks, respectively, according to the official competition tracks. In a practical demonstration, this method was integrated with a mobile app to assist drivers with pedestrian safety, specifically when interacting with in-progress reanimations at road crossings in Paris, France. The app provides the driver with early warnings about approaching pedestrians, as detected by an embedded camera, and presents the predicted trajectory in the correct reference frame, based on the specific event observed. This safety feature has been tested and shown to be effective in actual driving situations, according to a pilot study involving real drivers, which highlighted reduced risk ratings from very high to low. Three of the four participants reported no close calls during the app-aided drive, and the in-app report confirmed that two of the participants had received the warning just before a close call with a pedestrian would normally occur in the baseline case without using the app. In particular, they reported that the alert allowed them to avoid a close call with a pedestrian who had suddenly stepped off the curb in one case and in another case a pedestrian was walking towards the driver's car along the street. In a third instance, the driver reported that the alert had been given because of a reanimation event at a crosswalk and the driver had been able to avoid a close call because the pedestrian was standing still. This pilot study demonstrated the potential of this technology to significantly reduce pedestrian collisions involving vehicles. This technology has been successfully demonstrated

This research aims to compare and contrast these measures objectively by exploring their core similarities, disparities, and limitations. To achieve this, a Boltzmann machine architecture is employed as a reference model to analyze how system complexity evolves in response to variations in network dynamics and parameters. Furthermore, a variant of an information-based measure of complexity is applied to examine the emergence of ordered and chaotic phases within a simple recurrent neural network that adapts incrementally through Hebbian learning. The latter network dynamic is chosen for its ability to mimic human cognitive development and learning over time. This study demonstrates that different measures of complexity can yield results that align with one another, yet also highlights situations in which these results diverge. It is found specifically that all measures exhibit a consistent, albeit asymptotic, agreement between their calculations and the actual complexity of the system being studied. The difference between their results is greatest as the systems or measures in question become increasingly disparate. This research confirms that various metrics of complexity are applicable and equivalent in their capacity to evaluate complexity across a wide range of scenarios, yet also indicates that these measures differ from one another. The outcome suggests that the use of multiple, diverse complexity measures is necessary to gain a comprehensive, thorough, and complete understanding of the complexity of a system. This paper showcases initial research on an innovative technique for facilitating communication between humans and a swarm of robots. Our solution involves merging a compact hand gesture recognition model with the advanced \emph{ros2} system to enable a swarm of robots to execute complex actions in response to distinct hand signals. Our experiment, utilizing a series of hand gestures that instruct different swarm behaviors, was successfully implemented with three Turtlebot3 robots. This enabled these robots to automatically adjust their distances and evade collisions with obstacles in various simulated environments as well as in a physical testing setup. This research aims to enhance the effectiveness of human-robot collaboration in swarm robotics, thereby amplifying the quality and speed of interaction. Our code and hand gesture data have been made publicly available on our GitHub repository for future research purposes. Additionally, this work sets the stage for investigating more intricate issues related to swarm robotics, such as autonomous decision-making and optimization. Furthermore, this research can expand to other applications such as autonomous driving, utilizing a combination of hand gestures to signal specific actions to robots. This could significantly simplify the process of training these systems. In the future, our solution can be adapted to various robotic platforms operating within diverse environmental conditions. This would substantially reduce the complexity of research focused on human-robot collaboration in swarm robotics. The study aims to assess the performance of composite deep learning models consisting of Recurrent Neural Networks and Convolutional Neural Networks for identifying diverse White Blood Cell types, a feat that could revolutionize automated medical diagnosis and blood analysis in pharmaceutical and healthcare settings by analyzing image samples, thereby aiding in disease diagnosis for patients. The analysis utilizes a unique dataset comprising 55,000 WBC-stained image samples across 28 distinct cell types. To facilitate efficient comparison, a novel composite convolutional neural network model is developed and tested against the existing state-of-the-art performance benchmark, thereby achieving an impressive 99.44% accuracy. The study demonstrates the effectiveness of composite deep learning models with robust generalizability for multifaceted WBC identification tasks. The proposed model's capability to integrate expertise from specialized models can significantly aid medical diagnosis, thereby creating a valuable tool for medical professionals. We've shown that this approximation remains valid even when the full wave function is not available and demonstrated its effectiveness in optimizing adiabatic control circuits and reducing fluctuations in quantum drives. We examine the RDF data exchange process based on relational data, constrained by Shape Expression schema. Our research involves addressing two critical issues: first, determining the feasibility of solutions for source data instances; and second, developing a single comprehensive solution that represents all possible outcomes. To achieve this, we incorporate typed IRI constructors to form RDF IRIs from relational values and translate Shape Expression constraints into target dependencies. Additionally, we have identified certain data exchange settings as 'key-preserving', a determinate subset. For this key-preserving scenario, we found that the solution space can be represented by a fixed, compact database structure. Our approach involves using finite relational structures to interpret typed IRI constructors, which enables us to apply known techniques to analyze the solution space. Furthermore, we demonstrated that this structure accurately represents all possible solutions within the key-preserving class. Consequently, we can use this structure to simplify the solution process, making it comparable to standard data exchange problems. Our results also imply that the solution space may become exponentially large, rendering it impractical for 'key-nonpreserving' data exchange cases. To address the general data exchange challenge, we developed two sequential composition methods: the first combines Shape Expression constraints with target key dependencies; and the second combines target key dependencies with Shape Expression constraints. Our initial results show that the first composition method yields a positive solution for source data instances that meet the key-preserving conditions. Conversely, we identified a representative set of 'anti-Shape Expression' constraints, whose combination with Shape Expression constraints would result in an unsolvable data exchange case. Similarly, we discovered that pairing target key dependencies with Shape Expression constraints may result in an unsolvable data exchange case. Our research is an initial attempt to analyze the RDF data exchange process using Shape Expression constraints and relational data. We now propose this theory as a foundation for developing new exchange composition methods, while also highlighting areas for further investigation. Specifically, we have not explored the impact of advanced typing in IRI constructors, nor have we considered the effect of advanced data features, such as data fragmentation and data parallelism, on the exchange process. Our framework can accommodate these complex data characteristics, but these specific issues are yet to be addressed in future research. Our work has been presented in terms of an extensive formal theory, requiring a deep understanding of advanced data concepts and semantic generalization. Pre-trained language models possess the ability to capture syntactical information, as established in previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. This work presents two unsupervised constituent parsing models, UPOA and its enhanced version UPIO, both of which use the syntactic distance as a loss function to guide self-attention in Transformers through query and key matrices. These matrices are projected linearly, and their inner products with the vectorized tokens constitute the self-attention scores. The novel contribution lies in utilizing the syntactic distance as a local measure in the training process of the Transformers model. The loss function is defined as the sum of the syntactic distances between the root words and their respective children in the parse tree. The additional channel in the enhanced model, UPIO, combines the linear projection of the token vectors with the self-attention scores, thereby learning to integrate syntactic information alongside other traditional self-attention channels. Experimental results demonstrate the improved performance of the unsupervised models compared to prior approaches [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019] across various parsing tasks. The enhanced model UPIO outperforms the state-of-the-art in parsing with small contextual representations, achieving an Labeled Attachment Parse Score (LAS) of 40.1 on the Penn Treebank shift-reduction dataset, accompanied by semantic information. The models' source code and pre-trained models can be found on the GitHub repository at https://github.com/ghasp/2020nlpsemu. Our unsupervised models also exhibit robustness in shift-reduction parsing with minimal word embeddings, similar to previous studies [Tenney et al., 2019, Jawahar et al., 2019, Hewitt and Manning, 2019]. The improved performance of the models is attributed to the linear projection of the query and key matrices, allowing for better internal representation of syntactic information in the self-attention scores. The internal structure learned by the models is consistent with the underlying syntax, as the models consistently produce shift-reduction parses with minimal word embeddings. The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR). Despite having access to advanced ASR tools, the lack of sufficient training data for languages other than English severely hampers progress in these fields. To fill this void, we utilize Kaldi to develop German acoustic models utilizing datasets under a Creative Commons license. This has the added benefit of making these models redistributable and significantly lowering the barriers for researchers and developers working with German ASR. Through experimentation with various data combinations and Kaldi configurations, we evaluate the performance of these models across different training data sources, including the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus, the Open Source Audio Distribution (OSAD), and the Transkriert Leben dataset. Interestingly, our results indicate that incorporating the Spoken Wikipedia Corpus data yields superior WERs for ASR models trained with OSAD-based training data. Consequently, we make available our trained models, the associated data, and the custom data preprocessing code through the OSAD repository. Moreover, we suggest utilizing these models in combination with other data sources to achieve improved ASR performance. Finally, we propose the idea of creating a hybrid model by combining German acoustic models with similar models from other languages, thereby paving the way for multilingual ASR applications. While the concept is still in its infancy, the potential for significantly reducing ASR errors across languages is quite evident. To facilitate further research in this direction, we provide the code for generating the multilingual data from OSAD and the results of experiments conducted across 24 languages, including both speech data and ASR models. These results show that the accuracy of ASR can be enhanced by up to 71%. Additionally, the ASR models for the 13 languages with existing ASR models exhibit notable improvements when combined with the German acoustic models, thereby underlining their utility in cross-lingual ASR applications. The ASR models for the 11 languages where no prior models existed become competitive with baseline models for ASR after fine-tuning with the German acoustic models. These results suggest that the German acoustic models possess a level of generalizability that can be exploited in cross-lingual ASR applications. Deep neural networks, known for their robust performance across various tasks, are often difficult to understand. This interpretability issue severely hampers their use in critical areas like medical imaging. A promising approach, neural tangent kernel, offers some level of interpretation by mirroring a kernel machine's properties. In an effort to enhance classification and layer understanding, we've developed a novel network that combines multiple neural tangent kernels - one for each layer - as opposed to earlier work focusing on a single kernel to represent the entire network. The emergence of chimeric states could offer valuable insights into patterns observed in these coupled oscillators. Furthermore, the unique characteristics of chimeras may allow for a deeper and more precise evaluation of time series data from in vivo or in vitro experiments, where cells are in an asynchronous state, but close to a synchronized state. The possibility of a reverse transition from asynchronous to synchronized behavior could also be investigated in such real-world systems. Interestingly, the absence of chimeras in identical but randomly coupled populations hints at interesting applications for chimeras in topics such as cryptography, where data about population connectivity could be hidden, or revealed, depending on varying connection strengths. Lastly, the findings of our study also raise fundamental questions about the structure and dynamics of chimeras that inform theoretical analysis and investigation. These questions include whether similar configurations can be found in non-conservative systems, whether noise affects chimeras by solidifying their stability or reducing their stable population, and whether chimeras can be observed in non-identical population networks, such as those representing differing cell types within a tumor or immune response, for example. The answers to these questions lie outside the scope of this particular study and will require separate investigations to resolve. However, this study provides a significant theoretical foundation and new insights that inform these questions and pave the way for exploring chimeras in a broader range of coupled oscillator systems. Ultimately, the unique characteristics of chimeras make them attractive targets for study within various biological and physical coupled oscillator systems, and may also allow for a deeper and more precise evaluation of real-world systems studied in this research.

Quantum particles experiencing tunneling can be studied by analyzing the Larmor clock in a weak magnetic field. The clock registers two tunneling times,  $\tau_y$ and $\tau_z$, corresponding to particles approaching a potential barrier in the $y$ or $z$ direction. There is a discrepancy between the definition of tunneling time by B{\"u}ttiker and Steinberg, with the latter identifying the actual tunneling time (ATT) with the Larmor clock reading for the $y$ direction. Research, however, has shown that ATT is influenced by spin fluctuations in non-commuting spin systems. Consequently, we've established an ATT based on fluctuations that is given by the expression $\tau_y + \frac{\tau_z^2}{\tau_y}$. Our analysis reveals that at low barrier strengths, the difference between the two tunneling time measures is minimal but becomes significant at higher barrier strengths. Through an experiment using a two-level ion system, we've verified the ATT as being both physical and adjustable. Our work also indicates that ATT is unrelated to the phase factor in tunneling and provides an adjustable means of modifying tunneling times with the application of spin fluctuations. Finally, we've compared our work with existing tunneling time measures such as the geometric, peak arrival time and Steinberg's ATT. Our findings show that ATT is a universal and scalable method for adjusting tunneling times in potential barriers. For instance, at barrier strength equal to 0.5, the ATT is 0.5 times the classical tunneling time in the infinite barrier limit. Our work, therefore, offers the unique opportunity to manipulate quantum particles' tunneling behavior using magnetic fields and tunable frequency ranges. This could be especially significant in quantum information and may pave the way for developing tunneling time-based quantum information systems. Ultimately, we've demonstrated through the experimental realization and varied tuning of ATT that it offers an innovative means of handling quantum systems' tunneling behavior. As such, it may serve as a foundation for developing qubit-like systems based on the variable tunneling times in quantum systems. This could particularly facilitate the construction of qubits with variable geometric phases as proposed within recent research. Our work, therefore, not only resolves the different definitions of tunneling time but also highlights the significance of spin fluctuations in tunneling and may notably contribute to the development of tunneling time-based quantum information systems. However, the current understanding of BECs relies on complex descriptions, often through quantum field theory, which can make developments challenging. A more accessible alternative is offered by matrix product operator (MPO) methods, which facilitate the efficient simulation of one, or two, component BECs. Unlike traditional mean field approaches that imply no nonlinearity effects in quantum simulations, MPO techniques allow for the exploration of nonlinear effects in quantum simulations, even in the mean field regime. We examine the MPO formalism's connection to the Vlasov equation, which often arises in BECs, and discuss its implications. We then explore nonlinear quantum interferometer designs that outperform their linear counterparts in phase sensitivity, showcasing two new designs that leverage the nonlinearity to boost sensitivity without any post-selection. Finally, we investigate the practicality of implementing MPO-based simulations by examining the characteristics of BEC sources that produce wave packets with low Bloch number, thus facilitating efficient simulations. Along the way, we establish an analogy between quantum BEC simulations and classical fluid dynamics, which may have additional applications. Overall, our work demonstrates the efficacy of MPO methods in harnessing nonlinear quantum mechanics to enhance quantum interferometry and information processing. Moreover, our investigations focus on both theoretical and experimental feasibility, making our contributions relevant to multiple contextual settings, including closed-systems, open-systems, and interaction-free measurements. If an interaction-free measurement setup were employed, our interferometer design could potentially supersed the existing record in single-photon interferometry, which is currently held by a number of designs with high sensitivity, including the recent recorded value from 2020. Finally, our experiments also contribute to understanding the complex problem of BEC wave interference, which is difficult to tackle using mean-field theories, by leveraging the Vlasov equation and our MPO formalism to accurately forecast our experimental results. We establish that mean-field approaches, which often apply linear behavior even in the mean field regime, are insufficient for explaining our interferometer's behavior, which exhibits clear nonlinear effects. Therefore, we propose that our MPO-based simulations, which capture these nonlinear effects, are a reliable way to validate experimental research, particularly when simulated classical fluids are not applicable, due to the inherently quantum nature of the system. Nonetheless, the presence of intestinal parasites can typically be established via simple visual examination of feces. It incorporates both proportional reinsurance and loss-overlimit reinsurance models. To calculate the Nash equilibrium, a Markov chain approximation approach is developed. This involves constructing an iterative sequence of Markov chains, each corresponding to a specific state and time, which converges towards a Nash equilibrium as the state and time increase. An explicit Nash equilibrium solution is derived for a simple, two-player game in this context. Furthermore, numerical case studies examining investment and reinsurance relationships in the presence of credit risks are conducted. These case studies demonstrate the efficacy of the Markov chain approximation approach and validate its ability to support the analysis of equilibrium strategies under varying conditions. In particular, it is shown that although equilibrium strategies do not depend on specific model parameters, calculated Nash equilibria do exhibit dependence on these parameters. Additionally, players may benefit from knowing the characteristics of their opponent in certain situations, but this advantage is lost when the opponent's information is unavailable. An example case study illustrating the emergence of Markovian behavior in a player's optimal strategy is also presented. In this study, it was found that when certain conditions relating to player knowledge and credit risks are met, a player's optimal strategy does indeed exhibit Markovian behavior. are described within the context of partial-wave unitarity. The formal framework is then
applied to pion-nucleon scattering with partial-wave unitarity constraints combined with
sensitivities to the low-energy constant $C_5^1$. Our approach also encompasses the construction
of an in-medium modification for the pion-nucleon interaction, critical for understanding the properties
of finite nuclei and nuclear matter. The role of this interaction in the context of finite nuclei and the ground-state
energy of nuclear matter is evaluated. The units of $C_5^1$ for pion-nucleon coupling are established,
important for understanding the collective behavior of particles. The relationship between $C_5^1$ and the pion-nucleon
sigma term is critically examined, given that the latter directly impacts the ground-state energy of nuclear matter. The
determination of $C_5^1$ also influences the characteristics of finite nuclei and is seen to be closely linked to the pion mass. 
Ultimately, the pion-nucleon sigma term and $C_5^1$ play vital roles in understanding low-energy interactions and atomic and
nuclear structures. The experimental measurement of $C_5^1$ remains challenging due to its sensitivity primarily to the lowest-order

in an attempt to establish the value of the pion-nucleon sigma term, important for understanding low-energy interactions. However,
this approach is seen to be subject to significant uncertainties driven by the value used for the pion-nucleon sigma term,
critically limiting its accuracy. Two alternative methods for determining the pion-nucleon sigma term are identified,
important for understanding low-energy interactions. The chiral effective field theory and the partial-wave unitarity constraints

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) is one of the primary detectors in the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN, tracking particle interactions resulting from high-energy collisions. As part of the CMS system, the silicon pixel detector forms the innermost component responsible for navigating the trajectory of particles. Although initially operational between 2009 and 2016, it has been replaced with an upgraded variant in 2017. During a preceding period of shutdown for the LHC, an upgraded forward pixel detector prototype featuring a novel readout system and third disk was introduced, integrating eight pilot blades built using advanced digital readout chips. Through pilot module testing, researchers obtained practical experience in operating the upgraded detector. This study reports the results of analyzing data captured with these new components, including a detailed explanation of the reconstruction process and associated calibration steps. Furthermore, it includes illustrations of the hit finding efficiency and track-hit residual patterns. These outcomes serve as a basis for implementing improvements in software used to interpret the upgraded forward pixel detector's data output. Furthermore, designers have leveraged these test results to refine parameters for producing finalized electronic components for the full detector system. These advancements include enhanced design rules for the application of thin-wired components and optimized design rules for the generation of customized plastic molds. Finally, this study documents the initial experiences in manufacturing customized plastic molds, highlighting potential issues resulting from mold deformation during the molding process, as well as the detection of mold-related defects. These investigations have led to the development of recommended protocols for creating molds and thin-wired circuits, as well as the implementation of testing procedures for forward pixel forward pilot modules. These procedures have since been applied to the production of individual front-end modules, as well as the production of operational front-end modules, as demonstrated in the successful production of 50 QIE11 modules and 10 produced FEI4m modules. These advancements have significantly contributed to the achievement of production milestones, as the production of 288 front-end module units, as well as four production board lots, was successfully completed. These production milestones marked an important milestone in the progress towards meeting the scheduled installation deadline in 2022. However, as the COVID-19 pandemic persisted, production slowed due to the unforeseen complications arising from the conflict between supply demands and global restrictions. This research introduces SQUID, an open-source tool for developing and training hybrid Quantum-Classical classification algorithms. It utilizes PyTorch for the classical components, allowing for the creation of multiple quantum models that can be optimized with back-propagation. We demonstrate SQUID's capabilities by showcasing its implementation in a standard binary classification task from the widely-used MNIST dataset. Notably, we discuss how the choice of output affects the scalability of quantum models when utilizing gradient-based optimization. SQUID comes with pre-built features for the VQE optimizer and a comprehensive validation process to ensure that each iteration of the code yields comparable results to the conventional PyTorch framework. It is compatible with IBMQ, AWS Braket, and Qiskit, making it a versatile tool for classification tasks. We make public the experiments conducted with SQUID on IQART dataset, showing strong performance even when the quantum model is relatively simple. We suggest that the SQUID tool can facilitate the growth of quantum classification research, paving the way for new findings and contributions. Additionally, we share useful suggestions derived from our experimentation that could benefit other researchers working on similar projects. This paper is part of a research line focused on developing quantum-classical classification algorithms. For more information, please refer to the corresponding paper from the research line, available at 10.1002/open.20220108. To replicate the results, visit the public repository at https://github.com/ingl/ingl-qc.
