Interpreting teaching instructions with natural language can be compromised by the complexity of meaning, often leading to misunderstandings. Learners may misinterpret the intentions behind teacher-provided information when object characteristics are ambiguously described, a problem known as referential ambiguity. We explore how principles from cognitive sciences, such as teaching strategies (tailoring instructions) and adapting to agent preferences, can mitigate referential ambiguities through induction. Our experiments involve training two artificial agents to accomplish a simulated robotic task through instruction. Although the teacher knows the object's true nature (a cube), the learner has limited knowledge, making it reliant on the teacher's descriptions. To combat referential ambiguity, the learner employs inductive strategies, such as learning a probability matrix to infer the object's attributes from the teacher's descriptions. We found that the teacher can reduce the negative impact of referential ambiguity by adapting her language to the learner's preferences. We also found that the teacher can further aid the learner by providing descriptions that maximize mutual understanding. Our results suggest that the complexity of natural language instruction can be mitigated through inducutive strategies, such as tailoring instructions, adapting to agent preferences, and learning probabilistic structures to infer object attributes, ultimately enhancing communication between the teacher and learner. These findings may inform the creation of more effective communication systems, including educational interfaces. Our source code is available online. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of inducutive strategies in mitigating referential ambiguities, setting the stage for advancements in robotic training through semantically-enriched natural language instruction. As a result, this work contributes to the development of more efficient communication systems and could inspire the creation of a universal training language for teaching artificial agents, including robots. Our source code can be accessed at https://github.com/arindamvi/inductive-RL. Our research involves simulated robotics tasks and can be applied to real robotic tasks in the future. Quantum process tomography is crucial for building quantum computers, establishing quantum networks, and developing quantum sensors. Like state tomography, characterizing an arbitrary quantum channel necessitates a massive number of measurements, exponentially increasing with the number of quantum bits involved. Recent advancements in shadow tomography, specifically in state measurement, have revealed the possibility of extracting crucial state information using only polynomially many measurements. This study brings shadow state tomography and quantum process tomography together, allowing the reconstruction of an arbitrary quantum channel employing just polynomially many measurements of its associated probability distributions. This process, called shadow quantum process tomography, relies on two key components: a quantum algorithm capable of simulating the quantum channel, and a classical algorithm using shadow measurements to optimize the reconstruction of the quantum channel. Furthermore, our results include developing an efficient quantum algorithm for simulating quantum channels and demonstrating the quantum advantage in certain multi-qubit scenarios. This study lays the groundwork for more efficient and accessible quantum communication over complex networks. It also marks the first instance where quantum process tomography has outperformed classical processes, showcasing the significance of quantum advantage in multi-qubit systems. This research further opens doors for further optimization, enabling the creation of more precise channel estimators and potentially aiding in solving challenging problems, such as generating helpful quantum channels for efficient data transfer. The internet of things encompasses a network of interconnected devices, which includes various non-standard gadgets, traditionally unlinked to the internet, at an exponentially growing pace. Data security and user privacy concerns loom large over the IoT landscape, where devices operate on low power. Conventional encryption methods are unsuitable for these devices, necessitating a need for contemporary lightweight algorithms tailored for IoT settings, which this paper aims to address. A novel lightweight encryption method, inspired by permutations, is presented here. Its underlying idea stems from factoring a given number into a product of small prime factors, which is a well-established approach. This method employs a permutation of alphanumeric characters, followed by a finite field multiplication-based diffusion process to achieve both confidentiality and integrity, outperforming established permutations in terms of computational efficiency. Several evaluations, including the Resilient Encryption algorithm test, reveal the proposed method surpasses the confidentiality aspect of a comparable permutation-based algorithm. Moreover, this method requires minimal computational resources, making it suitable for devices with limited processing capabilities, thus highly suitable for IoT applications. A proposed implementation strategy using an RF energy harvester wireless sensor node demonstrates its feasibility. A real-world implementation shows the proposed method's computational overhead is roughly 0.11% of the energy consumed by the entire sensor node. Furthermore, this research investigates the potential for further developing this method into a full encryption algorithm. Its future directions for expansion are also explored. A possible extension of this method is examined using the AES algorithm. Specifically, this method can be used as the initial round of a modified AES algorithm, which also incorporates the data compression algorithm, ZIP. A simulation using the National Institute of Standards and Technology test suite reveals the expanded algorithm surpasses the confidentiality aspect of a full AES encryption by a significant margin. This method's unique aspect lies in its ability to achieve confidentiality and integrity with an exceptionally low amount of computational resources, making it an attractive candidate for IoT settings. Its implementation as an open-source project aims to accelerate adoption. Further scope for future research is also identified. A possible direction for this research involves exploring the use of steganography for IoT applications, which is also explored in this paper. A novel concept for embedding secret text within images is presented, specifically designed for low-power wireless sensor nodes that operate within energy constraints. Due to the limited battery life, these nodes have to be turned off when not in use, resulting in the presence of periodic power-up and power-down noise in their transmitted signals. This unique periodic noise presents an opportunity for the proposed method to hide the secret text

Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct scales. From a geometric perspective, a multi-scale centrality is defined by a node's relative position or distance to its boundary points within a given network. Theoretical frameworks enable the derivation of metrics like the triangle inequality excess (TIE) and information entropy excess (HE) for nodes, depending on multi-scale considerations. For scale up to a certain value, TIE significantly outperforms HE in differentiating central from peripheral nodes, although it struggles with differentiating highly connected central nodes. In contrast, HE surpasses TIE in this distinction and is more robust to node connectivity. The study introduces a novel multi-scale centrality metric, HE or TIE, to characterize nodes, then develops an algorithm combining these metrics to calculate geometric (Gromov) centrality. The analysis shows Gromov centrality is more sensitive to TIE and HE, with the latter outperforming the former in distinguishing central from peripheral nodes and requiring fewer inputs, despite incuring a computational cost. The study also demonstrates the application of Gromov centrality in various applications, such as community detection, shortest path optimization, and finding the network's geometric center. The practical effectiveness of these applications is validated by comparative analysis with existing methods. The research is accompanied by an open-source software implementation for the metrics and algorithm in this study. Sets of matrix pencils sharing the same Kronecker canonical form are classified under strict equivalence into infinite groups called bundles. Introduced in the 1990s, this concept is an extension of the earlier idea by Arnold in 1971, relating to matrices under similarity transformations. Despite substantial research on the topic, a general formula remains unknown even to this day. However, a new approach presented here involves using a matrix fraction description to generalize the formula originally developed by Arnold for matrices to matrix pencils. Key properties of the new method include its ability to be applied backwards for matrix matrices and its reliance on a fundamental concept: the minimal realization of a matrix fraction. This technique is illustrated through examples that also highlight its capabilities and weaknesses. Furthermore, it builds on existing theory by generalizing the method for finding canonical structures previously established by Arnold. While the new method shares many similarities with those already existing, it is shown that, in some cases, the reverse approach is not equivalent to existing ones, leading to the concept of double infinite groups, which are associated with pairs of matrix pencils. Lastly, a new method is proposed for determining the order of finite groups based on a matrix pencil's minimal realization. This approach is shown to be effective in identifying the order of both finite groups associated with matrices and finite groups associated with matrix of size 2x2 or greater. This technique is illustrated through examples that also highlight its capabilities and weaknesses. Programs written in MATLAB and MAPLE are provided to support the new theory and methods. They allow for the calculation of various properties such as indices, orders, and canonical forms for both matrix and matrix pencil sets. They also enable the computation of minimal realizations in both directions and are capable of handling matrices of any size, including square, rectangular, and non-singular ones. They are specifically designed to handle matrix pencils of rank n+p-1, with n and p being positive integers. We removed the extra logarithmic factor by developing a new embedding technique that replaces the random selection of treewidth vertices with a deterministic process. As an important contribution to the field, we also show that under a widely assumed hypothesis regarding the lower treewidth bound, $O_{\epsilon}(n^{\frac{1}{5}}\log^2 n)$ is the actual treewidth bound for graphs with diameter $D$ and minor-free property. Furthermore, we enhanced our results by applying them to research previously conducted by others, such as efficiently solving the single-source shortest paths problem on minor-free graphs and approximating non-uniform metric facilities location problems. The existence of a primordial stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) is highly likely, having been predicted by multiple theories including inflation, the process of cosmic string formation and more. A SGWB of this type could have significant consequences, altering the universe's expansion pattern and altering distance relationships in a way that could impact cosmological measurements. In this study, we explore how a SGWB produced via cosmic string loop collisions would appear in gravitational-wave observations, and find that it could be discerned via its anisotropy. By applying this same method to a SGWB generated during inflation, we discover that it would be impossible to distinguish from a SGWB produced via cosmic string loop collisions, with the resulting constraints being highly restrictive. Our research also makes provision for other potential sources such as binary black hole mergers and magnetar magnetization, demonstrating that they do not significantly contribute to the anisotropy of a SGWB. In the case of a SGWB produced via the Ekpysis model, we identify a unique characteristic in its pure scale-invariant spectrum within a particular strain range ($10^{-3}$-$10^{-2}$), with the resulting Ekpysis model Anisotropy (EMA) being highly restrictive. In all our models examined, the resulting SGWB anisotropy, $A$, places a limit on model parameter values: for a SGWB produced via cosmic string loop collisions $G\dot{\Omega^2}\le 8.9\times 10^{-16}$; for a SGWB produced via the Ekpysis model $H_{f}\le 1.6\times 10^{-2}$; for a SGWB produced via inflation $G^{(I)\rho}\psi\psi$ no limit exists while for a SGWB produced via magnetic fields $B_{10}$ no limit exists. In near future observations, it may be possible to use the resulting anisotropy, $A$, to discern whether SGWBs originate from Ekpyris, cosmic string loop collisions or a combination of the two models. In all our models examined, the resulting SGWB spectrum exhibits significant breaking of rotational symmetry. Our study presents the first survey of molecular emissions from a comet's volatile substances. We utilized spectroscopic technology to analyze the spectral lines from multiple species in the tail of a specific comet, C/2015 ER61. The data collected through three observations in 2016 were analyzed using various astronomical methods, resulting in the detection of several species, including CH4, NH3, H2O, CO2, and H2S. These molecules were identified through specific spectral lines that were then quantified to determine their relative concentrations in the comet's tail. The binding energies for these species were obtained from theoretical models, providing a comprehensive understanding of the comet's volatile substances. The data analysis indicates that CH4 and H2O are the primary sources of carbon and oxygen in the observed species, while NH3 was found to be more abundant than expected. Additionally, we discovered an unusually high ratio of CS to CH4, which may be attributed to the presence of complex organic molecules in the comet. The findings reveal the diverse composition of the comet's volatile substances and its potential link to the original interstellar materials that formed its parent body. The data also highlight CS as an indicator for CS2 in CS-bearing astrophysical sources, and its presence may be related to the degradation of organic matter. The dataset and spectra are available online at the Digital Object Identifier System. Our study contributes to the understanding of comet compositions by providing high-accuracy volume emission rate measurements for potentially biogenic molecules. Furthermore, a subsequent experiment showcases the unsupervised system's ability to scale more efficiently in terms of processing time. Lastly, a corresponding audio demonstration can be found at https://danielkoehrsen.github.io/demos.html.

Multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems frequently arise in real-world contexts, notably in mechanical engineering. A novel approach, combining multi-criteria branch-and-bound and non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, is proposed for approximating near-optimal solutions for such problems. A computational study, comparing this hybrid method to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, demonstrates its efficacy in obtaining high-quality solutions within a reduced computational time. A real-world engineering design example and the well-known multi-objective problem of distributing goods and collecting refuse are used to test the proposed algorithm. Compared to non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, the hybrid method, considering approximation ratios, computational times, and solution quality measures shows a substantial improvement. Additionally, the hybrid method, branching from high-quality non-dominated solutions, significantly enhances the search process by focusing on promising regions. A theoretical convergence analysis of non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm 2, supporting the hybrid method, is also established. Therefore, the proposed hybrid framework holds great promise for solving multi-objective mixed-integer non-linear programming problems. Its potential is further underscored by a real-world biomedical design example, where it successfully solves challenging multi-objective problems. Furthermore, a multi-objective version of the multi-layer neural network learning problem is investigated using the proposed algorithm. This enables the formulation of a Lie theory framework, focusing on local connected Lie groupoids. The development of this framework lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive Lie theory. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a particular aspect within product reviews. Approximately one-third of reviews lack explicit opinion words, yet clearly convey human-aware sentiment, classified as implicit sentiment. Unfortunately, neural network-based methods have overlooked implicit sentiment in reviews. To address this, we utilize a supervised pre-training approach on extensive sentiment-annotated datasets drawn from relevant linguistic sources. By aligning implicit sentiment phrases with their matching sentiment labels, this pre-training method significantly improves the capture of both explicit and implicit sentiment orientations in reviews towards specific aspects. Our technique exhibits superior performance on the SemEval 2014 benchmarks and an in-depth examination demonstrates its ability to extract implicit sentiment orientations. Moreover, we present a benchmark dataset for aspect-based sentiment analysis, which comprises of 15,000 reviews, each containing three instances of different aspects with accompanying sentiment orientations. This dataset is constructed by merging existing datasets with explicit sentiment orientations, while our model is also put to test on this new dataset. Our source code is available at https://github.com/achutkedia/Absa-Implicit. This research is an extension of our previous work, with significant enhancements in code quality through the adoption of state-of-the-art practices in machine learning. By raising the bar in reproducibility, we aim to set new standards in the field. Unfortunately, our model still shows limited capability in detecting implicit sentiment when practical applications require zero-shot learning, i.e., identifying product aspects a user has never mentioned before. As a result, this paper investigates a simple approach to enhance explicit sentiment orientations using purely unsupervised methods, thus resulting in implicit sentiment orientations to match the product aspects a user has expressed, but never explicitly stated. This approach is tested on a popular dataset and reviewed. Our work is finally concluded by highlighting the limitations of the Absa task in capturing implicit sentiment orientations. This research delves into secure communication systems for multiple users that utilize reconfigurable intelligent surfaces to compensate for hardware limitations.
We simultaneously adjust the base station's beamforming vectors and the phase shifts on the RIS to achieve the highest possible weighted minimum secrecy rate under constraints for the base station's power output and RIS elements.
To address this optimization challenge, we split the problem into two simpler subproblems and use the block coordinate descent approach to iteratively solve for these subproblems.
Our numerical results confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm in reaching a secure rate threshold, and we also compare its performance to an algorithm that ensures the sum rate is maximized for multiple users without considering security constraints. This comparison reveals that the proposed algorithm can achieve a substantial rate increase over its counterpart.
Finally, to further demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency, we evaluate its computational complexity and observe that the number of required iterations to converge is significantly lower than the number of RIS elements. This performance characteristic enables the algorithm to be seamlessly extended to scenarios with either a large number of RIS elements or a limited number of iterations. Moreover, this analysis highlights that the number of required iterations can be made arbitrarily small when the RIS has a large number of elements. Conversely, this dependence on the number of iterations when the RIS has a limited number of elements can be arbitrarily decreased by increasing the RIS size. To facilitate the usage of this algorithm in practical applications, we compare its computational complexity under two scenarios: one with a large number of RIS elements and one with a limited number of iterations and RIS elements.
Our analysis indicates that the algorithm has a computational complexity that is directly proportional to the number of RIS elements in the first scenario and to the number of iterations in the second scenario.
To make the algorithm more suitable for real-world implementations, we investigate its convergence rate and observe that it can reach a substantial part of its maximum value within a number of iterations that is linear with the number of RIS elements.

This study provides the first detailed analysis of the solar wind energy flux observed near the inner solar corona, following the Parker Solar Probe's missions conducted near the Sun's equator. During these missions, the solar wind energy flux, measured in units of W/m^2, was recorded in a lower-than-expected state. Specifically, the spacecraft observed an average energy flux of 20.2 W/m^2 with a standard deviation of 7.7 W/m^2 at a distance of 0.75 solar radii from the Sun's center. As the Sun's coronal radiation exhibits significant variability, the researchers considered and calculated the average energy flux, denoted as $\langle \xi \rangle$, when the solar wind trajectory intersected the Sun's equatorial plane at a distance of 1 solar radius. After offline training, the neural network model can be used in conjunction with a finite volume scheme, which requires mesh adaptation. One distinct advantage of this approach is its ability to eliminate CFL restrictions, permitting a wider range of time step sizes. Furthermore, when solving the Heat equation, convergence rates and error magnitudes show dependence on the spatial mesh size while being independent of the time step size. Moreover, when incorporating a finite difference term, the neural network model can achieve a Schrodinger equation solution accuracy of $O(\tau^2+h^2)$. The Unruh effect can be created by quantizing a electromagnetic field in a different way - by considering acceleration instead of simply translating to a new frame. This approach can be used to derive the Unruh effect without relying on adiabatic methods. When accelerated, a vacuum state of the electromagnetic field appears as a mixture of photons with an infrared spectrum. This phenomenon can be studied using soft photon behavior in quantum electrodynamics. It was discovered that photons behave similarly to charged particles during acceleration and help manifest the vacuum state's quantum entanglement properties. These observations align with experiments in relativistic heavy-ion collisions, which allow for the emulation of electromagnetic field dynamics in a quasi-classical state. This emulation is due to the collective movement of charged particles in the process, ultimately connecting the Unruh effect to photoproduction in ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions. Furthermore, it was found that photons generated during such collisions can serve as a probe of the Unruh effect. This probe can reveal key details, such as temperature and chemical potential, which are essential for understanding the quantum field dynamics in these collisions. Lastly, collisions that emulate the Unruh effect are also expected to exhibit a violation of Lorentz invariance, according to research, a concept that has been studied in various experiments. However, this expectation is still at odds with the results of a number of optical ladder experiments, which have not yet observed such a violation, despite being capable of detecting similar phenomena with higher precision. This discrepancy remains an open challenge in the field of fundamental physics.

It is based on a proposed new gravitational potential and derived from a mass distribution where matter outside the radial distance orbits in a clockwise direction. This model assumes a continuous, uniform flow of mass that adapts to the orbiting object's influence. To evaluate its effectiveness, we have calculated several astronomical parameters, including orbital potentials, forces, orbital periods, and perihelion time delays. These parameters are mathematically compared with Newton's and Modified Newtonian Dynamics models. Our research identifies a suitable range for the potential's parameter that accurately reproduces the perihelion advance in Mercury's orbit when compared with other alternatives. It also shows that the theory can potentially explain orbital light distribution, orbital velocity, and surface gravity data for the Earth, provided that the assumed mass distribution is adjusted accordingly. Recent observations of fast radio bursts (FRBs) have led to ongoing debates over their origins. While some theoretical models predict certain characteristics that have not yet been observed, others are supported by available data. Notably, optical studies of FRB 180924 provided valuable insights into flare dynamics, suggesting that lower energy flares may be less visible due to ionization of surrounding material. Our research examines the potential to detect FRB-associated transients using telescopes like the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Very Large Telescope, finding that such events would need to occur with extremely short durations to remain undetected. This has implications for coherent radiation theory, which predicts lower energy flares but may be at odds with observational limits on such events. Ultimately, the lack of detectable transients has tangible consequences for astrophysical models like magnetar burps and jet ejections, necessitating an adjustment in the predicted radiation emission patterns. Our research demonstrates that while optical observations constrained FRB-associated transients, they did not eliminate the potential for such events in certain models, and the incompatibility of observed FRB radiation patterns with those of certain burps necessitates an adjustment in the magnitude of the radial struggle. Our data suggest the possibility of detecting radiation associated with FRB 20190428 using ascribed telescopes, and further studies are needed to determine the compatibility of FRB 181025 radiation patterns with those from magnetar burps. 

Our research has led to the creation of an optical detection tool that enables the assessment of the likelihood of detectability for individual FRBs based on their radiation patterns. This assessment is based on the parameters that determine the duration and energy of radiation-associated transients produced in the context of magnetar burps. Our results confirm that burp-produced radiation would be detectable by telescopes like the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Very Large Telescope for events like FRB 180924 but not for FRB 181125; furthermore, burp-produced radiation would not be detectable by telescopes like the Gran Telescopio Canarias and the Very Large Telescope for events like FRB 20190428, FRB 20151225, and FRB 20191124. Our research indicates that the non-detection of radiation-associated transients in FRBs raises questions about the compatibility of observed FRB radiation patterns with those from magnetar burps; alternatively, burp-produced radiation would not be detectable by telescopes like the Very Large Array and the Chandra X-ray Observatory

Multimodal language generation capabilities of models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 can be leveraged for producing high-quality text, but it is still uncertain how they can be directed by image guidance during the generation process. A new framework called MAGIC was introduced to address this issue by developing an approach for image-guided text generation. Unlike existing methods that use a two-stage process, MAGIC combines the image and language objectives into an iterative process where image-guided text generation is performed in a balanced manner of image and language information. As a result, MAGIC achieves the goal of image-guided text generation by treating it as a balloon inflation problem where image information causes text to expand in specific ways based on the given image guidance. For training objectives, MAGIC utilizes a unique loss function called the cosine balloon loss function and novel image-guided loss functions. By demonstrating its efficacy, MAGIC was shown to outperform state-of-the-art models like GPT-2 and GPT-3 in image-guided text generation tasks and existing loss function-based methods. Additionally, MAGIC was used to set new performance standards for image-guided text generation and existing image-guided text generation baselines. Further experiments were conducted to examine the effects of specific image guidance mechanisms, text generation model capacities, and varying image guidance strengths on the performance of MAGIC. Interestingly, it was observed that MAGIC is resilient to overfitting image guidance and text generation overfitting, but fails when the two sources of guidance conflict. Moreover, MAGIC was found to successfully direct the generation process using multiple images, varying image guidance strengths, and raw image inputs. Finally, MAGIC was used to introduce a new task called image-to-capacity text generation to study how image guidance affects the generation process. For the complete implementation of MAGIC, please see the attached supplementary material. The final results show that MAGIC outperforms prior image-guided text generation approaches and baselines by achieving higher scores in existing image-guided text generation evaluation benchmarks, and sets new performance standards in image-guided text generation tasks. The MAGIC framework offers an alternative approach for image-guided text generation by balancing image and language information during the generation process and demonstrates its efficacy and robustness to various image guidance mechanisms, text generation models, and varying image guidance strengths. Moreover, MAGIC is a universal image-guided text generation framework that can be used with any text generation model and image guidance mechanism. The final objective is that MAGIC can be used to direct the generation process in a more balanced manner in image-guided text generation and active learning settings.

In 2015, CERN introduced "Emittance Scans," a new fast luminosity separation scanning method at the Large Hadron Collider. These scans were consistently carried out during physics production runs, utilizing full-intensity beams at the CMS experiment's interaction point. The emittance scans allowed for the simultaneous measurement of beam properties and closed orbits at the level of individual bunches, yielding precise insights into long-range beam-beam effects, as predicted by the improved TRAIN code. The dataset obtained enabled a precise correction of beam alignment at the level of individual bunches, a development known as "beam-based kick correction." This correction process was applied in real-time via the Global Alignment system and was effective as of 2016, an approach that was effectively used in Run II of the Large Hadron Collider. This document provides a comprehensive review of the emittance scan implementation, including the related setup, measurement, and analysis, as well as physical insights gained from the emittance scan dataset. The document concludes by exploring potential applications of the emittance scan method to other particle accelerators. While this document primarily focuses on the CMS context, the described methods are equally applicable to other experiments using the LHC. The document opens up opportunities for integration with other beam physics tasks, such as improvements to beam alignment and tuning, simulations of beam-beam effects, and beam physics analysis. As such, the document is relevant to a broader community involving particle physics experiments and beam studies. The document is available in PDF format. Nevertheless, a challenge persists in neural networks' tendency to 'forget' previous tasks after training on new ones. This drawback restricts cooperative advancements since modifying an existing model to solve a new task often interferes with previously acquired skills. This work demonstrates the effectiveness of two continual learning methods, against which the performance of three techniques is evaluated. These techniques utilize memory: either storing samples from each task (EWC) or generating data similar to each task (DALE) or creating data similar to each task ( DACO). This research aims to facilitate collaborative development among the mechanics community by providing valuable insights into cooperative modeling. Verifying facts using structured data can be a difficult task. A recent approach involved predicting evidence scores for specific claims based on available data, but this method requires a significant amount of labeled data and a particular type of output - a binary score that can be hard to obtain. To tackle this challenge, we develop an alternative approach called structural inference, which leverages underlying structures to support the analysis of multiple evidence sources. This approach transforms difficult inference problems into more manageable and interpretable outcomes. To demonstrate its potential, we apply structural inference to the context of verbal scores - a valuable resource in fact verification. Here, claims and evidence are represented as directed relationships within a graph, and associated verbal scores serve as edge labels. Building upon this concept, we introduce StructED - a novel method that predicts verbal scores by considering not only individual edge properties but also their connections to surrounding nodes. This method demands less labeled data compared to existing approaches, offers better performance, increased fidelity, and provides more accurate insights into claim validity. Ultimately, we believe that structural inference has a bright future in handling complex structured data across multiple inference challenges. The source code for our method can be found on the GitHub repository https://github.com/PracticalAI/StructED. We are proud to have achieved an 8.4% increase in peak performance on the FactCite dataset while reducing data requirements by 50%. The StructED model is now available for public use, enabling fact verification facilities to enhance their output quality and transparency. Additionally, we hope that our method may be applied across a broader spectrum of multi-modal structured data challenges in the future. A public demo of our method can be accessed at https://demostruced.github.io. We truly believe that our method has the potential to be expanded to other important applications, allowing us to better analyze and understand the validity of information presented to us. A humanitarian example of this is fact verification for medical purposes where accurately assessing the reliability of presented information is crucial. For instance, suppose a patient is considering whether radiation treatment is effective for their specific type of cancer and comes across an unverified statement claiming that such treatment increases patient survival rates. We explore the potential of leveraging object category information to guide the generation of synthetic images from limited real images. Unlike unsupervised approaches that often result in a lack of diversity and poor quality, we demonstrate that incorporating ground truth object category data enables precise control over the generated images, allowing us to isolate specific object categories within complex scenes. This research introduces a novel supervised image synthesis framework, Partitioned Generative Adversarial Networks (PGANs), which efficiently exploits detailed real images to create high-resolution synthetic images. The core innovation of PGANs lies in partitioning the input image into distinct object categories and generating each entity. The performance of PGANs is compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, including a standard generative adversarial network (GAN) approach. Experimental evaluations using the Sun database 24 (SUN24) dataset reveal that our approach surpasses other methods in terms of synthesizing accurate and diverse images, particularly for complex scenes involving multiple object categories. Furthermore, we showcase the ability of PGANs to detect errors in scene parsing annotations, a capability not previously demonstrated in unsupervised image generation techniques. The generated results and source code are publicly available on https://github.com/Ankittg/PGANs. To the best of our knowledge, this research marks the first successful application of object category-guided image generation using ground truth data, thereby opening new avenues for the supervised synthesis of complex scenes and object-driven visual retrieval applications. The PGAN model has also been made available on https://anekvision.github.io/pgans/. Lastly, a web-based interactive demo of our results can be found at https://anekvision.github.io/pgans-demo/. The research was conducted at the Adobe Research department.

Unlike other algorithms that leverage a fixed point approximation, these methods use a branching approximation. They display a marked improvement in high-dimensional problems and are robust across low and high dimensional scenarios. Our work presents an algorithm that provides a labelling scheme with a specified length (O(log(n)/log(3.5)) times a minimal number) for any connected graph containing any number of nodes. This allows us to efficiently adapt to changes in the graph structure by only modifying the labels of affected vertices in O(log(n)) times the number of affected vertices, producing a more adaptable version of an existing algorithm with similar label length. Additionally, we propose a variation that maintains consistency, achieving nearly identical label length while ensuring the labels adapt uniformly across the deleted or modified structures, operating in O(log(n)k-1 log(n)/log(3.5)) time and preserving the original distance measurement precision, where k represents the number of the vertices involved in the deletion or modification. This variant also holds significance in the realm of remote updating, allowing us to efficiently update complex graphs while retaining the ability to accurately calculate distances. In this theoretical study, we explore two-particle correlations in time and frequency for a Bose-Hubbard model subject to external driving and dissipation, specifically at and around the point where dissipation triggers a phase transition. We calculate a temporal two-particle correlation function and observe oscillations that decline when the model's imaginary Liouvillian gap narrows, a behavior that indicates a transition is imminent. When parameters deviate slightly from this transition, our findings suggest that super-bunching and anti-bunching regimes coexist, a behavior revealed when super-Bloch oscillations are analyzed in the many-body wave function. We also uncover an approximate relationship between the driving-induced frequency shift of the Liouvillian gap and this super-Bloch oscillation frequency, a behavior that holds at and around the transition. Moreover, our super-Bloch oscillation frequency at the transition matches the driving-induced frequency, a behavior that holds at and predicts an approximate linear increase in two-particle correlation frequency for small deviation parameter values. We have also derived correlations based on number conservation using an effective model, and these show similar behavior to the findings from exact calculations, specifically a single minimum in the two-particle correlation function, a behavior that holds for and out of the transition. We compare these findings with two other methods, mean-field theory and a model with conserved particle number, and observe that the last two only correctly predict the two-particle correlation behavior that closely mimics boson sampling, a behavior that holds directly after the transition. We conclude that the super-Bloch oscillation frequency at the transition is a robust signature of the model's driving-induced transition, a behavior that can be identified from two-particle correlations in time and frequency. Given that such a behavior can be seen in a variety of systems and is relatively easy to measure, it provides a very general test of driven-dissipative dynamics, a behavior that falls under the broader class of many-body dynamics. Moreover, our calculations reveal that while number-conservation correlation behavior and super-Bloch oscillations are distinct, they are not independent, a behavior that can be predicted through analyzing super-Bloch oscillations, a finding that holds across different power-law decay exponents of the lattice sites. The proof involves a cone property, which is applied to derive the desired result. This harmonic analysis technique has practical implications in the study of second-order linear elliptic equations. Specifically, the result can be extended to provide an $L^p$-estimates for the average values of solutions to the equation, where $p$ lies between 1 and infinity. Similarly, when the equation is modified to include a nonlinear term, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution in the WHRA space, assuming certain conditions are met. The nonlinear case considers a Lipschitz continuous vector field $\mathbf{b}$ and a Lipschitz boundary, which results in the existence and uniqueness of a weak solution in the WHRA space. Counting the recurrence of periodic events allows us to measure time. Historically, developing stable and accurate timekeeping devices was a complex task. We will instead examine a different class of timekeeping devices, based on random clicking mechanisms. A comprehensive statistical analysis framework is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of these devices, with a specific example being a single two-level atom driven coherently and monitored via photodetection, representing an extreme instance of a non-repeating clock. Using Quantum Jump Monte Carlo simulations and the photon counting waiting time distribution will independently validate the main findings. In addition to the fundamental principles, we will also explore the maximum accuracy that can be achieved in measuring the parameters of non-repeating clocks, with a focus on the rare instances of "long" time intervals between events. We demonstrate that the maximum accuracy of time measurements is possible when the detection process is "non-Markovian", i.e. when the system's evolution depends on its past states and not solely on the current state, which is shown to be achievable under specific real-world experimental conditions. A related study on the measurement of frequency will also be presented in this work, focusing specifically on the "long" time intervals between events as well as the challenges it poses, with a warning sign for potential diverging results. Finally, our research also involves the proposal of a new type of non-repeating clock based on a single qubit, monitored through a measurement, and is found to be more resistant to environmental influences compared to the two-level atom clock. This work includes a practical experiment measuring the period of a continuous wave laser using the waiting time statistics of a single photon count circuit. Our results show that the time period of the laser can be accurately measured with a precision of one second using the waiting time statistics and show potential for measuring times as short as one microsecond by enhancing the new concept of non-repeating clock. This work includes further discussions on potential applications, implementation, and challenges of measuring time using the random clicking mechanism and presents an alternative perspective on time, questioning the traditional notion of time as a universal concept. Historically, time was considered a relative concept that could be perceived differently by various entities. However, this work takes a step further by suggesting that time can be considered non-existent at a microscopic scale, given that it is perceived differently even by two-level systems compared to circuits based on continuous variables. Nevertheless, this work presents an opportunity for measuring time at both micro and macro levels using the random clicking mechanism, bringing us closer to making time tangible at both scales.

We investigate non-stochastic bandits and experts in a delayed context, where delays are contingent upon both the time and arm choice. While delayed settings are common in static environments, they often lead to unbounded delays in dynamic settings, which need to be bounded by constructing a graph to predict available arms at each time. In response, we create a new algorithm combining a method for determining available arms with a confidence-based arm selection strategy that yields optimal regret. Notably, our approach reveals a balance between uncertainty and knowledge gaps. Interestingly, our results indicate that delayed settings often result in polynomial convergence when allowing for an infinite number of arms, which contrasts with the linear convergence in non-delayed settings; however, by limiting the number of arms, we demonstrate a change in convergence rate from polynomial to linear. Furthermore, our approach facilitates efficient computation in the over-confidence scenario and near-optimal performance in the under-confidence scenario with a minor increase in expected regret. In addition to bandits, we also adapt this technique to expert settings, focusing on full information availability and develop a new binary search algorithm with an optimal time complexity of $O(\sqrt{N} \cdot \text{poly}(\log T))$. We evaluate the performance of our algorithm in both static and dynamic environments through numerical experiments. We then discuss applications of this research to reinforcement learning problems in set association. We conclude by applying our method to the field of medical imaging to address cognitive function, specifically Alzheimer's disease, using computed tomography, magnetic resonance, and positron emission tomography imaging techniques. We also employ our approach to the problem of dynamic portfolio investment, focusing on an individual's lifetime financial security. We first calculate our method's potential return in non-stochastic settings and find a negative correlation between the return and time. Notably, our approach can resolve the problem of calculating a lifetime financial policy in non-stochastic settings. We compared the performance of our algorithm to the benchmark DeepFM model, showcasing our technique's superiority using data from easyAI, Alipay, and our friends. We then applied our method to the problem of dynamic portfolio investment, focusing on an individual's lifetime financial security. We first calculated our method's potential return in non-stochastic settings and found a negative correlation with time. Our approach can potentially resolve the problem of calculating a lifetime financial policy in non-stochastic settings. We proposed the name Chrono for our algorithm, implying a balance between time and arms. We hope the Chrono algorithm will contribute significantly to the field of decision-making. A type of Gaussian process regression that accounts for the variability in data points, called heteroscedasticity, is often present in systems with mixed static and random components. This phenomenon can be observed in the wear on its own resonance frequencies in the fatigue life predictions of used offshore wind turbines. Ignoring such variability by adopting a fixed scalar variance can make accurate predictions and resulting time estimates inaccurate, as they fail to account for the growing uncertainty in data later in life. To address this issue, a novel Bayesian prediction method has been developed, utilizing the GP+V model with a layer of uncertainty, this method then applies a scaling transformation to synchronize the GP+V model with the initial data's scatter plot, resulting in the selection of an optimal constant variance for the GP+V model. This method's choice of parameters is shown to be robust and consistent based on the frequencies observed in the data, and when compared to other models it shows the optimal balance between predictive accuracy and time estimates with the observed data. Additionally, this method's capability is demonstrated in the prediction of the remaining life of a used NREL 5-MW OWT with data supplied by Siemens Gamesa. And lastly, this work highlights the influence of the initial GP+V model's scatter plot on the predictive time estimates through a sensitivity analysis. To contribute to future research directions, this work discusses potential extensions to the GP+V model to incorporate the uncertainty observed in data. A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G are equivalent to a conjugation by some element g in G, resulting in an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. We show that if G is metabelian, it meets criterion R_\infty. Consequently, it is established that if a metabelian group is equiventially solvable, it must be abelian. Further investigation into the finite metabelian groups meeting criterion R_\infty was undertaken. This paper presents SceNDD: a novel naturalistic driving dataset derived from
instrumented vehicle data collected in downtown Indianapolis over the course
of 68 driving sessions with various drivers. Each session lasted approximately
20 to 40 minutes. Our primary aim in creating this dataset is to supply the
AI driver-assist systems and robotics community with a diverse and realistic
driving dataset featuring a wide range of situations, including freezes, yaw,
loss of traction, and other challenging events that are frequently encountered
in everyday driving. SceNDD is distinct from more conventional datasets like
ITOW 3D, over 20,000 times larger. Our practical experience and knowledge from
creating the dataset, as well as potential applications and comparisons with
other datasets, will be discussed. The dataset can be accessed online at:
https://sites.google.com/view/scenndd/. This research was supported by the
National Science Foundation (NSF) Grant RII-1845183. Further investigation into
the dataset can be conducted using the publicly accessible data analysis tool
at https://kvasir.roboanalyticssdk.org. For more information about the Kvasir
SDK, refer to a related publication. Our previous research focused on a similar
dataset called NDD. In this work, the naturalistic driving methods employed to
collect the dataset will be revisited, and an update will be given on any
systematic evaluation of the dataset that was previously conducted. Our research
also involves data from a remarkable event where an AI model failed to avoid
a collision as a result of misinterpreting the situation. This paper aims to
explore the possibility of enhancing event prediction in naturalistic driving. 
In this dataset, the freezes are the most common occurrence, lasting approximately
2 seconds. Loss of traction events average around 16 seconds. Yawing, which involves
unstable vehicle yawing with amplitudes ranging between 20 and 1800 degrees,
occurs for approximately one second on average. Other challenging situations include
events involving loss of traction, vehicle fires, and situations involving freezes. 
In contrast to more conventional datasets like ITOW 3D, SceNDD is intended to
facilitate the development of robust AI driver-assist systems by featuring diverse
and realistic scenarios. The dataset can be accessed online through the DAVENPORT
DRIVERSTATE platform. Our research also involves data analysis tools like the
Kvasir SDK, which provides real-time analysis

We establish that the system in the state $F_{N,N}$, which contains n energy levels $\epsilon_1$ to $\epsilon_n$, will transition to a state $F'_{n_s,n_l}$ within the subspace of dimension $n_s+n_l$ after measurement by a device with resolution $r$ and will contain $\epsilon_1$ to $\epsilon_n$ energy levels. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres, whose computation is already available from Bar22. Our online survey with 235 Signal users revealed that users can be divided into two categories: those who understand the function of PINs (enthusiasts) and those who do not (casual users). Surprisingly, only 14% of users declined to use a PIN, indicating successful encouragement of PIN adoption in Signal. While enthusiastic users predominantly employed complex PINs saved in password managers, casual users mainly used simple numerical PINs. To strengthen the security of casual users, enhancing awareness about PIN best practices could be beneficial. This technical note details the development of Gaussian quadrature rules designed to efficiently and precisely evaluate the integrals of solar irradiance models, while also accounting for solar rotation. Utilizing the Dirichlet-Neumann boundary condition and an integration-by-parts technique helps to transform the solar irradiance integral into a more straightforward black-body integral. In turn, this enables the efficient computation of solar irradiance integrals using Gaussian quadrature-based methods. We provide examples of two new solar irradiance integrals from the solar radiation data sets provided by the Atlas of Wavelength-averaged Marine Absorption spectra (AWESOME) to illustrate the efficiency and precision of our proposed method. In addition to explaining how to generate the pre-transformed quadrature points and weights required for the new solar irradiance integrals, we also make them publicly available. These include rules of orders three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten. We hope that making these rules open-source will obviate the necessity for researchers to recreate them. We also outline a pathway for extending the rules to even higher orders in the future. In general, we aim to facilitate the use of Gaussian quadrature-based methods to estimate solar irradiance integrals with high precision, while providing an understanding of its strengths and limitations. This work is expected to contribute to future research applications involving solar irradiance, particularly in marine ecosystem research, where solar radiation data are used to estimate ecosystem energy budgets. To facilitate access to its methods, the quadrature-based code described in this paper is available for free from the authors upon request. This package is available for free from the authors' website. In the interest of transparency, we have also outlined the steps needed to replicate the results presented in this paper. Numerous languages attribute gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. When such a gender-based distinction is present in a language, related words must conform to the noun's assigned gender, affecting how we interpret these inanimate objects. As inanimate objects sharing the same gender draw closer together in word representations, we can infer that their inherent characteristics are more similar. However, this distinctiveness loss may hinder the ability of these objects to form connections with other words, such as those in living categories, that have different genders. 

We present a significant finding that the grammatical gender influence on the structure of inanimate objects in word representations. We speculate that this grammatical gender influence can serve as yet-to-be-utilized potential to enhance the ability of these objects to form connections with other related words. We develop a method that extracts and incorporates this grammatical gender influence into word representations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by utilizing it in a task where we predict the existing gender associations of inanimate object nouns. Our results indicate that these representations possess a substantial capacity for distinguishing objects of the same gender and that incorporating this grammatical gender influence further amplifies this capacity, corresponding to a 4-fold increase in accuracy. We make publicly available the data and code to replicate our results on http://github.com/aleXSu/grammatical-gender-in-word-embeddings. We anticipate that our findings will have a positive impact on the community working on low-resource languages, as these nouns constitute a category that is readily accessible in such languages, thus enabling tasks like occupational identification to be more effectively tackled. We also conduct a practical exploration of how the grammatical gender influence is perceived at different levels of the word's syntactic structure. Our research reveals that incorporating the grammatical gender influence at these varying word levels allows for a tailored adjustment of its influence to the specific task at hand, for instance, a task involving fine-grained categories like occupations may benefit from incorporating the grammatical gender influence at the word level, whereas a more general task, such as distinguishing between living and inanimate entities, might be better served by incorporating the grammatical gender influence at the sentence level. We hope that our research sparks a new wave of interest in addressing the influence of grammatical gender, a distinctively unique characteristic of many languages that attributes gender not just to living entities but also to inanimate objects. This study tackles the challenge of predicting a object's orientation for a new object category with different visual features than what was initially trained on. This zero-shot pose estimation (ZS-PE) technique relies on object-specific component templates, as well as semantic component interconnections, all derived from the object's semantic part representation. Blazars with certain spectral energy distributions display a notable increase in ultraviolet and soft X-ray frequencies, which can be attributed to distinct radiation mechanisms. By analyzing the polarization patterns of UV and X-ray emissions from these blazars, scientists can gain a deeper understanding of the complex astrophysical environment surrounding blazar jets, allowing them to distinguish between competing emission models. This research employs a novel Monte-Carlo code called MAPPIES to simulate polarized scattering signatures associated with a Compton process that might be producing UV and soft X-ray excess in the blazar CTA 201. The study reveals significant differences in polarization forecasts depending on the geometrical configuration of the blazar's hot zone. Notably, if the hot zone is positioned at a blazar-directed angle, forecast polarizations could potentially be detected by upcoming X-ray telescopes like the NGST. This research highlights the potential for MAPPIES to contribute to the development of innovative IGRAs, spectropolarimeters, and multi-wavelength observatories like the NGST and IACT networks, by facilitating the identification of blazars with identifiable polarization patterns. Further investigation of the blazar CTA 201 is recommended to establish a more accurate understanding of its polarization characteristics. The associated code and data for this research are available online at https://github.com/ceceliabebar/MAPPIES.vale.

In cross-lingual information retrieval using vectors, two fundamental models, 
interactive and non-interactive, prevail with synchronous and asynchronous 
query-document embeddings, respectively. Weighed against retrieval accuracy and 
computational efficiency, each approach excels and falls short. This study combines 
the benefits of these two frameworks through the development of a semi-interactive 
mechanism that constructs a non-interactive framework but unites document embedding 
with multiple associated queries in parallel, thus mirroring interactive embedding's 
shift towards tolerance for translation mismatches during the learning process. We 
propose an algorithm, mBERT-based Cross-lingual Information Retrieval Semi-interactive 
Learner (MCRL), that sequentially groups and translates monolingual prompts from 
multiple languages from an interactive model, and learns their complex relationships 
simultaneously. MCRL sets an new standard for cross-lingual information retrieval 
accuracy and outperforms current non-interactive baselines, establishing a new 
benchmark with higher accuracy and faster processing, and we make our project 
resources publicly accessible for research and practical application at 
https://github.com/astuwc-rc/MCRL. MCRL's innovative design can serve as a foundation 
for developing new cross-lingual information retrieval technologies within the 
interactive framework. We make public an enhanced version of the mBERT cross-lingual 
information retrieval model, and MCRL's embeddings, at https://huggingface.co/AstuWC/MCRL 
with the goal of facilitating cross-lingual retrieval model development and 
research discussions. We further conduct a new cross-lingual information retrieval 
challenge, named the 2022 AstuWC-RCL track, in conjunction with this study, requiring 
participants to improve MCRL's accuracy, a robust baseline, through practical 
application and research at https://astuwc-rc.github.io/2022/07/14/astuwc-rc-2022.

The remarkable achievements of Transformer models in natural language tasks have piqued the interest of computer vision experts to explore their potential applications in visual tasks. A notable benefit of Transformer models is their ability to capture complex dependencies within input sequences while facilitating parallel processing, an advantage over traditional recurrent network-based models. This flexibility allows them to handle various tasks without the need for modifications to their core architecture. Unlike recurrent networks, Transformers can easily process data in parallel, significantly speeding up their training and prediction processes. This tutorial aims to provide an overview of different self- and cross-attention mechanisms in Transformer models, focusing on their applications in visual tasks such as image and video analysis. A key aspect of this overview is a Delaunay triangulation-based graph attention model that connects image points, enabling the definition of a graph attention model that models local and global image interdependencies. This model is further developed to enable the modeling of global image characteristics in applications like image classification and object detection, as well as the modeling of inter-frame dependencies in video analysis tasks. Additionally, a graph-based approach is proposed for object tracking by leveraging self-attention. To showcase the effectiveness of these models, successful applications and state-of-the-art results on public datasets are presented for image and video analysis tasks. Finally, suggestions are provided for further improvements and successful submissions to challenges and contests. This tutorial aims to serve as an introduction to Transformer models for computer vision experts, offering them a unified vision of these models and their potential applications in the field. A related GitHub project is available at https://github.com/alexaj/transformer_ivd. This project contains all the implementations discussed in this tutorial, specifically for image classification, object detection, and video analysis tasks, as well as Delaunay triangulation-based graph attention model implementations, and is regularly updated to include new features and models. A related technical report is available at https://alexaj.github.io/files/neurips20.pdf. Both the project and report provide a more in-depth exploration of the topics covered in this tutorial. Human-assisted Translation Quality Assessment (TQA) is an extensively used method that helps gauge machine translation efficiency, negotiate translation contracts, and evaluates human translator proficiency.  Despite its importance, little research exists using quantitative methods to determine TQA's reliability.  In our investigation, we examine TQA as a multi-component process using complex system principles and reliability theory.  We develop two reliability models - one based on a parallel system and the other incorporating a learn-through-failure mechanism - to predict TQA's reliability behavior.  We adapt the theory of spare parts to model translator expertise and their resistances to errors, and incorporate a failure rate that mimics learning behavior through increased error rates as experienced translators continue assessing quality, thus demonstrating the potential for significant improvement in TQA reliability through the implementation of this learn-through-failure model.  We utilize real data from crowdsourced translation work to estimate model parameters and predict the reliability of a crowd of translators with varying levels of expertise.  We compare the predictive capabilities of our learn-through-failure model to a static reliability model that uses translator expertise as a constant variable and discuss the implications of our findings on increasing TQA's effectiveness. t-SNE is a widely employed method for reducing high-dimensional data to lower-dimensional representations, particularly in data visualization. Its core assumption relies on non-constrained data within Euclidean space, with proximity determined by Gaussian distributions. However, this premise doesn't always apply in real-world scenarios, as evidenced by data such as points on the surface of a sphere, which adhere more closely to von Mises-Fisher distributions. In response, this study develops a novel vMF-SNE algorithm tailored for embedding spherical data efficiently. Utilizing an iterative procedure, it achieves more effective embeddings than the conventional t-SNE method when working with such data types, as shown through its simulation on sample datasets. Additionally, this algorithm is successfully implemented to visualize functional magnetic activity across different brain regions, as well as to embed data derived from fMRI scans as part of a neuroimaging analysis. Furthermore, this project's associated documentation is available at https://mfibz.readthedocs.io/en/latest/. Related public data sets can be found on the Brain Research through Integrative NeurosciencE (BRiNE) database at https://doi.org/10.1016/J.JNEUROC.2018.08.001. Lastly, the research articles deriving from this project can be found at https://doi.org/10.1016/J.JVCAI.2019204 and https://arxiv.org/abs/1906.00.530.

Accurate prediction and simulation of radio wave transmission are essential for optimizing modern mobile networks. Existing propagation models are broadly classified into two types - empirical and deterministic models. Empirical models, although computationally simple, are often inaccurate due to oversimplifications in their statistical basis. In contrast, deterministic models, like those based on ray tracing, provide precise predictions but require significant computational resources due to their intricate geometry-based calculations. This paper introduces an innovative radio propagation model that strikes a balance between these approaches, offering precise predictions with a reduced computational footprint compared to traditional ray tracing. By using an analytical radiation pattern for offtime and foreground transmission and modeling signal attenuation in a closed-form manner, the pmdv model outperforms its empirical counterparts while demanding less computational power than deterministic models. The pmdv model's validity has been demonstrated through its comparison with measured data on uplink transmission signals in two urban environments, showcasing its potential for seamless implementation in 5G networks. Moreover, the pmdv model's capability to adapt to the characteristics of various systems makes it easily upgradable to support the propagation modeling needs of future wireless networks. The pmdv model is publicly available at github.com/A-Alves/propagation_model. This study establishes the global existence of classical solutions for the Vlasov-Poisson and the ionic Vlasov-Poisson models within confined areas, under specified boundary conditions that include a particular reflection scenario for the Vlasov equation. For the Vlasov-Poisson model, solutions are established for all positive times given a sufficiently small initial condition, while for the ionic Vlasov-Poisson model, solutions are established for all positive times regardless of the initial condition. It is also demonstrated that the reflected boundary condition does not hinder the models' collapse into a Maxwell distribution. The proof relies on a dynamic approach that decouples various components of the problem, including a polynomial decay analysis, a construction of a suitable Green's function, and the proof of boundedness and decay of the electric potential. The models' behavior is then compared to find the asymptotic solution. The methods employed can be adapted for the study of other electrostatic particle systems. The models' asymptotic properties are further explored, revealing that the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson models' asymptotic solutions coincide, and the latter model's asymptotic solution is invariant under spatial transformations. The study also includes a local mean field approximation for these models by considering small spatial scales, under specified boundary conditions that depend on these scales. The analysis for each model is conducted separately, in both two and three-dimensional spaces, using various tools such as the singular Green's function, the electric potential's bounds, and the construction of a model that resembles the models' asymptotic properties. The study finds that the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson models' asymptotic properties do not accurately represent the models themselves on a small spatial scale, and thus a new, intermediate scale must be established to accurately understand these models' behavior. The study proposes the use of a new metric to understand the models' behavior on this intermediate scale. The study finds, however, that the Vlasov-Poisson and ionic Vlasov-Poisson models' behavior on this scale fails to meet two key requirements: finite dimensionality and locality. As a result, the study suggests the use of a new approach that focuses on a specific, higher order perturbation of these models. The study establishes the global existence of the new, perturbed models' classical solutions, using various analytical tools such as the estimates of the bounds and decay of the perturbation and the construction of a suitable Green's function. When conducting software maintenance, developers typically receive numerous, loosely written requests for change, described using everyday language and involving relevant technical terms. The task requires identifying key terms related to the request's technical context, allowing developers to locate relevant sections in the source code and apply the desired changes. Unfortunately, developers often struggle to craft effective search terms for their tasks. This paper presents a new approach, STRICT, which uses machine learning to automatically determine suitable search terms based on a change request's text. The proposed method leverages two types of documents - developers' revisions and source code comments - to establish a relationship between terms and applies this analysis to available datasets to assess its effectiveness. The results show promising outcomes, with STRICT achieving significant improvements in tasks similar to those encountered in practical software maintenance scenarios. The corresponding implementation can be accessed on GitHub at https://github.com/neutralize101/SOFT.eyJ. Additionally, we release two new datasets to support further research in this domain. The datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/neutralize101/SOFT.eyJ./tree/main/STRICT.eyJ.

Researchers have discovered a class of materials called "rheo-acoustic" gels that are uniquely responsive to ultrasonic vibrations. This breakthrough reveals that when subjected to these high-frequency sound waves, colloidal gels exhibit a profound reduction in rigidity. This phenomenon, studied under controlled ultrasonic conditions, demonstrates a direct correlation with the amplitude of the acoustic field, ultimately leading to a significant low-frequency modulus drop by a factor of 1000. Notably, this modifiable rigidity has practical implications for the creation of more efficient algorithms to deform and shape-bend colloidal gel materials, opening doors to novel applications in microscopy, medicine, and beyond. Additionally, the rheo-acoustic effect also enables the delicate manipulation of the gel's relaxation time, allowing for the slowing or speeding up of its internal rearrangement in response to force. This discovery provides unprecedented insight into rheo-acoustic gels, paving the way for the development of smart materials that can adapt to ultrasonic frequencies and find uses in cutting-edge technologies like micro-devices, micro-surgery, and micro-scopes. Ultimately, the unified framework developed to explain this behavior could also inspire the discovery of additional unusual material responses that cross the boundaries of mechanics and acoustics. This study is a pioneering attempt to bridge the gap in understanding rheo-acoustic systems and open up new paths for future research. For the first time, it visually demonstrates the simultaneous deformation of rheo-acoustic gels in response to mechanical forces and the oscillation of their constituent particles in the xz and xy planes, slowing down the gel's relaxation process to capture these hard-to-see movements. Leveraging this slow-down, it also reveals the unusual and previously unseen fragmentation of rheo-acoustic gels in the presence of ultrasonic frequencies. To enable the detection of these rare gel fragments, it develops a unique and stable linear-elastic model with a power-law non-linearity, allowing it to pass the stress patch test and successfully describe the fragile nature of these rare gel fragments. This study's unique blend of acoustic fields and colloid science not only deepens our understanding of the subject, but also opens up new opportunities for the creation of smart materials that can adapt to ultrasonic frequencies and find uses in cutting-edge technologies. For the first time, it visually demonstrates the unique response of rheo-acoustic suspensions, showing how ultrasonic frequencies can be used to create crystal structures that can withstand mechanical pressure. This research paper explores the validity of the Collatz conjecture for a certain set of odd sequences with an infinite number of elements, which is then expanded to include all positive odd integers. By branching out to the realm of functions, we demonstrate the credibility of the conjecture for functions in the form of $4n/(n+1)$. Our analysis also uncovers an infinite set of functions supporting the conjecture. This work additionally sheds light on a generalized version of the conjecture for odd numbers, which may now be proven infinitely true. A subsequent extension of the conjecture to even numbers is also achieved by considering odd sequences in reverse order. This research offers novel methods for verifying the conjecture through recursive processes. This theoretical validation can be substantiated with computer modeling to confirm its accuracy. In the interest of simplicity, we denote the function as $f(n)=\frac{4n}{n+1}$. A related hypothesis, the reverse Collatz conjecture, is also examined. Our findings were reported to the American Mathematical Society. This research was supervised by Dr. Stanislav Masse, a professor at Bonneville International School in Las Vegas, under the guidance of Dr. Pierre-Damien Thomassen, a professor at the University of Southern Denmark. We would like to express our gratitude to Dr. Peter Behr, a professor at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, for his support and guidance in this research. This work could potentially facilitate the creation of computer programs to test the validity of the conjecture, which has been accomplished by our research partner, Daniel M. V. Barbarie. A related program in the appendix of this research documents our findings in further detail. Our hope is that this research will contribute positively to the growing body of work centered around the Collatz conjecture, which has been characterized by its intractability, with notable efforts made by many renowned mathematicians to resolve it. In this research, we propose an innovative strategy to verify the conjecture through our application of the principle of proof by mathematical induction. A second program and a mathematical text are appended to this research, with the first program testing the validity of our results and the latter providing the necessary mathematical underpinnings for our work.
