One widely accepted method for evaluating electronic integrals in complex molecules involves a modified version of Becke's partitioning scheme, originally designed for functions that decline rapidly over distance. This method employs overlapping spheres at specific atomic sites to approximate the integrals in question. The original algorithm then uses the finite-difference method to solve the resulting system of equations. However, since the spheres don't precisely align with the molecular geometry, the symmetry of the integrals might be lost. In our alternative approach, we address this issue by first transforming the sphere coordinates into a standardized reference system to maximize symmetry preservation during the numerical computation. Following this transformation, we utilize a modified version of the conjugate gradient method to solve the system of equations. Our method exhibits comparable computational efficiency to the original algorithm while successfully recovering the symmetry of the integrals. This method is applicable across second-order perturbation theory frameworks. We compare our approach with the original scheme, considering hydrogen, methane, ammonia, and water molecules. Our results show that our method outperforms the original algorithm in symmetry, with minimal sacrifice in computational speed. This suggests our method could facilitate the practical application of high-precision electronic evaluators to large molecules with symmetry. Furthermore, our method could serve as a foundation for developing similar schemes for other polyatomic molecules. We also conclude that our abstract optimization method can be freely extended to other parameter sets without compromising the substantial gains in symmetry we've achieved. In a graph, a subset of vertices forms a resolving set if, for any two vertices, a single set vertex is positioned at different distances from the two vertices. The problem of finding a resolving set of size at most k, called the Metric Dimension problem, has been a subject of research since the 1970s. The problem was found to be NP-hard, with parameterization by the vertex cover number yielding fixed-parameter tractability. However, the complexity under different parameters remained unclear until our recent discovery, where the problem was found to be W[1]-hard when parameterized by the feedback vertex set number. Additionally, we found that parameterization by the vertex cover number results in the problem not admitting a polynomial kernel unless a significant assumption holds. While the problem remains open under the vertex cover number, we found fixed-parameter tractability when parameterizing the problem by distance to cluster or co-cluster. The results also include the disproof of the existence of a polynomial kernel under these parameterizations. Furthermore, we found the problem to be fixed-parameter tractable when parameterizing the problem by the maximum degree. The complexity under the maximum degree parameter shows that the problem cannot admit a better kernel when applying the Bidwatcher technique. The techniques employed include the construction of suitable non-decomposable graphs as well as an algorithm for listing all vertices starting from a given vertex that are at a specified distance from it. The algorithm for the latter problem is based on a novel application of the Horsnel's algorithm for the Longest Path problem. The former problem's complexity under the maximum degree parameter was previously considered open, with the discovery showing the minimal size of the listing, affecting the complexity of the Metric Dimension problem under that parameter. Domain theory's powerdomains hold significant importance in the semantics of non-deterministic programming languages.  This paper extends powerdomains to directed spaces - a concept equivalent to T_0 monotone-determined spaces.  Powerdomain-like spaces (upper, lower, and convex powerspaces) of directed spaces are defined through free algebras, and their existence and structures are shown for any directed space.  Notably, these spaces have distinct structures compared to powerdomains of directed-complete partial orders with Scott topology and other previously-introduced powerspaces.  Relations between these spaces and directed spaces are studied using model-theoretic methods to establish their significance as semantic objects for directed calculus and lambda calculus.  Furthermore, the paper examines the equivalence of definitions for upper and lower powerspaces, and concludes that powerspaces completely capture the directed properties of directed spaces.  Finally, the paper presents examples of directed spaces, including Glushkov automata, for which the powerspaces provide meaningful interpretations of their properties.  The work extends to the domain-theoretic interpretation of (non-deterministic) directed calculus and lambda calculus.  The paper includes a survey of previously-introduced directed spaces and their powerdomains, including Selinger's and Bierman's powerspaces, which are shown to be special cases of the powerspaces.  The results provide insights into the relative strengths of the different approaches to interpreting non-deterministic programming languages.  The work appears as a revised version of an older technical report and is subsequently published as a book.

Past and potential future Earth climate states have included extremely warm 'hothouse' environments with unknown atmospheric behavior, characterized by the absence of stable mechanical dynamos that create and maintain storm systems. As a result, there is confusion about how hothouse climates regulate water cycles and weather patterns. This research investigates the effects of geographical factors on hothouse climates using a simplified two-dimensional climate model that replicates the Earth's atmospheric circulation patterns. The application of deep neural networks in medical image classification has shown great promise due to their advanced image mapping capabilities. Despite this, current deep learning-based methods rely heavily on a perfect set of labels with no accounting for noise that may be introduced during the labeling process. Consequently, this noise can have serious consequences, such as misleading patients or causing treatment delays. To combat this issue, we propose a novel method that incorporates a pre-label refinement step using a combinatorial optimization algorithm, facilitated by a discriminative power metric. By refining the initial labels before feeding them into a deep learning network, our method seeks to minimize the influence of noisy labels in the training dataset. Through thorough experimentation, our method has achieved the highest possible Dice score for each of the three datasets we tested, surpassing that of the 90th percentile of alternative compression methods that rely on a robust deep learning network to refine labels. However, our method outperforms these alternatives without experiencing significant increases in computational time or energy consumption. In order to facilitate the use of this algorithm in a variety of applications, the code and models have been made open-source. Furthermore, our method may also be applied in scenarios beyond medical imaging, such as chemical and geological image analysis. The pre-label refinement method may also be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/zwang4/DeepRefine. In the future, our plan is to expand upon this algorithm by using more sophisticated optimization techniques, such as local relaxation methods, and exploring its applications in the field of hyperspectral imaging. Additionally, through collaboration with Regents of the University of Minnesota, we intend to conduct additional, larger-scale experiments to verify the efficacy of this method in real-world applications. Smoothed particle hydrodynamics possesses innate capabilities for maintaining the conservation of momentum, energy, and enthalpy due to its nature, which arises from the basic principles of the method. This paper delves into the fundamental principles that govern the conservation properties in SPH, providing a clear understanding of the inherent laws that govern the algorithm. The paper also outlines specific prerequisites and guidelines to ensure precise energy conservation in SPH simulations. Additionally, it highlights the potential sources of error that might obstruct momentum conservation and provides simple remedies to overcome these issues. To validate the conservation laws, a specially designed enthalpy-preserving SPH scheme is implemented and used in a series of tests, which include ranining, periodic heat transfer with boundary conditions, and non-periodic heat transfer simulations. The results of these experiments strongly substantiate the claims of momentum, energy, and enthalpy conservation in the scheme. Furthermore, using the validated method, a real-world non-periodic heat transfer simulation was conducted and analyzed to verify its non-periodic characteristics. Along with the theoretical findings, this research also includes a detailed analysis and discussion of several applications where incorporating mass conservation may be crucial to achieving accurate outcomes in SPH simulations. The investigation delved into conductance and spin polarization oscillations caused by varying barrier heights, which can be regulated with gate voltages, in addition to analyzing the effects of varying widths on the band gap and contact nature. In 1972, Erdos demonstrated that a graph on n vertices with n larger than 4k to the fourth power and an independence number of k will always contain all cycles. After his findings, he suggested the independence number squared value should also be sufficient for this, later proven otherwise by subsequent results and further improved upon by the presented work which now shows that there exists a constant c, that n being larger than ck to the 7/3 power guarantees a graph with an independence number of k contains all cycles. In relation to Hamiltonian graphs specifically, a result by Bondy showed if a graph is 2-factor Hamiltonian and has an independence number of k, a cycle of size n is present. This paper sets out to solve a key problem of quantum mechanics by developing a method to calculate resonance parameters in the context of particle decay. Current theoretical frameworks, such as S-matrix theory, pose difficulties when trying to calculate these resonance parameters. To address this, a new method based on Cauchy integral has been formulated. This method can calculate resonance parameters located near the real axis in the complex plane and also handles cases with moving poles. Furthermore, it is influenced by non-resonant terms, making it a widely applicable tool. This method has been tested with a simple model that features a straight line in the complex plane, after which it was used to analyze the $\Lambda(1672)$ particle. Using the $\Lambda(1672)$ as an example, the method can produce consistent results for partial decay widths that align with existing experiments. This tested method will be particularly useful for analyzing the decays of hadrons. To facilitate the use of this method, a corresponding algorithm has been written in Python, making it suitable for widespread adoption. This method can also be extended to calculate non-resonant terms and will be explored in future research. The full source code for this method has been made available at https://github.com/WeilunYang/ResonanceDecay. Furthermore, a detailed explanation of the method's theory and implementation has been provided in the documentation at https://github.com/WeilunYang/ResonanceDecay/tree/main/doc. Additionally, a list of implemented particles and decays can be found at https://github.com/WeilunYang/ResonanceDecay/tree/main/doc/known_states. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic years compared to pre-pandemic years, with particularly stark differences observed in areas where face-to-face interactions play a more pivotal role, such as in eating establishments. Furthermore, counterintuitive to initial predictions, pandemic-related declines in urban diversity were found to surpass rural diversity declines. Building on the understanding that cross-city mobility patterns are influenced by urban transportation systems, researchers created a model that simulates social diversity loss due to reduced face-to-face interactions. This model revealed that such losses are largely irreversible (at least within a two-year timeframe) and that pandemic-related declines in urban diversity were predominantly caused by reduced mobility rather than increased fear of virus transmission. Focusing on urban areas known for their vibrant street life (such as Times Square in NYC), researchers found that efforts aimed at reviving these areas through enhanced landscaping and seating could help mitigate COVID-19-related declines in urban diversity, at least in such contexts. However, in other urban settings, increased investment in these areas may not be enough to recover lost diversity. Furthermore, using data from dating apps, researchers found that COVID-19 accelerated declines in urban diversity to be accompanied by a shift towards homophily (similar individuals associating with one another) in urban areas over a one and a half year period. Building on prior research indicating post-pandemic recovery of urban diversity to be critical to mitigating long-term social effects, researchers identified policies aimed at reviving urban diversity as vital measures to be implemented immediately. These policies include designing urban areas that encourage increased face-to-face interaction and investment in these areas, especially in settings where diversity was disproportionately affected. Additionally, researchers recommend exploring ways to leverage digital technology in support of these efforts. Researchers also propose monitoring cross-city mobility patterns to optimize urban transportation systems with a view to enhancing urban diversity. Finally, researchers see the potential for incorporating pandemic-related concerns into existing urban planning frameworks as another policy option. The property of chirality exists ubiquitously in various sizes of geometric patterns - ranging from organic life forms to DNA and proteins - across different scales. Chiral matter responds to chiral light with specific polarization properties that allow for the identification and separation of enantiomers within molecular pairs. Developing an optical cavity capable of efficiently interacting with chiral matter using chiral light is of great importance. The concept of chirality in cavities remains an area of ongoing research due to its novel light interactions. Either a cavity is designed to induce chirality in its surrounding medium through the absorption of left- and right-circularly polarized light with varying rates or a medium is placed inside a cavity to amplify a specific enantiomer's signal. Either method is influential in studying and detecting chiral phenomena. We have created a semiconductor microcavity that interacts with chiral matter through chiral light, resulting in an induced chiroptic signal within the medium. The strength of chirality in the signal depends on the relative strengths of coherences between states with the same energy but opposite spins as well as incoherent interactions. Notably, the strongest chirality is observed in energy transitions where the spins' components are either +1/2 or -1/2. The presented findings represent an advancement towards developing and implementing new methods in chiral research and could be applied in detecting and identifying chiral molecules. The novel technique is set to contribute significantly in future applications in chiral detection and identification of chiral molecules. The study and understanding of chiral interactions between electromagnetic waves and chiral matter could also be pivotal in the development of new and efficient methods in medical diagnosis and new technologies in laser-based medicine, where chiral molecules play an essential role. The induced chiroptic effects caused by chiral matter in the absence of coherences may also lead to a new approach for detecting and identifying chiral molecules using chiral light. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match, significantly influenced by boundary terms, extends to annulus amplitudes. We also explore the boundary BCFTs in the JT gravity context and show the presence of a time-like Liouville BCFT creating a boundary with a gravitational potential. Furthermore, we derive the partition function for the time-like Liouville CFT and a related scalar field, with implications suggesting that the string theory with a primary twist solvable and yielding two BCFTs with negative c values. Additionally, we resolve the holographic duality of this scenario by relating the boundary variable to the gravitational potential of the anti de-Sitter space, with a time-like version of the entropy formula demonstrated. We also discuss the string theory with a primary twist in the context of time-like non-rational CFTs as an alternative to the JT gravity model with a specific potential. We further show the presence of two BCFTs with negative c values in this context, one of which might be related to a proposal by Anninos, Cardona, El-Showk, Guica, Kabat, Myers and Siegel. A warp drive metric proposed by Alcubierre is capable of creating a region where objects can move without violating the speed of light limit. This research extends Einstein's field equations to incorporate the shift vector in the metric. This analysis is confined to spherically symmetric shift vectors, resulting in a simplified equation compared to the overall field equations. Various mathematical and numerical methods are used to demonstrate that an exact solution exists. Additionally, a warp drive metric with a single massive source is derived, and a relationship with the shift vector is established. This solution meets the requirements of the shift vector equation. This research also shows that a pure general relativity warp drive metric with a single massive source, proposed by Fairhurst, corresponds to a specific limit of the shift vector-free solution. TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. This research involves creating an algorithm that can accurately determine the Raman signal optimization in TERS experiments. Signal improvement is primarily attributed to the spatial concentration and field amplification mechanisms. Through simulation, we found that the proportion of signal contribution from these factors can be quantified and varied depending on the type of tip used and the sample being analyzed. Our algorithm can calculate these factors by utilizing a pair of Raman spectra crossed by a sharp metal tip. One cross section is parallel to the metal surface, while the other is perpendicular to it. By analyzing the ratio of these factors, we can determine the specific type of tip used, whether it's a bulk or a sharp layer metal tip. This algorithm showed high effectiveness in various simulations, retaining an average accuracy of 93% in different metal materials. It was also found that the presence of a low-intensity band in the Raman signal can help pinpoint the type of metal material used. This method offers a simple and easy analysis process that can be integrated into a computer program for quick diagnostics. Even with the presence of a scatterer on the metal surface, our algorithm remains reliable and can be used under experimental conditions to identify the characteristics of the metal material used. This finding provides a significant breakthrough in the understanding of the underlying mechanisms of the TERS signal enhancement process. It also opens the possibility of utilizing this approach to measure the specific type of enhancement provided by the sharp metal material on or near the surface. This research can be applied in various fields, including surface science, chemistry, and biological analysis, to name a few. A computational program that can utilize this algorithm has also been uploaded to the following GitHub link: https://github.com/chemstremo/Signal-analysis.git.

There's a common perception that organisms learn from experience by comparing predicted outcomes to actual results, adapting strategies accordingly.  However, research suggests a simpler model, "probability-matching," where individuals simply choose the better option more often, might adequately explain observed behaviors.  We argue that probability-matching suffices to explain learning without the need for an adaptive process, and such explanations should be preferred over others that involve complexity.  We also propose a test, "the cut-off point method," for determining when to favor probability-matching over a learning process in modeling a particular data set.  When applied to data from a well-known experiment on probabilistic learning in rats, our method reveals that a simpler model, where probabilities simply increase over time, is sufficient to explain the data without the need for an adaptive model.  We also discuss the implications of our findings for understanding both the biology of learning and the effectiveness of different experimental approaches.  Finally, we propose an extension of the probability-matching model that may be more applicable in certain contexts, such as when data are unavailable or likely biased.  Our new approach, "probability-matching with adjustments," can be applied not only to probability-matching but also to other models, like the drift-diffusion model, to find the most suitable fit.  Furthermore, it's worth noting that probability-matching with adjustments consistently favors the simpler model, leading to an improved description of human data on signal detection tasks using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).  Our method, "probability-matching with adjustments using reverse inference," generates more meaningful results than traditional models, like the drift-diffusion model.  Our approach may be a valuable tool for making sense of neuroimaging data and other complex observations, leading to a deeper understanding of the underlying biology.  In cases of uncertainty regarding the suitability of a particular model, our approach can help to clarify the situation.  Our method may also enable researchers to avoid over-interpreting complex data, using its iterative process to switch from one model to another as preferred.  Our approach may be a valuable addition to other tools, like reverse inference, by providing a framework for choosing between different models when faced with uncertainty.  Our extended approach may be applied to probability-matching in its simplest form, offering a framework for choosing between different models when faced with uncertainty. To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques known as measurement error mitigation (MEM). A key limitation of these techniques is the tradeoff between scalability and validity: methods that handle a large number of qubits tend to produce negative probabilities, whereas those that guarantee a correct probability distribution cannot be scaled. To address these concerns, we propose a new scheme that combines both principles. Specifically, we adapt and implement a standard iterative Bayesian unfolding approach commonly used in high-energy physics experiments in a way that scales effectively with the number of qubits. Our approach is validated by successfully mitigating measurement errors in experiments involving up to 127 qubits and 26 qubits using Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger and Bernstein-Vazirani algorithms, respectively. An added benefit of our method is its ability to extract measurement probabilities directly from the posterior distribution. By doing so, we are able to estimate the actual variational gradient in conjunction with MEM, which is particularly valuable in quantum machine learning applications. To facilitate the deployment of MEM in near-term quantum computing, we have implemented the technique in TensorFlow and made the code available publicly. Furthermore, we highlight some general challenges and potential solutions associated with the implementation and scalability of MEM based on current approaches. As such, we suggest the use of our proposed scheme as a practical solution to mitigate measurement errors while overcoming scalability limitations. Furthermore, we recommend exploring alternative implementations of quantum algorithms to reduce the requirement for MEM in the first place. Ultimately, we believe that the strategies outlined in this work will contribute significantly to the development of quantum computing by helping algorithms perform at the current level of performance without the need for extensive postprocessing. Moreover, we are able to make more accurate predictions about the behavior of quantum algorithms without the constraints of measurement errors. As such, we are able to make more informed decisions about the deployment and tuning of these algorithms. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings, having a clear and precise sense of place is crucial. We propose a mobile robot localization system that uses a cutting-edge algorithm to analyze data from an IMU, GPS, and wheel encoders simultaneously. By integrating a novel form of machine learning called the Kalman filter, our system can accurately determine the robot's location, even in situations where one or more of the sensors may not be reliable. We tested our method using real-world data collected from a mobile robot navigating a circuit while experiencing varying levels of noise input from an IMU, GPS, and wheel encoders. The results show that our localization method can achieve high levels of accuracy and precision, with a mean error rate of less than 0.8 meters and a standard deviation of less than 0.7 meters, even in situations where the noise input exceeds a certain threshold. The findings suggest that our proposed localization method is suitable for use in outdoor navigation applications. However, the data also reveals that the system's accuracy can be affected by significant amounts of noise input in situations where the robot deviates from its predetermined path. A proposed remedy could be the integration of additional navigation sensors, such as LiDAR or cameras, which could provide more direct and accurate spatial awareness. Furthermore, the system's reliance on GPS signals can be problematic in areas with high levels of interference. A potential alternative could be the use of dead reckoning techniques to maintain robot localization, especially in situations where GPS signals are lost or blocked. The data shows that our proposed localization method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches, such as sensor fusion, by significantly reducing the mean and standard deviation of the location error by nearly 300% and 85%, respectively. The findings suggest that our proposed localization method offers improved performance and accuracy, which could make it more suitable for use in various robot navigation applications. The data analysis revealed that the system's mean and standard deviation of the location error are directly proportional to the magnitude of the noise input. The data further shows that the proposed localization method yields a standard deviation of the location error that is five times lower than the mean, which could indicate that the distribution of the location error is skewed. The findings suggest that incorporating direct spatial awareness from sensors, such as LiDAR or cameras, could enhance the robot's navigation capabilities. The data presents an opportunity for future research to validate the proposed distribution of the location error. In this paper, we explore a user-centered system for retrieving COVID-19-related information that enhances user involvement in tasks such as identifying crucial terms from news stories. We found that manual term selection by users reduces the query size by almost 90% while maintaining 65% of the original performance. The system is enhanced through a user-centered design that integrates a rich display of news stories and user feedback. This includes a rich display of news stories and user feedback. We also compared the system to an automated approach using part-of-speech filters and discovered that manual selection by users is preferred over the automated method. The system is designed to be accessible through mobile devices. We presented the system at a workshop during an ACM Conference for Information Systems for Crisis Management. The paper is a reflection of the research presented at the workshop. A live demonstration of the system can be accessed at https://alvar-ros.es/covidws2022.live. Time-based data refers to information measured against the backdrop of time, giving it a distinct structural context that forms the foundation of its constituent parts. When dealing with multi-variable data sets that change over time, we anticipate observing interconnected patterns, long-term fluctuations, seasonal variations, and correlations across different variables. In contrast, longitudinal data often displays relationships between and within individual units over time, including both intra- and inter-subject correlations. While analyzing time series typically involves examining relationships between variables, longitudinal data focuses on tracking the development of characteristics within each unit. Given these considerations, we need to account for the unique properties of each unit and apply advanced methods to analyze its features. Our approach can be applied to a wide range of problems, including simple multivariate analysis and complex neural network predictions. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we have compiled datasets from the COVID-19 Health API, providing accessible examples of both time series and longitudinal analysis. Our goal is to enable the creation of self-contained models that incorporate context, including mean and standard deviation calculations for feature scaling. By following the principles of minimalism and making the underlying logic of our code visible, we have developed a straightforward and adaptable framework for building custom AI models. Our aim is to provide researchers with a simple way to turn raw data into informative insights, enabling them to create powerful time series and longitudinal analysis models. In this study, we have achieved a precision score of 93.7% and a recall score of 92.7% using deep learning techniques on a dataset with 83.7% positive cases. Our model's unique approach allows it to interpret the features as mean and standard deviation calculations, providing insights into what the model is learning. By making the code simple to understand and minimalistic, we have achieved a F1 score of 93.1% higher than a similar model reported in a different repository, 0.6% lower but with significantly improved code quality and understandability. Our approach has also resulted in a recall score 4.1% higher than the aforementioned model. Our goal is to provide researchers with a simple way to build upon our model, enabling them to create powerful time series and longitudinal analysis models. In this study, we have achieved a precision score of 93.7% and recall scores of 92.7% and 94.1% for datasets 1, 2, and 3, respectively. Our approach has also resulted in a recall score 4.4% higher than the baseline on dataset 2, 4.

The promising potential of extracting valuable insights from Electronic Health Records (EHRs) lies in machine learning models, despite issues with data completeness. To enhance healthcare quality, research has focused on developing advanced machine learning algorithms using complex EHR datasets. This paper introduces a new ensemble-based method called FinEn, designed for classification and regression tasks using rich, incomplete datasets. The proposed method leverages a unique feature partitioning approach and an enhanced loss computation technique to optimize performance. Experimental evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrated that FinEn surpasses existing methods, including gradient boosting and deep learning approaches, in terms of classification accuracy and regression precision. Notably, the method outperformed state-of-the-art performance without employing data augmentation. This study's findings suggest that FinEn can serve as a high-quality tool for processing and analyzing medical data. The method's source code will be made accessible to the scientific community to support future research. This research aims to improve the field's understanding of machine learning algorithms for diagnosing medical conditions and hopes to inspire similar research. Using a mean-field approach and considering the fixed charges within a mean field, the non-equilibrium electric properties of a micro-electrochemical system involving a flat, negatively charged cathode were studied when in contact with a solution of mobile ions and a non-polar, polarizable solvent. For a system where the solvent does not move as a unit, the solvent's rapid response time generates a non-equilibrium electric potential that is attracted to the cathode, thus reducing the thickness of the double layer. In contrast, when the solvent behaves as a unit, the solvent's collective movement time is comparable to the ionic collective movement time, resulting in a thicker double layer and an out-of-phase potential relative to the cathode. These findings imply a role for solvent polarization in the operation of devices such as capacitors, electrochemical sensors, and energy storage. Moreover, the importance of solvent polarization in micro-electrochemical systems might be enhanced at lower temperatures due to increased collective movement times. In micro-devices, the unequal dielectric properties of solvents should be taken into account when evaluating and optimizing performance. In line with the present study, the equalization of solvent and ion collective times could serve as a relevant criterion for optimizing device operation conditions. In specific contexts such as energy storage and charge storage in electrochemical devices, the optimization of device design conditions could be evaluated based on a combination of factors including dielectric properties, operating temperature, and device design. In an effort to bring micro-nano electrochemistry to the forefront of modern technology, the present findings emphasize a critical need to understand and analyze the unequal dielectric properties of solvents in order to optimize device operation and design under real-world non-equilibrium conditions. Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT model with this dataset and compared its outcomes with well-established models like fastText and ELMo. To challenge the model with more complex text, we compared PURE's performance with experiments conducted on less formal Request For Information texts and more formal Semeval-2010 datasets. Our results indicate that the proposed model outperforms existing models on all datasets. Additionally, we investigated the model's behavior across various domains, considering the influence of written language, domain, and text complexity on its performance. A deeper analysis revealed the strengths and weaknesses of the model regarding false positives and false negatives. Based on these findings, potential future research paths are proposed to improve the model's capabilities. The PURE dataset, code, and project repository are publicly accessible at https://github.com/harshvarma90/PURE.

This research investigates the relationship between network coding and energy efficiency in a system that also prioritizes diversity. By assuming a source node sends data to two destination nodes over a same-path wireless channel while a helper node chooses the optimal transmission strategy to minimize energy usage and maximize diversity, we developed an algorithm to find the best encoding methods and transmission modes given the nodes' positions and desired level of diversity. Our results show that employing a helper node can decrease energy usage despite the extra transmission required. Furthermore, we found that the benefit of helper node assistance is more noticeable in scenarios with a higher priority given to diversity over interference reduction. In addition, we identified the point at which the helper node's assistance negatively affects performance, which occurs when the angle between the source and destinations is less than half the angle of the helper node. Using the cross entropy method, we also investigated how varying the helper node's position affects energy efficiency and found that it reaches the minimum at a specific angle of around 2.5 times the angle of the source. Lastly, we found that the maximum energy savings that result from using a helper node increase as the number of sources grows. For two sources, this value is 33.3%; for three sources, it reaches 66.7%; and for n sources, it reaches $\frac{n-1}{n} \times 100\%$. All these findings demonstrate the importance of optimal coding and transmission strategies in achieving energy efficiency. Although these strategies can bring benefits, they also highlight the limitations of using specific techniques and how they negatively affect performance in certain scenarios. For instance, if the angle between the source and destinations is less than half the angle of the helper node, using an optimal coding strategy leads to almost the same performance as using no helper node assistance. Consequently, this behavior indicates that general methods that apply one technique worldwide without consideration for diversity may work well in local areas but fail in more complex global environments. Using the cross entropy method again, we also found that the maximum energy savings that result from using a helper node increase as the number sources grows. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local density of states to analyze the influence of different material parameters on the YSR spectrum. A dual-band structure in the local density of states, resulting from the differing energies of spin-up and spin-down impurity states, is a key feature of the YSR states within certain magnetic materials. To illustrate the applicability of the developed theory, this approach is applied to analyze the YSR states presented in recent experiments conducted using scanning tunneling spectroscopy on chromium and nickel. Furthermore, the influence of various material parameters on the YSR spectrum is evaluated for iron, with implications for ongoing and future experiments. This theoretical framework is intended to facilitate comparison between material-specific theoretical predictions and experimental observations. With continued advancements in resolution and precision, this approach is well-positioned to support the identification and study of magnetic impurities that are present but not easily detectable, such as non-magnetic impurities with spin. This theoretical framework is potentially capable of detecting up to one in a thousand potential magnetic impurities, with potential applications for precision measurements in various material specific applications. Comprehensive and material-specific theoretical data is presented here for iron, with additional data including plots of the local density of states for a range of magnetic materials including manganese, nickel, and chromium, with relevant code available online from GitHub, with corresponding reference number: $\href{https://github.com/LaRgeScaleMagnon}{0}$. Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) are effective for registering 3D point clouds when the environment remains stationary, but they fail when the scene changes. This is due to a poor balance between computational complexity and the trade-off between registration accuracy and computational efficiency. Our proposed solution, PCR registration, improves upon traditional methods like NDT by integrating a robust point cloud representation with a direct deep learning registration algorithm. Our approach achieves registration by minimizing the distance between two point cloud descriptors, collected from pre-trained networks that have been trained on a wide range of discrete Gaussian distribution cells. This is done while ensuring that the cell points remain accessible, thereby ensuring a feasible search space for optimal solutions. Our method can process point clouds with any resolution and has a search space comparable to its parameter count. We outperform current methods in dynamic scenes with respect to computational efficiency, as demonstrated by results from evaluating our approach on the KITTI odometry benchmark. Our source code is available at https://github.com/utnride/point-cloud-registration. Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for processing. Deep 
learning methods have recently gained traction for analyzing satellite images. 
Although incredibly efficient, they have inherent limitations, necessitating 
specialized computing infrastructure. In the context of edge computing, which 
involves processing data locally, the lack of powerful GPUs or CPUs can be 
overcome by leveraging the potential of neural networks within Field-Programmable 
Gate Arrays (FPGAs). Our proposal, named EdgeFPGA-Net, integrates an FPGA-based 
 neural network designed for edge computing and showcases its adaptability with 
the lightweight EfficientNet model. Our proposed combination of this model with 
FPGAs significantly enhances performance for image classification on the DAVIS 
dataset, achieving an accuracy of 72.19% compared to 43.67% for a purely 
software-based approach. Moreover, on the semantic segmentation ILIDS dataset, 
our proposed system achieves a mean IoU of 74.23%, representing a mean 
improvement of 1.16% over traditional software-based methods. Our results 
demonstrate the viability and efficacy of EdgeFPGA-Net for real-world 
applications. Furthermore, our source code and models are publicly accessible 
at https://github.com/HiDynamic/EdgeFPGA-Net.

Subjecting solid materials to an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse from a free-electron laser causes drastic electronic excitation, triggering rapid changes within the material's electronic system that evolve over time. The degree of excitation is often quantified by X-ray fluorescence yield, which increases with higher X-ray fluences. To better comprehend the dynamic screening of core electrons and their impact on the material's structure, researchers must analyze time-resolved X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy data. The shape of this near-edge spectrum significantly correlates with the material's core-hole localization and number, core-hole states, and electronic configuration. Initially, disordered core holes cause spectral shifts, which gradually subside as the material's ground-state structure reasserts itself; however, a residual shift sometimes persists and is linked to changes in the material's valence electronic configuration. The time-evolution of near edge shape and phase can provide direct insight into the time-dependent development of valence electronic configuration, core-hole dynamics, and their interplay. The appearance of a disordered core-hole peak is linked to dynamic behavior, while a residual shift is indicative of post-excitation changes in valence electronic configuration. The following is an investigation into the disordered core-hole peak and related valence changes in four different materials: N$_2$MDC (a high pressure cubic phase of CN$_4$ at 5.5 GPa), a C$_8$O$_2$ molecule, CO (carbon monoxide), and a NiO$_x$ thin film (where $x$ is between 0 and 1). The research highlights the potential for time-resolved near edge spectroscopy to reveal the dynamic, time-dependent reorganization of electronic configurations following an ultra-intense, femtosecond X-ray pulse. The phenomenon can offer a unique insight into the short-term changes in core and valence electronic configurations. The appearance of a disordered core-hole peak is typically associated with valence changes over a relatively short time scale. Importantly, the research indicates that the shape and phase of near edge spectroscopy can provide direct insight into the dynamic reorganization of electronic configurations, a phenomenon that is linked to a range of unique and fascinating properties. The potential for time-resolved near edge spectroscopy to reveal the dynamic, time-dependent changes in the disordered core-hole peak is demonstrated. The application of a Deep Neural Network in Automatic Modulation Classification (AMC) exhibits enhanced performance compared to traditional methods even with low-resolution received signals. However, some received signals are completely degraded due to severe distortion from factors such as frequency offset, channel attenuation, and multi-path delay. These distorted signals cannot be classified using conventional methods. Thus, a new AMC approach has been proposed to classify weak received signals that cannot be properly aligned through conventional means. To overcome this challenge, a novel low-resolution complex-valued convolutional neural network has been developed. This proposed network can classify signals with normalized SNR as low as -10dB without pre-processing. During the training phase, a normalized cross-correlation step is implemented to correct for residual frequency offset and subsequently, a classification model is constructed. The approach was tested using a specific set of wireless signals and compared with traditional methods in terms of classification accuracy, showing improved performance at extremely low SNR levels. The classification accuracy of this proposed approach was found to be around 90% at an SNR of -10dB, significantly outperforming conventional methods. Furthermore, this approach was also evaluated in various Scenarios of varying complexity and its advantages were highlighted over traditional methods. The approach was found to be generalizable across different channels, frequency configurations, and levels of multiplexing. Overall, this proposed classification approach demonstrates the generalizability and robustness of the Deep Neural Network model. Detailed descriptions and mathematical explanations of the approach have been provided. The advantages of the proposed method over traditional approaches are due to its ability to correct for residual frequency offset and its simplicity. The classification model can be modified to accommodate different parameters such as number of antennas, number of frequency configurations, number of multiplexing, and power distribution among various signals to enhance its flexibility and generalizability. The approach was found to be computationally efficient as it can operate at an SNR of -10dB without pre-processing, thereby reducing implementation complexity and power consumption of base stations. The concept of low-resolution AMC using a collaborative neural network is highly relevant to modern wireless systems that aim to minimize power consumption and complexity while providing high-quality services to users. The idea has the potential to be applied to other fields such as image classification, seismic data classification, and speech recognition in future. The approach can be further simplified by reducing the resolution of the received signals from 64 to 16 points, showcasing its ability to operate efficiently at reduced scales. Recent studies propose using artificial intelligence-based techniques but most
methods are one-dimensional and lack the analysis of multi-dimensional lesion
characteristics. A more complex approach involving bidirectional attention
mechanism has shown promise, yet it remains computationally expensive and is
not suitable due to technical limitations. A proposed model addresses the first
issue of dimensionality by leveraging bidirectional attention and integrating
multi-dimensional data from MRI scans. By using a memory mechanism to store
intermediate results, the model overcomes the second issue of computational
complexity by avoiding the recollection of previous steps. 

Evaluation of the proposed model showed that it outperformed existing methods
on data from 180 patients. A comparison of baseline models revealed that the
one using a memory attention mechanism had the best results. A proposed method to
evaluate the quality of segmentation is also introduced. An investigation of the
quality of segmentation on data from 180 patients revealed that minor gaps in
segmentation accuracy are mainly due to two issues. A proposed method to
address these gaps involves combining clinical expertise with multi-dimensional
data from MRI scans. By leveraging these two areas of study, the method is
able to identify lesions that were initially missed. A proposed ensemble model
outperformed existing methods on a related benchmark dataset.

the experts was combined with the model for lesion segmentation. A proposed

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity. This new 
metric comparison is called strictly 1-WL and is more delicate than Alexandrov comparison. 
This comparison leads to a proof that MTW is equivalent to finding a potential function 
that minimizes an optimal transport cost between two measures, with the constraint 
of being 1-logarithmically smooth. Furthermore, using Douglas-Rachford dynamics in 
combination with the metric comparison technique, it is demonstrated that metric 
continuity is preserved during an iterative process for solving the OT problem. This 
research also explores the relationship between OT costs and Wasserstein distance when 
the target measure is a point measure. Finally, using optimal transport, it is demonstrated 
that MTW is equivalent to a metric comparison involving 1-smoothness via a novel notion 
of curvature bounds derived from the MTW condition, allowing for the metric 
continuity of OT costs when the source measure is absolutely continuous with respect 
to the Lebesgue measure and the target measure is a point measure on a complete, non-compact 
Riemannian manifold with non-compact cut locus. This new concept of curvature bounds 
is related to lojasiewicz exponent in homotopy theory and 1-WL comparison is more 
delicate than Hessian metric comparison when the OT problem has a solution with 
logarithmically smooth potential function. From a computational perspective, it is 
demonstrated that an iterative process using Douglas-Rachford algorithm to solve the OT 
problem with an initial starting point moving towards a conic point on a complete, 
non-compact Riemannian manifold with bounded sectional curvature is feasible, as well 
as on manifolds with positive sectional curvature bounded away from zero. This 
research, in addition to its applications, provides novel metric comparison theorems 
that highlight the connections among OT and geometry. A significant outcome of this 
research is the development of two flexible and efficient algorithms for solving the OT 
problem, one being an adaptive hybrid algorithm based on the metric comparison technique and

This framework can be applied to different machine learning models, both continuous and discrete, and handles different types of model errors. 

Firstly, we've explored the impact of a specific type of error that isn't influenced by past events and proved that the accuracy of predictions is closely tied to the duration of the training data.

To address the challenge of these models often requiring complex representations with extensive environmental dependencies, we've incorporated an efficient method for simplifying these representations and demonstrated that the relevance of these representations is closely tied to the duration of the training data.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores, in terms of mass. Protostellar cores have a significantly greater mass than their starless counterparts, on average, by a factor consistent with the mass spectrum of cores observed in the cloud. It is hypothesized that protostellar candidates are more massive because they have undergone greater accretion, largely due to outflow-induced feedback looping back onto the core and reducing surrounding material's kinematic support. This feedback loop is thought to be the primary factor regulating the core's collapse and subsequent disk formation in protostars within the drag cloud. 

Data for the analysis were collected through the Submillimeter Array with a resolution of 4.5" and were made publicly available through the astro-ph pre-print platform as <arXiv:2106.08881>.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific star-related signals resulting from gravitational lensing. A simulation tool called PopSyCLE allows users to study this phenomenon and predict the occurrence of detectable microlensing events. To assess the likelihood of detecting PBH-related stars, we employed PopSyCLE to simulate various scenarios of dark matter composed of these black holes. We calculated the overall abundance of these black holes based on different mass specifications and used the mean and median values to determine the expected number of PBH-related stars per Galactic event. Our results indicate a maximum number of approximately one PBH-related star per 100 Galactic microlensing events, assuming a dark matter composed solely of 10^14-10^17 gram black holes formed during the late formation period of stars. We presented maps of the Galactic center that could reveal the presence of these black holes by identifying specific stellar anomalies. We found that detecting a PBH-related star is more feasible than identifying a black hole directly from X-ray emissions, but this can be achieved for a small number of events with a high degree of uncertainty without excluding the PBH scenario. However, identifying PBH-related stars may become more difficult due to background contamination from 2015-2020 data from the PS1 catalog. Additionally, our analysis of the Gaia data revealed minimal evidence for PBH-related stars due to a limited survey area. We discovered that nearly all stars potentially created as a result of a black hole merger existed outside of the 2000 parsec boundary of the Gaia and had a relatively low mass of less than 2.8 solar masses. We conducted a research study into self-assembly systems consisting of uniform-shaped molecules with a wedge-shaped design, utilizing molecular simulation software to analyze the material science aspects involved. The system's equilibrium structures were determined in relation to packing density variations. When the packing density was at lower levels (below 0.5), we observed liquid crystalline phases consisting of nematic and smectic A types. At higher packing densities (above 0.55), a crystal solid phase emerged. Moreover, for systems with a wedge-shaped molecule's width greater than 0.9 times the thickness, an additional polar nematic phase was detected at intermediate packing densities. The research provided detailed visual representations of these phases, as well as their temperature variations in the context of thermal energy. The study confirmed the existence of specific phases not previously reported in a recent article by Ye et al. Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters.
Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune models, with applications across various deployment scenarios for handling multiple tasks, and underlines the crucial importance of special tokens in pre-trained language models. The code and model weights for our implementation are publicly available on GitHub. Our primary findings will be presented at the ACL 2022 conference.

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences between options, which prompts the use of context-dependent preference modeling. To tackle this issue, we examine two distinct Siamese network designs, contrasting one that compares the resultant collections after an addition with another that considers each item's individual contribution to the existing collection. Through experiments involving a real-world task of learning Magic: The Gathering deck-building preferences, we found that the triplet network outperformed its counterpart and surpassed previous performance levels in this area. The triplet network's success suggests that its architecture is more effective in capturing the context-dependent nature of preference learning. By analyzing the top-ranked model after ablation studies, we found that incorporating a layer that extracts vertical transformations in the data significantly improved the model's accuracy. This discovery highlights the importance of vertical comparisons within the context of weakly ordered preferences. Additionally, our results show that our model is capable of providing actionable insights to decision-makers in the deck-building process. With a deeper analysis of our model's underlying mechanics, our findings imply that the model's preferences are influenced by horizontal and vertical data patterns, as well as the complexity of the vertical transformations, which corroborates the results of the ablation studies. This research contributes to the field of preference modeling by elucidating the effects of data transformation on preference-learning models, as well as providing an innovative solution for context-dependent preference learning in the absence of absolute preferences. The proposed preference-learning model also offers practical applications in the real world, as evidenced by its applicability to the deck-building problem in Magic: The Gathering. The model's code is available for further review at https://github.com/amiwjs/pref-learning. The dataset used in this research can be accessed at https://github.com/amiwjs/deck-preference-dataset. This study underwent institutional review to ensure compliance with relevant regulations, as detailed in the appendix. Appendix A contains additional information on the institutional review process, as well as a comprehensive discussion of the research methodology. 

Replication details can be found at the following link, along with the necessary materials to perform the experiments described in this paper: https://github.com/amiwjs/pref-learning. Using the lattice cluster theory, we develop a framework for molecular fluid theory based on the principle of entropy's temperature dependence. Grounded in the entropy's expansion, our approach integrates configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy in a unified framework, uniquely relating thermodynamic properties to each other in polymer fluids. To validate our model, we adapt the Pratt-Chandler formalism to calculate the configurational part of the free energy and assess its applicability to the binary blend and supercooled states of a model molten polymer. A corresponding DiMarzio-Lipps-like behavior is observed in the supercooled state, supporting the idea that the configurational part of the free energy plays a key role in understanding supercoolability. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the dientropic temperature function plays a crucial part in understanding the temperature dependence of configurational entropy and enthalpy. Finally, our model is related to the lattice cluster theory's entropy-based formalism to provide insights into the relationships between its parameters and the configurational cluster concept. This understanding enables speculation that the principle of entropy's temperature dependence may help resolve the question of how living organisms acquire heritable variability. In this context, early organisms may have utilized compact, congested configurations to explore their surroundings, thereby facilitating adaptive innovations. In the field of materials science, this concept could lead to the creation of living systems with customized, orderly structures by introducing specific cues that trigger specific reconfigurations within the systems. In the accompanying Supporting Information, a comprehensive derivation of the dientropic function is provided, offering a flexible approach for parameter calculation through analytical or numerical methods. Moreover, two additional appendices examine the relationships between the Pratt-Chandler formalism and the Gibbs ensemble, as well as the parameter relationships between the dientropic and DiMarzio-Pratt functions. A specialized software tool developed for this work, named Fluxion, is available at fluxion.net. Fluxion is a Python package that automates the derivation of thermodynamic properties using the principle of entropy's temperature dependence, potentially serving as a replacement for existing software, such as NIST's CHEMCODES, to provide a more systematic approach. Additionally, an interactive 3D model of the lattice cluster structure can be accessed through this tool to visualize the thermodynamic properties of molecular fluids. A tutorial introducing the software and its capabilities can be accessed at https://fluxion.net/tutorials. Transformer-based language models have difficulty with logical reasoning, especially when involving negation, as they tend to rely heavily on memorization. We've developed a method to enhance their capability by introducing a new training objective based on logical forms, in addition to existing objectives. This novel approach leads to significant improvement in performing tasks that require logical reasoning, with notable results on GPT3 and RoBERTa variants, where performance on Sample-Specific Generalization tasks increases substantially, a phenomenon not observed under the original training paradigm. Experimental results indicate that different models excel in various Subtasks, with EBNFT GPT3 achieving the top score in four out of six tests, while RoBERTa 4B outperforms in two tests. Notably, leveraging the strengths of GPT3 and RoBERTa, we are able to surpass the performance of the original GPT-3 model in three tasks, in a more efficient manner, as our model utilizes the 13B parameters of the full GPT-3 model, without requiring it. The newly designed training objective based on logical forms, is also found to facilitate Improved Negation Handling, an effect that is not confined to GPT3. We've applied this same training paradigm to RoBERTa 1M, leading to comparable outcomes. Multiple control experiments are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the novel training objective. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, a phenomenon known as conditioning effects. This phenomenon poses limitations to traditional attention models, limiting their performance in sequence-to-sequence tasks like translation, summarization, and machine transcription. This study proposes an improved attention model, called orthogonal localization that utilizes target word interconnections to boost the translation quality of NMT. The proposed OR-LA model leverages a context monotonic constraint to utilize orthogonal symmetries in the attention matrix, thus localizing to both source sentence parts and previous target words, or initial padding symbols. The proposed model is examined through 30 pairs of datasets, including 14 from the standard WMT datasets, and 16 from datasets of domain and low-resource languages, showing improved performance with significant speedup, outperforming 20 pairs of state-of-the-art baselines. These oscillations produce oscillating spectra in the power spectrum and bispectrum, signaling the presence of massive particles. Understanding how complex visual models work is crucial, and developing techniques to explain these models can be particularly challenging. To address this issue, a framework called LaViSE is proposed to enable convolutional neural networks to describe their internal workings in plain text. By using a large vocabulary related to images, this approach identifies key concepts that match the model's focus areas, thus making the interpretation process easier. Following a training phase that combines image analysis and text generation, LaViSE enables users to generate written summaries for given images without requiring extensive training, proving to be both fast and efficient. The LaViSE framework is further enhanced by achieving a state-of-the-art result in visual scene parsing, a task that also involves understanding the context of images, and it is applicable to other tasks like image classification and object detection. To promote a deeper understanding of computer vision, the LaViSE code and data are fully open-sourced on https://github.com/fintainl/LaViSE. Our approach is demonstrated to be effective in a video clip where a child asks about an image on an Amazon Alexa device and the LaViSE model explains the child's question to another human. This real-world application showcases that the state-of-the-art computer vision techniques have finally reached a level where they can communicate complex information in a simple and easy-to-understand manner, leading to a potential capability to teach children. In the future, this technology has the potential to enable a more natural dialogue between humans and machines, and it is consistent with the idea of a knowledge graph, which is a concept currently being explored in the field of explainable artificial intelligence. A similar line of research in the 90's on understanding images through language is called image semantics, and it is also related to other areas of research such as visual linguistics, image psychology, and cognitive sciences. By making computer vision models understandable, this technology has the potential to open new avenues for collaboration between artificial intelligence and human intelligence, leading to a unification of these two fields. Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study, we found evidence that long-range electron-phonon coupling plays a prominent role in cupate compounds, particularly in the formation of the superconducting energy band associated with d-x^2 - y^2 orbitals. Additionally, we observed that long-range electron-phonon coupling causes a shift in the superconducting d-x^2 - y^2 orbital state towards the anti-Feynman spectrum, thus facilitating its formation. This phenomenon is comparable to an optical phonon mode observed through polarized Raman spectroscopy. We also discovered that the superconducting density of states, triggered by phonon condensation, exhibits a lower energy compared to the anti-Feynman spectrum, which aligns with experimental observations. Our research suggests that cuprate superconductivity can be explained by a simplified model involving long-range electron-phonon coupling, resulting in the Feynman spectrum's suppression and the phonon-induced superconducting spectrum's upward shift. This model can potentially be used to describe other superconducting systems involving angular momenta, such as Fe-based and Fe-chalcogenompounds. Furthermore, our simulation results highlight the distinct effects of long-range electron-phonon coupling on the superconducting spectrum, thus advancing towards a microscopic understanding and a simplification of cuprate superconductivity. As a result, our simulation method may be applied in the future to uncover the microscopic mechanisms behind superconductivity in other materials. Additionally, our simulation method may be adapted to analyze and identify Raman active phonon states in other materials. In this context, our simulation results provide an original and simplified explanation for cuprate superconductivity that is distinct from the conventional model based on the Resonating Valence-Bond picture involving short-range electron-phonon coupling, yet it is compatible with it. This compatibility is confirmed by our simulation results showing the failure of the RVB model in explaining the photoemission spectroscopy study within the scope of this contribution. Lastly, our simulation results highlight the broader implications of long-range electron-phonon coupling, thus paving the way for a potential application in the future to uncover the microscopic mechanisms behind superconductivity in Fe-based and Fe-chalcogenompalstes. As an extension to this contribution, our simulation results may be adapted to analyze and identify Raman active phonon states in other materials

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To implement the Bayesian approach in the context of reversible steganography, we use Type I uncertainty, which reflects the model's limitations, and Type II uncertainty, which can be alleviated through correction. By applying the BNN framework, we are able to distinguish between uncertainties that cannot be separated and those that can be disentangled. To demonstrate the practical implications, we examine the emergence of double binary steeganographic algorithms utilizing BNNs, which can reduce distortion and significantly increase the embedding capacity. Moreover, experimental results show that the proposed algorithms outperform their non-Bayesian counterparts in both metrics. Ultimately, our study contributes to the advancement of reversible steganography and serves as an example of the practical application of the Bayesian approach in computer vision and other related fields. Additionally, this research opens up avenues for addressing uncertainty in application areas where reliable data is scarce. To address this challenge, we propose the concept of online learning, which involves training the model on data as it becomes available in real-time. Ultimately, our study serves as an exemplification of the practical application of the Bayesian approach in the context of reversible steganography and the challenges associated with uncertainty in machine learning. The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers around the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within local dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of active nuclei in these galaxies. The article also considers the cosmological implications of nearby galaxies, which can provide insight into the galaxies thought to dominate the cosmos at an early stage. The authors propose that dwarf galaxies may play a crucial role in the formation of the cosmic metal-rich clouds thought to give rise to the first stars and potentially the Milky Way. The discussion also touches on the galaxies' potential as templates to study and replicate the formation of the cosmic baryonic components, particularly the process of star formation and the evolution of galaxies. This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the sweeping process, first proposed by J.J. Moreau in the early 1970s as part of plasticity theory. The proposed modification involves a novel combination of the prox-regular moving set and two types of perturbations: a Carathéodory mapping and an integral forcing term with an integrand dependent on time variables. To address this new integro-differential sweeping process, a semi-discretization method is developed and used in conjunction with an original Gronwall-like inequality to prove that it possesses a single, absolutely continuous solution. The prevailing subspace randomized methods used to compute the t-SVD require 2q + 2 passes over the tensor data, where q represents a positive integer variable for iteration refinement. In this paper, we introduce a new randomized algorithm for t-SVD computation, requiring exactly q passes over the tensor. Through theoretical proof, we establish the reliability of our approach, comparing favorably with existing research in terms of data sample size requirement. We experimentally validate the efficacy of our method, demonstrating superiority over current models through notable reduction in data sample size needed for similar accuracy. We showcase its practical application in low-rank matrix multiplication. This research presents an innovative method to efficiently compute the t-SVD, maintaining or improving current performance levels while reducing computation cost associated with data sample size. Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters helps us better understand their internal dynamics and chemistry. Melotte 72, an open star cluster located 2344 parsecs away, has significant implications for our comprehension of Galactic disk chemistry due to its close proximity to the Sun. Through our in-depth analysis of the cluster's stellar population, we have derived key values including age and distance. Our findings are based on an extensive dataset of Gaia DR2 photometry and the ground-based photometry collected by M.K. Soyuz. Our research reveals a fascinating age structure, consisting of two distinct periods - the cluster was born simultaneously, but one subgroup was affected by a shift in the IRON-iron abundance pattern around 650 million years ago. To verify this phenomenon further, we propose a thorough examination of the cluster's chemical composition, particularly focusing on the iron group elements to explore the role of stellar mergers or other complex dynamics. Gaia DR2 data also reveals a mysterious, highly blurred radial gradient within the cluster. Our analysis further suggests the presence of binary stars, which could have a substantial impact on determining the fundamental parameters of stellar objects. Our research findings provide valuable insights into the evolution pattern of the Galactic disk stars, particularly the Melotte 72 cluster, paving the way for future investigations to expand our understanding of these stellar objects. The dataset used to derive the findings of this study is open-access at doi:10.1051/00040631 (for Gaia data) and http://ultravista-thuorsen.org/index.php/MK_Soyuz2008/Melotte72 (for ground-based data).

Keywords: Gaia, Melotte 72, Open star cluster, Evolution pattern of Galactic disk stars, Binary stars, Global iron abundance pattern.

In robotics, calibrating an eye-in-hand camera using image information is an essential task that has been extensively researched. We investigated using artificial intelligence-based methods for this purpose by leveraging only a single color image, utilizing exclusively simulated data to train the models. Our experiments involved comparing three approaches: one method predicting the camera's positioning directly from the image, another using 2D keypoints and subsequent PnP calculations, and a third method using estimated depth and segmentation maps to calculate the camera's position through iterative closest point alignment. When evaluating the methods against each other and established traditional approaches, we found an unexpected result in which direct prediction outperformed other strategies. Further analysis into these findings involved assessing the methods' performance under various noise levels. Our methodology and code have been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/sbrc-uom/image-camera-pose.
