We found that using simulated data allowed us to achieve accuracy of 0.5 km in the camera's position when using the direct prediction method. When evaluating the methods in real world conditions where the object was viewed from behind, we noticed a significant drop in direct prediction accuracy of 2.5 km. Our results showed that the method using estimated depth and subsequent ICP outperformed other strategies in this scenario. Our results highlighted the promising use of AI-based methods in calibrating eye-in-hand cameras exclusively using simulated data. While these algorithms are not yet ready for real-world use, they represent an important stepping stone towards achieving this goal. In real-world settings, RL systems face issues due to their unpredictable nature and innate tendency to explore beyond safe limits. Consequently, they can cause harm or generate unproductive content. Constrained Markov Decision Processes provide a mathematical framework for addressing these constraints, but constraints based on state and action are difficult for RL agents to comply with. On the other hand, trajectory constraints that consider policies can be used to enforce rules, but specifying these constraints and implementing them across various policies is computationally intensive. Therefore, a more effective and efficient approach is for the agent to directly identify safe actions, avoiding the need for pre-identifying constrained policies and trails. However, an algorithm that only relies on line-of-sight to improve policies is generally incapable of handling long-term goals. VisionRT, an algorithm for the agent to identify safe actions, utilizes a model that predicts potential obstacles and trails that result in harm by analyzing current images and trail data, which includes previously visited trails and imagined futures. It views the prediction of trails that result in harm as a object detection task that uses visual information, allowing it to incorporate this information into reinforcement learning and resulting in an algorithm that learns from experience without requiring an external task manager or an explicit trail specification. A substantial portion of network information comes from edge weights and their directionality.
Most network measures were initially developed for simple undirected networks.
As a result, weighted network extensions were created to incorporate weight-based information, particularly for calculating the local clustering coefficient.
We discovered that not all edges in these extensions contribute equally to clustering results, which we call fully-weighted.
We analyzed the different components of the local clustering coefficient and found that some are affected by degree, while others are influenced by edge weights and their interaction.
Based on our findings, we developed three new, fully-weighted local clustering coefficients.
Our mathematical analysis shows that these measures capture unique aspects of the network.
We applied them to real-world networks, revealing their effectiveness in characterizing weighted networks.
In doing so, we found correlations similar to those noted in previous studies between clustering coefficients and modularity, as well as interesting connections between weights and clustering in biological networks. 

Additionally, an open source code for the calculation of the proposed clustering coefficients can be found on the GitHub platform under the repository name "clustering-coefficients-for-weighted-networks".

One notable strategy to embed prior knowledge about physical systems into machine learning models is physics-informed neural networks (PINNs). These models have been observed to perform well both within and beyond the training dataset, partly due to their capacity to incorporate data and physical laws simultaneously. Nevertheless, they are prone to convergence issues during training, primarily due to instability caused by non-convergent layers, which hinders their widespread adoption. Building on prior improvements, our proposal involves leveraging an adaptive loss adjustment technique, coupled with a flexible adjustment factor, to mitigate the instability of PINNs. When incorporated into PINNs, this approach yields significant enhancements in convergence, as evidenced by our experiments using a variety of benchmark problems. These tests demonstrate that the hybrid method outperforms existing enhancements in PINNs and supports our analytical findings. Our assessment further indicates that the technique is robust across different network architectures and datasets, and ultimately, may be adapted for use in other types of neural networks. These benefits are exemplified in our analysis of two case studies – a Darcy's law-based inversion problem and the estimation of a period of a pendulum. These examples showcase the hybrid method's enhanced convergence, ultimately enabling more accurate predictions. Our code is openly accessible for review at https://github.com/krishnaiitk/adjustpinns. Overall, our results show that the hybrid method's adaptability and robustness make it an attractive choice for PINNs. These benefits are further highlighted in our analysis of a real-world example involving groundwater model inversion, which demonstrates the hybrid method's ability to leverage geophysical and engineering prior knowledge to generate more accurate estimates of unknown model parameters. These estimates are found to be in strong agreement with the actual values. On the other hand, purely data-driven neural networks fail to produce accurate results in this case. These outcomes further establish the hybrid method's ability to effectively utilize data and physical laws simultaneously, as observed in our experiments. To facilitate the hybrid method's use in practical applications, our results show that the approach is relatively straightforward to implement, as evidenced by our code's open accessibility and the ease with which it yields superior results on diverse problems. Graphene with gaps has been proposed to showcase the valley Hall effect, where different types of electron flows, determined by specific indices, are observed.  Our research, however, demonstrates that this effect can be more accurately described by the orbital Hall effect, where the indices representing "valleys" are replaced with a distinct physical measurement called the orbital magnetic moment, capable of being applied consistently across the entire range of the Brillouin zone.  Utilizing the orbital Hall effect offers the benefit of eliminating the valleys and relate the effect in question to well-understood movements within a two-dimensional periodic structure, simplifying the process required to detect and identify the effect.  Our new understanding also marks the first time the orbital Hall effect has been identified for a specific type of hopping network in a one-dimensional representation, known as the ternary chain.  Our predicted predictions regarding the amount of the orbital magnetic moment can be tested in future experiments using the same method of measurement. The growing significance of Adversarial Machine Learning within Computer Science can be attributed to vulnerabilities in models and crowd-sourced attacks on data. Over the past few years, research has revealed that Graph Classification is particularly susceptible to adversarial attacks, thanks to vulnerabilities in neural network-based methods. Notably, the problem is exacerbated by the limited availability of attacks and defenses tailored to directed graphs. Moreover, the constraints imposed by transferable attacks on graph data pose a significant challenge. To address this limitation, this study proposes an innovative attack that uses activation perturbations specifically designed for directed graphs, while also providing mechanisms for efficient model transfer. Our analysis includes an in-depth examination of the attack's performance, an assessment of its impact on state-of-the-art models, and an evaluation of the tradeoff between attack efficacy and model robustness. Our results demonstrate that the proposed attack outperforms existing methods, while also highlighting the constraints imposed by model transfer on graph data. Domain-specific knowledge is frequently captured using comprehensive, formally structured concept relationships called ontologies. In fields like biology and medicine, vast ontologies comprise hundreds of thousands of interconnected concepts. Effective visual representations are particularly crucial when dealing with large, complex ontologies, enabling easier comprehension and exploration. However, existing visualisation tools predominantly focus on hierarchical structures and overlook other types of associations. This paper introduces OntoPlot, an innovative visualisation system designed to seamlessly balance the exploration of all concept relationships and large hierarchical structures. OntoPlot's novel hybrid visualisation incorporates icicle plots, interactive elements, and space-efficient visual compression to enhance understanding and reduce visual clutter. Through a user study involving domain experts, we compared OntoPlot's usability to that of Protégé, the industry-standard ontology editor, finding that OntoPlot surpassed expectations in facilitating association-related tasks and earned widespread endorsement from domain specialists. With its unparalleled performance, OntoPlot is well-suited for visualising numerous ontologies across various domains. We anticipate that OntoPlot's success will inspire the development of novel visualisation methods addressing the inherent complexities of concept relationship management. We introduce an innovative technique that synergistically combines inter-domain loss and CycleGAN to facilitate semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition. Inter-domain loss aims to derive a common speech-text representation through a shared neural network, whereas CycleGAN leverages cycle-consistency and identity mapping to preserve input characteristics after cross-domain conversion. As both approaches can train end-to-end networks with unpaired data, we leverage their strengths to improve the speech-text mapping and, subsequently, speech-to-text transcription. This method's effectiveness is exemplified by our observation that the addition of identity mapping and inter-domain loss to CycleGAN-ASR significantly enhanced recognition accuracy across multiple datasets. Notably, for the Libri30 dataset, the accuracy increase was substantial, with word error rates decreasing from 18.95% to 3.70%. Furthermore, the results exhibited a notable increase in absolute word error rate reduction for the SWB dataset, with values of 5.95%, 1.95%, and 1.70% for the LibriSpeech, Fisher, and Swb datasets, respectively. Interestingly, the significance of inter-domain loss was found to be data-driven and, in some cases, performed better than the cycle consistency guarantee. For Fisher and Swb datasets, the importance of inter-domain loss was evident, with word error rates increasing by 2.70% and 3.40% when removed, respectively. Conversely, the importance of cycle-consistency loss was found to be data-agnostic and generally resulted in slightly higher word error rates. Overall, the results clearly demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed semi-supervised method. To the best of our knowledge, the integration of inter-domain loss and CycleGAN for end-to-end automatic speech recognition in semi-supervised settings has been pioneered by this work. Although inter-domain loss-derived loss functions can also be used in self-supervised scenarios, the presented framework is specifically designed for semi-supervised settings. Future investigations will examine the application of inter-domain loss to self-supervised scenarios, which is believed to be a promising area of research. The development of Automated Essay Scoring involves a fusion of expertise from Education, Linguistics, and Natural Language Processing. Effective evaluation of an NLP system's long-term dependencies is crucial, particularly when dealing with compositions that necessitate understanding and retention of information presented in introductory sections. A methodical investigation of an NLP system's performance across an array of temporal evaluation techniques can aid in pinpointing areas for improvement in both the system's architecture and the evaluation benchmark. Such an assessment is conducted in this study using an sophisticated Automated Essay Scoring system that incorporates a Graph Convolutional Network and a BERT-based model for extraction and reasoning. The study explores three machine learning challenge datasets from Gradescope and highlights variations and inconsistencies in the datasets that affect the model's performance. A comparison of the model's performance under established metrics demonstrates that a temporal assessment is both necessary and beneficial for evaluating its ability to grasp logical connections in complex essays. The study demonstrates that a temporal assessment results in a more accurate comprehension of the information and significantly reduces the gap between the model's human-equivalent scores on the GRE and TOEIC datasets. Specifically, the temporal assessment achieves an enhancement of 6.3% in Jason's module, 14.3% in Sarah's module, and 9.9% in the integrated module. An additional analysis of the model's layer and head optimization is also conducted, which reveals that a temporal assessment of the BERT model past its initial Layer 24 yields optimal results and stabilizes the model's performance consistent across various evaluation metrics. Consequently, a combined evaluation strategy for assessing the model's module and overall performance is proposed, which initiates future avenues for research. The vast majority of NLP text transformations have inherent limitations in their ability to expand coverage of input data due to the need to preserve the original class label. In order to overcome this constraint, we propose a concept called sibylvariance, which refers to the use of data transforms that can vary class labels as well as input data, thereby allowing for greater diversity in the generated data. To illustrate this point, we provide two case studies. Firstly, we demonstrate that a pre-trained BERT model, when utilized as a feature extractor for transformer architecture, can produce consistent outputs that are insensitive to minor variations in the input sentence. Secondly, we establish that a network trained for sentence similarity learning is capable of developing invariance to minor variations in the input sentence. In order to effectively harness the sibylvariance concept, we design a pre-training task called the Random Class Sibylvariance Reversal (RCSRR) that can enhance the ability of a network to vary class labels as well as input data. In addition, we develop another task called the Permutation Identification and Disentanglement (PIDE) that can produce a compact yet robust sentence embedding that is immune to variations in the within-sentence word order. Experimental results have shown that both tasks are capable of enhancing the sibylvariance of the network. Finally, we demonstrate that a network with sibylvariance can effectively contribute to the development of a robust sentence embedding that is immune to minor variations in the input sentence. In conclusion, the concept of sibylvariance combined with the proposed data transformation approaches offers a simple yet effective method for enhancing the robustness of networks designed for NLP tasks. The proposed methods have been successfully integrated into BERT, with the network achieving an 11.5% improvement in performance on the NLP task of sentence similarity assessment. The code for the network has been made available on GitHub at: https://github.com/quantumoran/2019_ICLR_Sibylvariance_BERT. In addition, our network has the capability of developing sibylvariance that is transferable to low-resource settings, with existing networks being capable of enhancing the sibylvariance of languages such as Indonesian and Javanese. As the importance of the model's representation becomes increasingly prominent, numerous approaches have centered on leveraging task information to optimize this representation, such as multi-task training and co-operative reasoning. In contrast, this paper introduces a novel, opposing strategy, which focuses on exploiting the initial data to extract a versatile representation through careful selection and manipulation of conditions. The proposed method achieves this by treating the model's conditions as part of the representation and incorporating them into backpropagation. The algorithm then identifies the conditions most crucial for the model's performance and retains only those, effectively pruning both the model's parameters and conditions. This paper proposes a unified image captioning framework that excels across various domains and can effortlessly adapt to multiple captioning styles. We incorporate a flexible prompt learning system that enables the model to absorb data from multiple domains, ensuring its performance remains strong in each domain. Previous attempts to define harm in philosophical literature have failed to address various real-world examples, leading some to consider abandoning the concept of harm. The existing definitions, primarily rooted in descriptive analysis, lack the ability to accurately capture complex scenarios. This work proposes a new definition of harm by employing causal models, which can effectively handle multivariable cases. By positing that a planner caused an event, and this event is adverse for an individual, our definition states that by using causal models, they can show that this event occurred because of the planner's decision, and this decision was not necessary for achieving their desired outcome, as they could have acted differently to avoid the adverse event. Our definition is based on objective criteria and is neutral regarding moral implications. This definition's technical underpinnings are built on existing concepts in computer science, making it cognizably applicable to autonomous systems. To illustrate the practical implications of this definition, we have identified and categoryically analyzed 9 challenging scenarios where an individual was harmed by an autonomous system as a result of the planner's decision. These scenarios are meant to serve as reference points for evaluating this definition, rather than providing an exhaustive list of all possible harm-causing situations. Our objective is to conduct further research into the varieties of negative outcomes and their relationship with justice, with a view to exploring more complex notions of justice in the future. In the context of autonomous systems, we have identified situations where an individual was harmed by a fellow user, as well as scenarios where both individuals were adversely affected. Our definition of harm highlights the importance of these systems for autonomous systems, as it necessitates a plausible explanation of the adverse event, rather than merely mitigating it. This definition of harm differs from existing concepts in computer science, such as harm and fault, as it incorporates elements of causality and intends to apply solely to autonomous systems. Our work aims to facilitate a proactive approach, as opposed to a reactive one, to handle harm-related issues. By integrating this definition into the design of autonomous systems, we can identify and rectify potential sources of harm at an early stage. This definition of harm is broader than other conceptual frameworks and is intended to apply beyond automated systems to areas such as compensable interferences with autonomy. Precise short-term forecasts of future energy consumption are essential for managing low voltage electricity networks efficiently, particularly with regard to highly disaggregated load distributions among a small number of customers, where individual behaviors tend to dominate aggregate consumption profiles. Since peak demand often drives energy distribution challenges, developing accurate timing and level predictions of daily peak demand is crucial, as traditional forecasting methods frequently struggle to characterize these spikes adequately. This issue highlights the need for the development of novel methods capable of identifying energy consumption spikes, which in this study is accomplished through a simple parameterized clustering approach based on peaks and then refined through a forward model to minimize the residual errors between observed and simulated consumption, ultimately enhancing the precision of short-term peak demand forecasts compared to conventional methods. This enhanced forecasting approach was applied to the energy consumption data of 170 residential customers, resulting in peak demand forecasts that were 15% more precise than those created using the existing method. Moreover, by analyzing the behavior of customers whose data contributed significantly to peak demand, it was observed that these customers tended to have lower energy consumption on peak days compared to non-peak days, which was reflected in the model's parameter estimation using generalized linear mixed models. Interestingly, these findings varied when considering customers who did not appear in the peak demand dataset, as these customers demonstrated higher energy consumption on peak days compared to non-peak days. This difference in behavior is consistent with theories surrounding single-bullet patterns in electricity consumption. The proposed forecasting approach, which effectively identifies and models peak demand, can be adapted to predict energy spikes in other contexts, such as clinical trends in patient data, by employing similar understanding and integration mechanisms. The challenge stems from the large number of classes in this multi-class problem and the lack of detailed annotations, leading to inaccurate results from methods that utilize edge masking during the segmentation process. To resolve these issues, we introduce a unique, multi-task learning approach, named Pathpedia, that simultaneously performs tasks such as semantic segmentation, path classification, and boundary prediction on chest CT images. The Pathpedia method incorporates a pathway mask that facilitates the identification of intrapulmonary lesions, thereby enabling more accurate distinctions to be made between COVID-19 and other abnormalities. The Pathpedia method achieves better performance compared to existing techniques on the DSB2022 dataset, with a high level of accuracy in path classification and boundary prediction. The Pathpedia method also addresses potential biases in data sources and demonstrates better adversarial robustness. We propose a novel neural network-based approach to regulating hybrid systems that model actuator dynamics as switched components. In a novel pattern generation strategy, central pattern generator neurons regulate the switching between different actuator states and modulate their transition times with gaitspecific parameters. The coevolution of neural and switch dynamics is explored using energy-based techniques in a simulated environment. We demonstrate this method with a spring-driven quadruped robot called HyQ-3p, showcasing the ability to produce robust and self-vibrating gaits across various settings for sit-stand and galloping gait phases. Notably, the controller requires no energy to maintain the standing phase and successfully transitions from a forced gait in movement to a natural gait pattern. Experimental outcomes confirm the effectiveness of the regulator in achieving desired gaits. The integration of actuator and switch dynamics in the controller further enables seamless transitions between gait phases, as seen in actual execution. This method has the potential to expand to additional robots and is compatible with various rigid and semi-rigid actuators. A surge in demand for search by image has led researchers to investigate fashion instance-level image retrieval, which involves finding matching images. Building upon this, the concept of fashion attribute manipulation, which modifies a specific attribute while retaining others, has emerged. This enables users to search not only identical items but also similar items with specific attributes. However, this task is challenging due to the difficulty in defining attributes and preserving query uniqueness. Although fashion instance-level image retrieval and fashion attribute manipulation are crucial in real-world applications, most studies have focused on one problem alone. In this research, we aim to achieve state-of-the-art results on both tasks. To accomplish this, we propose a novel method that translates a query into a representation that incorporates the desired attributes. This method employs a BERT-based contrastive learning framework to retrieve identical items and another framework combining class centroid and soft center to retrieve items with specific attributes. To validate our approach, we extend a widely used dataset, leading to an open-source dataset with 382,067 images containing four distinct attributes. Our approach achieves a retrieval rank one benchmark score of 66.2, marking the first time this score has been surpassed. Additionally, we achieve a benchmark score of 57.9 for manipulating attributes while retaining query uniqueness in a challenging setting. This research demonstrates the effectiveness of incorporating fashion attribute manipulation into instance-level image retrieval tasks. To apply this technology, the user selects an image of a product and specifies desired attributes using a list of options. Based on this input, the application retrieves identical and attribute-manipulated items, allowing users to navigate and interact with the search results to find the desired fashion product. To achieve this application's success, the underlying retrieval method must be enhanced to handle the complex task of fashion attribute manipulation. To contribute to this goal, we propose a method that addresses existing challenges in this area, ultimately aiming to improve the accuracy of fashion attribute manipulation. A dual-based method with two stages is proposed: first, inverting the equation while keeping the function parameters fixed, and then updating to minimize the regularized objective. This method is examined under the conditions of Hillbert space, and the convergence to the $\R$-optimal solution is proven through iterative applications of a proximal alternating linearized minimization algorithm. An efficient fast iterative shrinkage-threshold algorithm variant is developed to accelerate computations. This method is validated through simulation experiments of image de-noising in a Hilbert space context. When applied to vector Lasso, our technique is proven to converge at the same rate as the dual solution to the $\R$-optimal value, and to be within a bounded difference of the dual and primal $\R$-optimal values. Further evaluation of the proposed algorithm showed it to be equal in performance to the primal Tikhonov approach. These results show the proposed algorithm to be computationally efficient, and capable of accelerating Tikhonov regularization imaging applications. To future-proof home WiFi networks for the widespread adoption of immersive technologies like VR and high-quality altra-real video streaming, it is essential to enhance their capacity, speed, and quality of service. One potential solution for achieving this involves the use of Extensible WiFi Scheduling, a novel concept that enables traffic management in next-generation home networks. By extending available WiFi scheduling standards with enabling technologies such as network slicing, Extensible WiFi Scheduling provides more efficient and capable home WiFi networks. By prioritizing real-time data and extending the scope of WiFi scheduling to unrelated tasks, developers can enhance the performance of their networks. A test bed implementation was developed using a WiFi 6 access point and enabled with the aid of USM, a set of tools that includes a traffic generator, a network scanner, and a QoS monitor. By implementing EFJS, researchers were able to achieve substantial improvements in their home WiFi network's capacity. Specifically, the amount of simultaneous traffic the network could handle increased significantly when EFJS was applied, in one test doubling the capacity of the network. Furthermore, the accuracy of EFJS in prioritizing traffic and scheduling events was verified and found to follow an inverse relationship with the level of network congestion. When EFJS was applied, the average packet delay rate declined by half while the packet service rate increased by a similar margin. These gains in performance for next-generation home WiFi networks enabled by EFJS are expected to be even more substantial when even more advanced and bandwidth-hungry technologies are supported. Such an extension of WiFi to support 6G technologies such as vR-based telepresence, enhanced real-time data streaming, and machine learning/AI applications with mixed data types is anticipated to yield substantial improvements in terms of energy efficiency, bandwidth utilization, and overall end-user experience. As a result of EFJS's capabilities and potential, researchers believe that WiFi is an attractive candidate for the management and scheduling of network traffic in home networks. Furthermore, the incorporation of intelligent and self-organizing WiFi scheduling mechanisms such as EFJS is envisioned to pave the way for the development of a more autonomous, reliable, and efficient Internet of Home network. A roadmap detailing the requirements and necessary steps to implement and enable self-organizing home networks based on WiFi is also outlined. According to this roadmap, the key challenges and obstacles that need to be overcome include the enhancement of end-user experience through scheduling advancements, improved network resource management with features such as slicing, and increased energy efficiency through the selection of optimal subcarriers and bandwidth.
